The closing clause states the ground of the difference. Knowledge belongs to God in the matter under dispute, and the disputants do not possess it; the verse had already told its readers as much when it described the unseen news being recited to the Prophet.

The formula recurs in the Book where a dispute has reached the point at which the parties are asserting what they cannot establish. Its function is to close the argument by naming the only available authority, and it leaves the hearer with a choice that the sūrah has been building toward: to accept the account revealed by the one who knows, or to continue maintaining a position for which no evidence exists. The verse does not position itself as one opinion among the disputants. It states the fact that makes the dispute decidable.

**Why Abraham Was the Right Subject for This Charge**

The choice of Abraham as the matter of the argument is what makes the rebuke stick. He is the shared ancestor whose story both communities prized, and about whose religion they had no detailed record other than the traditions that had grown around his name.

The Book's own narrative about him is presented as revelation, which is precisely the point: knowledge of Abraham must come from God, because the period is closed and no witness remains. A community that had received a book must have known this about a figure who preceded its book by centuries. The verse's charge is therefore about method as much as about content. What the disputants were doing with Abraham was what the Book regards as the characteristic error of a community that has stopped treating revelation as its source of knowledge and begun treating its own position as the measure.

**The Standing of Argument in This Sūrah**

The sūrah is not opposed to reasoning; it has been reasoning throughout, and this verse is itself an argument. What is being corrected is argument conducted without a basis, and the distinction matters for how the reader understands the Book's repeated appeals to intellect.

The Book asks its hearers to reflect, consider, and understand, and its arguments move from premises its hearers accept to conclusions they can verify. Where the evidence is available, the Book presses for the inference; where it is not, the Book supplies revelation and expects it to be accepted as such. The verse above illustrates the second case. A dispute about a man who lived before the scriptures is a dispute that cannot be resolved by the parties to it, and the Book's answer is that the account has come from the only source that was present.

**A Question of What Can Be Known**

The sentence leaves the reader with a plain intellectual distinction: the disputants had knowledge of one thing and no knowledge of another, and they argued about both in the same tone.

That habit is not confined to the communities the verse addresses, and the sūrah's placement of the observation in the middle of its argument with them makes it available to any reader.

The Book's own answer to the difficulty is on the page in front of the sentence. A dispute about a figure who lived before the surviving records is settled in this sūrah not by weighing the traditions about him but by revelation from the one who knows, and the same principle governs everything the Book reports about the earlier prophets. The next verse gives the positive account of Abraham, and it does so in the form of a series of negations followed by a description, which is how the Book usually corrects a claim it cannot accept.

---
## Sūrah Āli ʿImrān 3:67

> Abraham was neither a Jew nor a Christian; he submitted in all uprightness and was not a polytheist.

**Expanded Commentary**

**Two Negations Before an Affirmation**

The verse answers the question of what Abraham was, and it begins by excluding the two categories that the disputants wanted him to occupy. He was neither a Jew nor a Christian, and he was not a polytheist. Only after clearing both names does the sentence say what he was.

The order is deliberate, and it is the order of a legal finding that first removes the parties' claims and then states the position. The Book uses this technique where an argument has become a competition over labels: it denies the labels and supplies the description, which is why the verse's middle term carries the whole weight of the sentence. What is affirmed after the exclusions is not a faction but a disposition.

**Ḥanīf: Turning Away and Turning Toward**

The word rendered "in all uprightness" describes a person who inclines away from the worship of anything other than God. In the Book's usage the term is tied to Abraham specifically, and it carries the idea of a deliberate turn — away from the practices of a people who had gone astray, and toward the one to whom worship belongs.

The Book pairs the term with Abraham in several places. The sūrah of the Cattle records the Prophet's own declaration of following the way of Abraham, the upright, who was not of the polytheists (6:161); the sūrah of the Bees describes Abraham as a model of excellence, devoted to God and upright, and again denies that he was a polytheist (16:120); and the sūrah of the Cow instructs the believers to say that their way is that of Abraham, the upright (2:135). The recurrence shows that the term functions in the Book as the name of a religion that existed before the books, which is why it can serve as the shared ground in this dispute.

**The Third Negation**

The clause denying that Abraham was a polytheist is not a repetition of the first two denials, and it deserves its own attention. A person could be neither Jewish nor Christian and still be a worshipper of other gods, since those were not the only options available in the ancient world.

The Book adds the clause because the argument it is conducting concerns the oneness of God, and the sūrah has been occupied with exactly that subject for many verses. Abraham's refusal of idols is the pattern to which the sūrah keeps returning, and the verse identifies his religion with that refusal before it says anything else. The positive content of his faith is stated as a combination of turning away from false objects and facing the one God, and the Book is careful to name both halves of the movement.

**What the Verse Removes From the Dispute**

The exclusions answer the claims of both communities at once, and they do so without insult. Neither community is told that its tradition is false; the verse simply declines to trace Abraham's religion to either.

That restraint is important for what the sūrah is doing. It has just criticised the two communities for arguing about the ancestor without knowledge, and it now supplies a description that neither can claim as its own property. The effect is to remove Abraham from the argument about communal standing and to place him where the Book consistently puts the prophets: in a category defined by conduct toward God rather than by membership in a later community. What the following verse does is to say who does have a claim on him, and the answer is stated in terms of following rather than descent.

**The Prophet's Own Position in the Sentence**

The sūrah's readers would hear this verse as a description rather more than a history, since the same three clauses describe the position of the Muslim community in relation to the older traditions. It is neither Jewish nor Christian, it refuses the association of anything with God, and its founding model is the man who did the same before any of the books existed.

That is why the verse can carry the argument forward with a single sentence. Abraham is being presented not as the property of a lineage but as the first instance of a stance that the sūrah wants its readers to recognise as their own, and the identification is made twice within the sentence: once by the word standing in the middle and once by the denial at the end.

**The Shape of the Argument**

The argument of the sūrah with the scriptured communities has been building to this point. It has shown that Jesus was created as Adam was, that the communities dispute about Abraham without information, and now that Abraham belonged to neither of them.

Each step removes a claim and leaves the reader with a smaller field of disagreement. What remains after this verse is the question of who can claim to be his descendant in spirit, and the Book answers it in the next lines with a definition based on following rather than ancestry. The description of Abraham as upright and free of partnership is thus not only a correction of the past. It is the criterion the sūrah applies to everyone who reads the verse.

The three clauses also read as a portrait of a man who stood alone. Uprightness in this vocabulary is a direction taken by an individual rather than a position inherited from a group, and the denial of polytheism is a statement about a person surrounded by it. Abraham's story in the Book is exactly that: a single figure arguing with his people, breaking the images, and being thrown into a fire for it. The verse's grammar is the grammar of that life.

---
## Sūrah Āli ʿImrān 3:68

> Indeed, those who have the best claim to Abraham are his followers, this Prophet, and the believers. And Allah is the Guardian of those who believe.

**Expanded Commentary**

**Who Has a Claim on Abraham**

Having said what Abraham was not, the verse says who belongs to him. Three parties are named: those who followed him, this Prophet, and the believers. The order runs from Abraham's own contemporaries to the messenger of the sūrah and then to the community that has accepted him.

The structure of the claim is the point. Belonging is defined by following, and the verse's first category consists of the people who followed Abraham while he was alive and afterward. Everything that follows is measured by the same standard, which is why the two later parties can be named in the same sentence as the first. What is being described is a continuous body of people united by a way rather than by blood.

**Follower Before Ancestor**

The disputes the sūrah has been answering turned on ancestry, and this verse replaces ancestry with adherence. The Arabic term used for the followers describes those who came after a person on a road, taking his direction, and the Book uses it for the relation of a community to a prophet throughout.

The replacement has consequences that the sūrah's readers would feel. A claim resting on descent can be inspected in a genealogy; a claim resting on following can be inspected in conduct. The Book consistently prefers the second test, and it does so without denying that the first exists, since the descent of the Prophet of this sūrah from Abraham through Ishmael is part of the tradition. What the verse refuses is the notion that the genealogy settles the matter. A descendant who does not follow the ancestor's religion is not being described here as the ancestor's, and the Book makes that point elsewhere in explicit terms when it denies that a covenant extends to wrongdoers (2:124).

**"This Prophet" — the Manifest Reference**

The second party named is the Prophet of the sūrah, and the phrase used is the standard designation for Muhammad in the Qur'an's argument with the scriptured communities. It marks the presence of a living claimant to Abraham's way in the middle of the dispute.

The wording also carries a claim the sūrah has already made in the passage about Abraham. If following is the criterion, then the messenger who has brought the clearest statement of the oneness of God and the rejection of all partners stands closest to the man who did the same in Ur. That is the argument's logic, and the sūrah states it directly here rather than leaving it to be inferred. The claim is not that Abraham was a Muslim of the later community, which the previous verse explicitly denies; it is that the religion of Abraham and the message of this Prophet are one, and that the people who follow that religion are his people.

**The Believers Included**

The third party is the believing community, and its inclusion extends the claim beyond the messenger. Nobody in the community has Abraham's lineage, and none of them lived in his era, yet the verse names them among those who have the best claim to him.

The extension is what makes the verse a statement about the religion rather than about a personal succession. A community assembled from different tribes and backgrounds is told that its relation to the founding monotheist is established by what it holds, and the same doctrine appears in the Book's account of Abraham's prayer for a nation to be raised from his descendants who would submit to God, which the Book presents as answered in the community of the Prophet. The sūrah's claim is that the answer is recognisable in the present community's confession rather than in its ancestry.

**God as Protector of the Believers**

The verse ends with a statement about God's relation to the believers: He is their guardian. The word used is the same one the sūrah employed in the passage about taking disbelievers as guardians, and the placement of the two passages within one sūrah is not accidental.

What the closing clause does is to state the source of the community's protection once it has renounced the protection of other parties. The sūrah warned the believers against seeking security from those who did not share their faith; it now tells them whose protection they hold in exchange, and it states it as a fact about God's relation to them rather than as a promise of what will happen. The community's confidence does not rest on its size or its allies, and the verse supplies the alternative in five words.

**A Definition That Reads Both Ways**

The verse's three parties are not merely names of groups who belong to Abraham; they are described as people who would recognise themselves in the description. Reading it, a believer is told that his standing rests on the same thing as Abraham's, and the sūrah leaves him to check whether that is where his confidence sits.

That makes the verse a criterion as much as a statement of fact, and it applies to the dispute the sūrah has been conducting as well as to its own audience.

It also explains the order in which the three parties are listed. The followers come first because they set the standard, the messenger comes second because he is the living instance of the same way, and the believers come last because they are the community being formed by it. A reader who works through the list finds his own name in the third position and his own standing in the first, since the question the verse leaves with him is whether he belongs among the people who followed. What follows in the sūrah is a description of the people who had the opportunity and did something else.

---
## Sūrah Āli ʿImrān 3:69

> Some of the People of the Book wish to mislead you ˹believers˺. They mislead none but themselves, yet they fail to perceive it.

**Expanded Commentary**

**A Wish Directed at the Believers**

The verse reports an intention rather than an act. Some among the People of the Book want to lead the believers astray — the verb describes a wish to pull a person off a road — and the sūrah states the desire without describing any particular attempt.

The wording keeps the matter at the level of motive while making the motive known. A community told that the pursuit of its members is hoped for by others has been warned about something that no incident will necessarily reveal, and the Book supplies the information so that the believers do not have to infer it from events. The sūrah's audience was a small community in a city where it negotiated with older groups, and the verse tells its members what is being thought about them behind the arguments.

**"They Mislead None but Themselves"**

The second half of the sentence reverses the direction of the harm. The wish to mislead is real, and the Book says its outcome falls on those who hold it.

The Book states this reversal repeatedly, and with a variety of images. The hypocrites are described as hoping to deceive God and the believers while deceiving only themselves (2:9); the community in the desert is told that those who broke faith wronged nobody but themselves (2:57); and elsewhere the Book says that a person's plotting encircles its author. The claim is not that the intended victims escape harm in every case, since the verse exists precisely to warn them. It is that the deeper damage of an act of corruption settles on the one who commits it, and the sūrah places that fact before it names the parties.

**The Envy Behind the Wish**

The sūrah's other account of the same situation names the motive: a group of the People of the Book wish to turn the believers back into disbelievers out of envy in their own souls, after the truth has become clear to them (2:109). The verse under discussion does not repeat the diagnosis, but the passages belong together, and the commentators read them as one report.

The identification of envy as the engine is what makes the wish intelligible. The groups concerned had argued against the message on doctrinal grounds; the Book's account says the argument was not the reason for their resistance. The mention of envy also sets a limit on any discussion held with them, since a disputant whose real concern is the standing of his community cannot be persuaded by evidence about the standing of a prophet. What the sūrah asks of its readers is that they understand the nature of the opposition they face.

**"They Fail to Perceive It"**

The verse closes by noting that these people do not notice what is happening to themselves. The Arabic describes an absence of awareness rather than of intelligence, and the Book uses it for the condition of people who cannot see the consequences of their own conduct.

That is the sūrah's answer to the appearance of competence. The groups being described were learned, established, and in possession of scriptures; they understood the arguments they were making. What they lacked was the perception to see that the damage they were arranging for others was being inflicted on their own position, and the Book's diagnosis is that the instrument they trusted — their standing and their learning — was exactly what their conduct was eroding. The warning in the verse is therefore for them as much as for the believers, and the sūrah continues to address them in the passages that follow.

**What the Verse Asks of the Believers**

The verse does not instruct the believers to withdraw from the members of the other communities, and it does not authorise any hostility. It tells them what is wished for them and what the wishing costs the person who does it.

What a reader is meant to take from that is a specific kind of caution. The sūrah has just told its audience that Abraham belongs to those who follow his way rather than to a lineage, and it now tells them that there are people who would like to detach them from what they hold. The two facts together produce the disposition the rest of the passage will appeal to: hold the religion firmly, argue fairly where argument is offered, and understand that the pressure on the community is an intention rather than an accident. The following verses address the parties responsible, and they ask them why they behave as they do.

**A Charge Addressed in Public**

The final note of this verse is that the Book addresses the group directly in the verses that follow. Having told the believers who wishes them ill, the sūrah turns to the other party and asks them three questions in succession, and the questions are not rhetorical in the sense of being unanswerable.

That combination of disclosure and address is characteristic of the Book's handling of opponents. The community is told what it faces, and the opposing party is told that its conduct is visible and that reasons are being requested. Nothing is kept back from either side, and no accusation is made that the accused is not invited to answer.

A reader can also measure the distance between the wish reported here and its outcome. The plan attributed to the group was to detach the believers from their religion, and the sūrah's own account of the community's later history records the opposite movement: the message travelled beyond the city, and the communities that had argued with it produced scholars who carried parts of its learning into their own traditions. The Book's remark that the planners mislead none but themselves is not a prediction of an easy outcome for the believers; it is a statement that a plan aimed at someone else's faith has its first effect on the faith of the person making it.

---
## Sūrah Āli ʿImrān 3:70

> O People of the Book! Why do you reject the signs of Allah while you bear witness ˹to their truth˺?

**Expanded Commentary**

**A Question That Puts the Accused on the Spot**

The sūrah now addresses the People of the Book directly, and it begins with a question about conduct rather than belief: why do you reject the signs of God while you bear witness? The form of the question assumes that the addressees have an answer to defend and asks them to produce it.

The Book uses this interrogative form repeatedly in its engagement with the scriptured communities, and the effect is to shift the discussion from a contest of doctrines to a matter of the parties' own consistency. The question does not ask what the other party believes; it asks why, holding what they hold, they do what they do. That is a harder question to deflect, because the premise on which it rests is supplied by the addressee rather than by the speaker.

**"While You Bear Witness" — the Heart of the Charge**

The clause about bearing witness is what makes the question incriminating. The commentators gave two readings, and both are damaging to the position being criticised. On one reading, the addressees themselves bear witness — that is, they have known the truth of the message and are acting against their knowledge. On the other, they are witnesses to the earlier prophets in their own tradition, and the message in front of them manifests the same truths those prophets brought.

Either way the charge is the same in structure: rejection here is not an absence of information but a decision made in the presence of it. The Book makes the identical point about the community that disputed the account of Jesus, describing a disagreement that continued after knowledge had come to them, and about the people whose hearts have swerved, who follow what is ambiguous while the clear verses stand in front of them. The charge in this verse belongs to that family, and its severity comes from the fact that the witnesses are the defendants.

**The Signs in View**

The word for signs covers both the verses of revelation and the events that accompany a prophet's mission, and the sūrah has just narrated a series of them: a birth without a father, a child who speaks, healings, a raising of the dead, and the removal of the messenger from the hands of those who plotted against him.

The question therefore points at a body of material, not a single proposition. A community that had argued about Jesus was being asked why it rejected the signs whose account it had heard, and the word choice keeps the argument on the evidence. The Book's habit of calling revelation itself a sign means that the recitation the community has listened to is part of the case against it, and the verse's question covers that recitation as well as the wonders it describes. What is being rejected, in other words, is not a foreign claim but what the hearers have been given.

**A Question to a Community That Argued About Abraham**

The verse's position in the sūrah matters. It follows the passage in which the Book denied that Abraham was a Jew or a Christian, described him as upright and free of partnership, and named his followers as the parties with the best claim on him.

The question about rejecting signs arrives immediately after an argument that turned on the other party's own history. A community that prized Abraham and accepted that he preceded both books is asked why its descendants are rejecting what has come, and the implication is left for the hearer: the conduct being questioned is a departure from the pattern of the ancestor whose name they invoke. The sūrah does not spell out the comparison, and the question is framed so that the addressee supplies it himself. That is the strength of the interrogative mode in this kind of passage; the accusation is carried by the listener's own premises rather than by the speaker's assertion.

**The Community Being Defended**

The versse also has a function for the Muslim community reading it, since it explains the nature of the resistance they were meeting without instructing them to retaliate. The sūrah has just told them that people wish to mislead them; it now shows them the shape of the opposition, which is a refusal made by people who have grounds to know better.

What the believers are given is therefore a way of understanding their situation that does not require them to treat their neighbours as ignorant. The charge is not that the other communities lack information. It is that they have it and are acting against it, and the Book's decision to address them directly means the disclosure is not a piece of gossip about a rival but a statement made openly to the party concerned. The following verses ask two further questions of the same people.

**A Pattern Repeated Across the Sūrah**

The sūrah contains, near its end, another question of the same kind: why do you turn those who believe away from the way of God while you are witnesses? The two verses form a pair separated by some thirty verses, and their agreement is a sign of how the Book's argument with the scriptured communities was conducted throughout the chapter.

The recurring formula is a question about consistency, addressed to people whose own tradition supplies the standard. The Book does not accuse them of following a different religion; it accuses them of failing to follow their own with integrity. That is a more serious charge and a more useful one, and it leaves the door open in the way the sūrah's later verses continue to do.

**The Warnings This One Echoes**

The same charge is made twice more in the sūrah. A few verses later the People of the Book are asked why they turn those who believe away from the way of God, seeking to make it crooked, while they are witnesses (3:99); the wording of that passage and of this one are close enough that the two sentences are read together by the commentators. The second part of the same warning, about concealing and confounding the truth, repeats the charge made in the sūrah of the Cow, where the recipients of the scripture are told not to mix truth with falsehood or to conceal the truth while they know it (2:42). The repetition of the same accusation at three points in the argument indicates how the sūrah treats the conduct it describes: not as an isolated error but as a settled policy.

**What Being a Witness Means**

Al-Ṭabarī read the verses as referring to the refusal of the Prophet's mission by Jews and Christians although, on the Muslim understanding, his coming is announced in their own books (7:157). The witness in the sentence therefore describes people who are in a position to recognize what they reject. Al-Qurṭūbī recorded another reading on which the witnessing refers to their own tradition: they bear witness to the truth brought by the prophets who preceded them, whose message agrees with what the Prophet is teaching, so that their rejection of him contradicts the testimony they already carry. On either reading, the question in the verse is not a request for information but a statement that the people addressed possess grounds for accepting what they deny.

---
## Sūrah Āli ʿImrān 3:71

> O People of the Book! Why do you mix the truth with falsehood and hide the truth knowingly?

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Second Question**

The verse keeps the same addressee and the same interrogative form, and it sharpens the charge. The first question concerned rejection; this one concerns the handling of truth and falsehood, and it names two acts: mixing the two, and concealing the truth while knowing it.

The pair is significant because the second act is hidden and the first is public. A person can hide a text, a reading, or a fact; he can also construct a presentation in which the true and the false are blended so that the distinction no longer shows. The Book's charge covers both operations, and its framing as a question means the addressees are being asked to explain a method rather than to deny a conclusion.

**The Image Behind "Mixing"**

The verb rendered "mix" describes the blending of one thing into another until they cannot be separated, and the Arabic term is the ordinary word for confusion and for murky water. What the verse describes is not the honest mistake of a reader who cannot tell two meanings apart; it is the deliberate production of a compound in which true material carries false conclusions.

The Book states the same charge in the sūrah of the Cow in almost identical words, warning the community not to clothe truth with falsehood nor to conceal the truth while knowing it (2:42). The two verses are usually read together, and the commentators treated them as describing one practice rather than two. The practice is the characteristic one of a community that wants to hold its position while retaining the authority of the revelation it holds. The truth is not denied; it is used as a vessel.

**Concealment and the Charge of Distortion**

The second act named is concealment, and the Book's treatment of it elsewhere is explicit about what is being hidden. In this sūrah's later verses, a group is described as distorting the book with their tongues so that what they say appears to be from it, and the verse ends by saying that they knowingly attribute lies to God (3:78).

The classical commentators developed the distinction between altering a text and altering its interpretation, and they disagreed about which the Book accuses the earlier communities of. The verse above does not need that dispute resolved. It accuses the addressees of hiding something they know, which presupposes that they still have access to it; a community that had genuinely lost the material could not be charged with concealing it. What the verse assumes, then, is the presence of the truth among these people and the decision not to present it.

**The Word "Knowingly" and Its Weight**

The sentence ends with the phrase that recurs in the Book's most serious accusations: they act knowingly. The word appears in the warning against mixing truth with falsehood in the sūrah of the Cow, in the account of people who attribute lies to God knowingly, and here.

The addition of the adverb changes the category of the offence from error to something else. The Book is consistently careful about the difference between a person acting in ignorance and a person acting against his own knowledge, and its severest language is reserved for the second. That is why the verse's question is put to the community rather than to individuals who might have been misinformed: the charge is corporate, and it concerns a policy rather than a mistake.

**What the Charge Implies About the Scriptures**

A reader might expect a passage such as this to deny that the other community possesses anything genuine, and the verse does not do that. It accuses the community of concealing and mixing what it has, which is an accusation that makes sense only if what it has includes the truth.

This is the sūrah's position on the earlier scriptures throughout. It treats them as genuine revelations, describes the Qur'an as confirming them, and places the failure of the communities in the handling rather than in the holding. The distinction matters for how the passage reads: the argument is not that the Torah and the Gospel are worthless but that their custodians have dealt with them in a way that obscures what they contain. That is a charge about conduct, and conduct can be changed.

**The Question as an Invitation**

The verse asks a question, and a question addressed to someone who is concealing something functions as a notice that the concealment is visible. The sūrah does not produce the evidence in this sentence; it states the charge in the form of an enquiry and leaves the question standing.

That form is the Book's usual way of addressing a party that still has a chance to respond. The verses that follow describe a stratagem the same community devised, so the sūrah is not naive about the likelihood of a change of heart; it continues to address them anyway. What a reader is being shown is a method of argument that states the accusation publicly, refuses to hide behind implication, and leaves the door open even after the conduct has been described.

**A Charge That Applies to Any Custodian of a Text**

Read without the immediate controversy, the verse states a rule for anyone who holds a revelation. The two acts it forbids — blending the true with the false, and withholding what one knows — are the ordinary operations by which a religious community defends a position it can no longer support from its own sources.

The sūrah's own community is not exempt from the warning, and the Book's habit of recording such charges against another party is not a licence for the reader. It is the earlier community's story told in advance, and the Muslim community is shown both what was done and what it looked like from outside.

---
## Sūrah Āli ʿImrān 3:72

> A group among the People of the Book said ˹to one another˺, “Believe in what has been revealed to the believers in the morning and reject it in the evening, so they may abandon their faith.

**Expanded Commentary**

**A Stratagem Reported in Full**

The verse reports what a group among the People of the Book said to one another, and it reports it as a plan rather than as an accusation. The members of the group are not named; the sūrah records the scheme in their own words, which is why the reader meets it as a conspiracy rather than as a charge laid by an adversary.

The Book's decision to disclose the plan has a purpose beyond warning the believers. A community that has been told what is being said about it in private can no longer be surprised by the manoeuvre, and the sūrah has been preparing its readers for exactly this information in the verses that precede it. The disclosure is part of the defence.

**The Manoeuvre: In by Morning, Out by Evening**

The plan is described with precision: the group proposes that its members appear to accept the revelation in the morning and publicly retract it in the evening. The point is not the acceptance, which is false, and not the retraction, which is intended. The point is the sequence, and the sequence is the weapon.

The reasoning behind it is easy to reconstruct and the commentators supplied it. When people who are respected observe a position being adopted and then abandoned by those who adopted it, they draw conclusions about the position rather than about the people. A message that its own apparent converts have left within a day looks unstable, and doubt about a message is easier to plant that way than by direct argument. The plan's target is not the Prophet's claim but the confidence of the ordinary believer who watched the performance.

**What the Plan Assumes About the Believers**

The stratagem is a piece of applied psychology, and its assumptions are worth spelling out, because the sūrah's answer to it addresses those assumptions.

The planners assumed that the Muslims' conviction depended on appearances — on who was seen to be joining and staying — rather than on the content of what they had accepted. They also assumed that a community of new believers, many of whom had left their families and their standing to join, could be destabilised by the sight of important people coming and going. Both assumptions would be reasonable in a community that had never been told what its own foundation was, and the sūrah's response in the surrounding verses is to keep telling them. The plan's weakness is that a person whose faith rests on an argument he has understood cannot be moved by a performance, and the Book's remedy for the manoeuvre is the account of that argument.

**The Verse's Reporting Style**

The sūrah introduces the quotation without commentary and lets it stand. The Book uses this technique elsewhere with the statements of opponents, and the effect is to let the reader judge the plan by hearing it.

There is a certain kind of dignity in the Book's restraint. The scheme is presented as it was formulated, in the plotters' own voice, and no adjectives are added. A reader who encountered the plan second-hand through polemic might suspect that it had been exaggerated; the Book's method removes that suspicion and leaves the reader with the words themselves. What the verse does not do is gloat, and it does not follow the quotation with a denunciation. The answer to the trick is delivered elsewhere, generally and without reference to the incident.

**How the Book Answers a Stratagem**

The sūrah does not tell the Prophet to expose the group publicly, and it does not instruct the believers to treat the retractions as a test of their loyalty to the people involved. What the Book does, in the passage as a whole, is to continue stating the case for the message with the same arguments it used before.

That is the Book's characteristic way of dealing with this kind of attack. A claim about the truth of the revelation is answered by the truth of the revelation, and the community is equipped by being given reasons it can hold onto rather than suspicions it must guard. The next verse records a second element of the same plan and the command given to the Prophet in response to it, and the response is neither a counter-conspiracy nor a public rebuke but a statement about where guidance comes from.

**The Vulnerability the Plan Exposes**

Read from the outside, the manoeuvre identifies something true about religious communities: their confidence can be eroded by the visible conduct of prominent people, and this happens whether or not the conduct is sincere.

The sūrah's answer to that vulnerability is not to deny it but to locate the community's certainty elsewhere, which is what the verses around this one have been doing from the beginning. The believers are being told about a group that intends to undermine them, and the same passage tells them that guidance is God's, that bounty is in His hands, and that He chooses whom He wills. What is being defended is not a reputation to be managed but a position the community holds by evidence and by gift, and neither of those is available to the tactics in this verse.

**A Record Kept for the Community's Use**

The verse preserves for later readers a picture of the environment in which the earliest Muslim community formed, and it shows that the opposition was not confined to argument. Some of it was designed to work on the perceptions of onlookers.

A reader in a later century can take the verse as a model of what to expect rather than as a story about others. Any community whose members are admired by their neighbours will face the same kind of pressure, and the condition for withstanding it is the one the sūrah keeps supplying: knowledge of what one has accepted and of the ground on which it was accepted.

---
## Sūrah Āli ʿImrān 3:73

> And only believe those who follow your religion.” Say, ˹O Prophet,˺ “Surely, ˹the only˺ true guidance is Allah’s guidance.” ˹They also said,˺ “Do not believe that someone will receive ˹revealed˺ knowledge similar to yours or argue against you before your Lord.” Say, ˹O Prophet,˺ “Indeed, all bounty is in the Hands of Allah— He grants it to whoever He wills. And Allah is All-Bountiful, AllKnowing.”

**Expanded Commentary**

**A Second Clause of the Same Plan**

The verse continues the report of what the group said among themselves, and the second part of their plan concerns who deserves to be believed at all. Their proposal is that only members of their own religion should be accepted as credible — a rule that closes the circle of trust around the community that made it.

The measure is presented as a matter of policy rather than conviction, and the sūrah's arrangement of the two elements is instructive. The first part of the plan was tactical: perform acceptance and then withdraw. The second is structural: hold that anyone outside our religion cannot be telling the truth about religion. The two together amount to a system in which the message can never be accepted on its merits and never accepted on testimony, because the only credible witnesses are those who have already refused it.

**The Interjection From God**

The sūrah breaks into the quotation with an instruction to the Prophet: say, guidance is God's guidance. The interruption splits the reported speech and answers it in the middle, and the commentators noticed the grammatical awkwardness and discussed several ways of reading the sentence.

However the syntax is resolved, the content is decisive. The claim that truth is confined to one community is met by the statement that guidance belongs to God, which places the matter outside the jurisdiction of any group. The sūrah has used the same principle earlier in a passage that described the well-grounded in knowledge accepting the whole of what was revealed, and it will return to it again when it states that bounty is in God's hands. What the remark does is to remove the question of credibility from the arena of communal authority and return it to the one who guides.

**The Fear Behind the Second Clause**

The group's second remark is reported in the same breath: do not believe that someone will receive revealed knowledge similar to yours, or that he will be able to argue against you before your Lord.

The reasoning is transparent, and it is not really a doctrine about revelation. It is a fear about standing: if someone outside the community can be given a book, then the community's possession of a book no longer guarantees its position in the argument. The sūrah reports the fear because it explains the resistance better than any doctrinal objection could, and the answer given to it is about God's freedom to give rather than about the merits of the recipients.

**"All Bounty Is in the Hands of Allah"**

The Prophet is told to say that bounty belongs to God, that He grants it to whoever He wills, and that He is All-Bountiful and All-Knowing. The sentence answers the objection at its root by placing the distribution of revelation in the same category as the distribution of everything else.

The Book uses the same argument elsewhere for the granting of prophethood itself, and the sūrah's opening verses made the same claim in their account of God giving authority and honour to whom He pleases. What is being asserted here is that no community holds a veto over God's generosity, and that the community which received a revelation earlier cannot determine who receives one later. The terms of the sentence also explain why the objection is misplaced: if the giver is all-knowing, then the choice of recipient is a matter of his knowledge rather than of the community's qualifications.

**The Names at the End of the Sentence**

The two descriptions chosen are bountiful and knowing, and each answers part of the objection. Bounty explains why gifts are given at all, since the giving proceeds from generosity rather than from the merit of the recipients; knowledge explains why the gifts specify the right recipients, since the one who grants them knows what each community can carry.

The pair recurs throughout the Book at the ends of verses about provision, prophecy, and mercy, and its presence here ties the distribution of revelation to the ordinary providence by which the world is sustained. The sūrah is telling its readers that the same hand which supplies food and rain decides where a book appears, which makes the jealousy in the previous clause unintelligible as a religious position and recognisable as what the Book calls it — envy.

**What the Verse Leaves With Its Readers**

The verse ends with a statement about God rather than with a rebuttal of the group, and the reader is left holding an argument that can be applied wherever the same reasoning appears.

Any community can arrive at the position described here: the true knowledge arrived with us, and anything arriving later or elsewhere is suspect. The sūrah's answer is that guidance and bounty are not community property, and it is an answer that applies to the community now reading the passage as much as to the one being quoted. The next verse continues the same thought, and it describes what the mercy of God does in the world.

**The Group and Its Representatives**

The sūrah does not say how many people held the position it reports, and the phrase it uses is a group among the People of the Book. That qualification has already appeared in the sūrah's accounts of the community, and it prevents the reader from converting a report about a faction into a verdict on a people.

The Book's practice in these passages is consistent. It names conduct, describes the reasoning behind it, answers that reasoning, and leaves the question of who else shares it open. The reader who closes the verse has been given a clear picture of a tactic and a clear statement of the principle that defeats it, and he has not been invited to assess the standing of anyone not mentioned in the text.

---
## Sūrah Āli ʿImrān 3:74

> He chooses whoever He wills to receive His mercy. And Allah is the Lord of infinite bounty.

**Expanded Commentary**

**A Sentence That Answers an Envy**

The verse follows the statement about bounty with a sentence about mercy, and it does so in the same key. God chooses whomever He wills to receive His mercy, and He is the lord of an abundant bounty. Read after the reported fear of the previous verse, the sentence explains what the group's objection had misunderstood.

The two nouns are close in meaning and the verse uses both. Bounty describes the generosity of a giver, and mercy describes the relief that reaches the one who receives it. The sūrah's arrangement places them in sequence: the mercy is what is chosen, and the bounty is the source from which the choosing proceeds. What the community had feared as a threat — that someone else might be given revealed knowledge — is thus classified as an act of mercy on God's part, and the classification removes the sense that anything has been taken from anyone.

**Chosen, Not Earned**

The verb describes selection, and the verse repeats the pattern the sūrah has used since its opening verses. Authority is given to whom God wills; honour and disgrace are His to confer; the families named at the beginning of the sūrah were chosen rather than self-made; and here mercy is granted by the same decision.

The recurrence of the theme across the sūrah is a running correction of the assumption behind the disputes. Every party in the argument had a claim resting on something it possessed — a lineage, a book, a history — and each was being told that the standing it relied on had been given rather than achieved. The sentence in this verse is the general form of that correction, and its brevity makes it harder to argue with than a long demonstration.

**Who Is Chosen in This Instance**

The commentators offered several identifications for the recipient of the mercy in this verse. Some read it as a reference to the Prophet of the sūrah, chosen for prophethood despite the objections of those who had expected the position to remain elsewhere. Others referred it to the Qur'an itself, and still others to the religion that had been established through it.

The readings are not far apart. In each case what is being described is the conferral of something that no community could award to itself and that no community could withhold from another, which is the point the verse is making. The sūrah's own account of the objection — that a messenger could not be raised from among the unlettered — fits the first reading, and the surrounding verses about the Book fit the second. What matters for the reader is the act rather than the object: the choice belongs to God, and the object of the choice is a mercy rather than a property.

**The Lord of Infinite Bounty**

The verse's final description uses a word that denotes greatness and abundance, and the commentators noted that it is used in the Book for gifts that are not measured out. The phrase appears in the Book in connection with the giving of knowledge, of provision, and of reward, and it is always a statement about the scale of the source rather than about quantity in a particular case.

The placement of the phrase here answers the fear in the previous verse a second time. If bounty is infinite, then the gift given to one party is not subtracted from another, and the reasoning of those who worried that someone else might receive something like theirs is exposed as a misunderstanding of the economy they were dealing with. A person who fears that another's gain is his loss is thinking in terms of a limited store, and the verse names the giver as the lord of a store without limit. That single word removes the ground on which the whole anxiety in the previous quotation rested.

**What the Verse Says About Religious Envy**

The passage as a whole diagnoses a condition that has recurred in religious communities. It is the conviction that one's own standing depends on the exclusion of others from the same gifts, and it produces the conduct described in the earlier verses: concealment, mixing, and stratagems aimed at the confidence of outsiders.

The Book's answer here does not argue that the gifts are distributed fairly, and it does not promise anything to the envious. It states that the distribution belongs to God, and it describes the distribution as mercy. A reader who accepts that statement has removed from his own religion the assumption that its value depends on anyone else's deprivation, which is a service the verse performs for every community that recites it.

**The Comfort and the Caution in One Sentence**

For the believers who had been warned that a group wished to mislead them, the sentence is a reassurance about the ground they stand on. What they hold was given, and it can neither be earned away from them nor taken by the manoeuvres described a few verses earlier.

For those who had made the plan, the sentence is a caution. The gifts they were guarding belong to someone else, and the choice of recipients has never been theirs. The Book states both readings in one sentence without differentiating its audience, which is how it usually handles a matter that concerns everyone in the argument, and it leaves the reader to work out which side of the sentence he is standing on.

There is one more thing the verse does, and it is easy to overlook because it is small. It describes the mercy as something God chooses someone *for*, rather than something a person qualifies for by rank, learning, or lineage. A community that has spent generations curating its standing will find the sentence uncomfortable for the same reason the disputants of this sūrah found it uncomfortable: it makes the criterion invisible from outside. No one can inspect another person's selection, and no one can certify his own, which is why the Book's readers are left with the practice the sūrah has been describing rather than with a status they can point to.

---
## Sūrah Āli ʿImrān 3:75

> There are some among the People of the Book who, if entrusted with a stack of gold, will readily return it. Yet there are others who, if entrusted with a single coin, will not repay it unless you constantly demand it. This is because they say, “We are not accountable for ˹exploiting˺ the Gentiles.” And ˹so˺ they attribute lies to Allah knowingly.

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Test of a Trust**

The verse describes a community by its behaviour with property, and it uses a comparison to make the description exact. There are those among the People of the Book who return a large deposit without being pursued, and there are those who refuse to return even a small sum unless the creditor stays at their door.

The choice of subject is deliberate. A community's religion is most visible not in its arguments but in its handling of what belongs to other people, and the sūrah puts the test where no doctrine can obscure it. The same Book repeatedly ties the truth of a person's religion to the fulfilment of obligations: the covenant that God made with the prophets concerned what they would do with what they were given, and around it the Book places warnings about trading the covenant for a small gain.

**The Small Sum and the Large Deposit**

The contrast between the two cases is not between honesty and theft but between honesty that costs nothing and honesty that requires effort. Returning a great deposit to a man who trusts you costs you nothing if you were never going to keep it; returning a single coin to a man who has been asking for it costs you a decision.

The commentators noted the practical dimension of the second case, which is that the creditor has to persist. The behaviour described is therefore not a single refusal but a policy of resistance that wears down the person who is owed. The verse's picture is of a debtor who calculates that the effort required to recover a small amount will eventually exceed its value and who is relying on that calculation. That is a description of a certain kind of dealings, and the Book presents it as a religious matter rather than a commercial one.

**"We Are Not Accountable for the Gentiles"**

The clause the verse reports is the justification the community offered, and the Book reports it as the reason for the conduct rather than as an excuse. The claim is that the obligations of the religion do not extend to people outside it, so that property belonging to an outsider may be treated differently.

The Book's answer to the claim comes in the next verse, where it states that those who honour their trusts and are mindful of God are the ones God loves. But the claim itself deserves attention, because it is the most dangerous position a religious community can reach. A rule of conduct that applies only inside a boundary turns the religion into a loyalty and dissolves the very obligations that the earlier scriptures had been given to establish. The Book elsewhere addresses this directly when it asks the community why they believe in some of the scripture and reject the rest, and the question applies to the position quoted here with exactness.

**"They Attribute Lies to Allah Knowingly"**

The verse's last clause attaches the conduct to a claim about God. The community had justified its policy by reference to what God required, and the sūrah says that what they attributed to Him was not His.

The charge is the same one the sūrah made two verses earlier about concealing and mixing, and it is worded in the same way, with the adverb marking the deliberate character of the act. What the community has done is not to reason wrongly about God but to invent a position and present it as His, and the Book treats this as the gravest form of the offence it has been describing. Everything in the passage about the groups' stratagems, concealment, and fears comes to its sharpest point in this clause, which concerns a statement made about God's own requirements.

**Trusts and the Book's Treatment of Them**

The vocabulary of trusts appears throughout the Book and is applied to several kinds of possession. Property entrusted to another person is one; time, knowledge, and the obligations of the covenant are others. The Book commands the believers to return what is held in trust to its owners, and its warnings about the misuse of entrusted goods extend to the inheritance of scripture itself.

Placing property in that framework is what makes this verse about religion rather than about commerce. A community that holds a book holds a trust, and the Book's argument is that a person's handling of a coin entrusted to him is an indication of what he will do with a text entrusted to him. The two are the same test applied at different scales, which is why the verse can move from a debt to a lie about God within three clauses. The reader is meant to see one habit of mind behind both.

**The Answer That Follows**

The verse ends with the false claim stated and attributed, and the next verse begins with the answer: those who fulfil their trusts and are mindful of God are the ones whom God loves.

The sūrah's arrangement leaves no gap for argument. The claim about Gentiles is answered by a statement about God's love, which is the currency the whole discussion has been conducted in since the passage opened. What a reader takes from the pair of verses is that the boundary of a community does not bound its obligations, and that the obligations themselves are the place where God's approval is decided.

**A Large Deposit and a Small One**

The two sums in the sentence are not close together. The word rendered as a stack of gold names a quantity many times larger than a single coin, though al-Rāzī noted that it is not a precise measure, and the Book uses the same word elsewhere for heaps of gold and for a great sum handed over at the end of a marriage (3:14; 4:20). The contrast is therefore between a sum worth protecting and a sum hardly worth pursuing, and the test is which of the two each person will honour. The commentators explained the thing entrusted in the widest sense: it can be a loan, the price of a purchase, or property left for safekeeping, since all three involve a claim that the holder is obliged to satisfy.

**The Claim and Its Correction**

Al-Qurṭūbī and al-Rāzī recorded explanations of the excuse the verse reports. On one account, some Jews held that agreements made with members of their own community who later accepted the message were void, and they justified the position from their teaching; on another, the attitude was a matter of tribal loyalty rather than of law. The word the verse puts in their mouths describes non-Jews, and the Book uses the same term elsewhere for those it calls unlettered, which is how the community is described when the argument concerns the possession of scripture (2:78; 3:20; 7:157–58; 62:2). The sūrah's own later passage supplies the corrective, since it states that the People of the Book are not all alike and names an upright group among them whose conduct the verse before the reader has just illustrated (3:113).

**The Correction Ibn ʿAbbās Gave**

The tradition preserved a report in which Muslims came to Ibn ʿAbbās and made a claim of the same shape against a non-Muslim community living under treaty, arguing that nothing prevented them from taking what belonged to those people. He rejected the claim and told them that no wealth might be taken from the treaty peoples beyond what they had undertaken to pay, the indemnity mentioned in the sūrah of Repentance (9:29). The report shows how the community's teachers used this verse: the argument about one group's misuse of a rule became a warning against the same misuse on the other side. Al-Qurṭūbī attached a further report to the passage, one that traces a chain from resentment to betrayal, from betrayal to the loss of compassion, and from there to the departure of faith from a person's heart.

---
## Sūrah Āli ʿImrān 3:76

> Absolutely! Those who honour their trusts and shun evil—surely Allah loves those who are mindful ˹of Him˺.

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Answer to the Previous Claim**

The verse responds directly to the justification reported a line earlier, where the community had defended its conduct toward outsiders by claiming that its obligations did not reach them. The answer is not an argument about the clause; it is a statement about who enjoys God's approval.

The Book often answers a false principle this way, by replacing it rather than refuting it. The claim under discussion was a rule about which people a community owed honest dealing; the answer given is a description of the conduct God approves of, and the description turns on the fulfilment of trust. The reader who compares the two sentences sees that the disputed clause has been set aside rather than engaged, and the ground of the comparison is what the Book is looking for in people, which the closing phrase names as mindfulness of God.

**The Word for What Must Be Honoured**

The term rendered "their trusts" covers more than a deposit held for safekeeping. It describes everything that has been placed in a person's care, including property, agreements, and the obligations of a role. The Book uses it for duties of office, for the treatment of dependents, and for the whole of a community's inheritance of revelation.

Reading the word in its widest sense explains why the verse can answer a question about commercial dealing with a statement about divine approval. The deposit of a coin and the inheritance of a book are both trusts, and the Book's treatment of the two is the same in kind: what has been entrusted remains the property of the one who entrusted it, and the person holding it is accountable for how he handles it. A community that had convinced itself that one class of trust did not bind it had, by that reasoning, loosened a principle that reached far beyond the case in front of it.

**Mindfulness as the Second Condition**

The verse names two things: the fulfilment of trusts and mindfulness of God. The second is not a decoration on the first. In the Book's usage, *taqwā* is the guardedness that keeps a person aware of his accountability; it is what makes the fulfilment of a trust a matter of conscience rather than convenience.

The pairing appears in the sūrah's earlier description of the people who inherit the Garden, and the same two elements recur in the Book's portraits of the righteous. What the sūrah is doing here is placing the conduct it has been describing against a standard the community itself would have recognised — honest dealing and awareness of God — and pointing out that the two belong together. A person who fulfils a trust because he fears consequences is performing the act; a person who does it because he is mindful of God has understood what the act is for, and it is the second kind of fulfilment that the verse attaches to God's approval.

**God Loves the Mindful**

The verse's last clause states the reward in the vocabulary the sūrah has been using since the passage about love opened. In an earlier verse the Book told its readers that if they love God, following the Prophet would produce love in return; here the love is attached to a specific conduct, and the conduct is the honest handling of what one holds.

The Book's attributions of divine love are instructive when they are gathered together. God loves those who do good, those who are mindful, those who rely on Him, and those who act justly; the list is made up of conduct rather than of status. The community addressed in this passage had a great deal of status and was in the middle of an argument about it, and the verse ends by naming the conduct God's approval follows. The verse therefore supplies both the answer to the claim and a description of what is being asked in place of the system the claim represented.

**What the Verse Confirms About the Community's Diversity**

The passage as a whole has been distinguishing between people within the same community, and this verse continues that work. The previous verse said that among the People of the Book there are those who return a large deposit and those who will not release a small one; this verse states the principle that decides between them, and the sūrah will later state explicitly that they are not all alike.

That pattern is important for how the passage is read. The Book is not conducting a case against a people; it is describing a conduct and naming the standard that judges it, and the standard applies inside as well as outside the group. The verses that follow continue in this vein, moving from the honest trustee to those who trade their covenant for a small price, and the reader is being shown a range rather than a verdict on a whole community.

**A Standard That Applies to the Reader**

The clause about trust is one of those sentences in the Book that addresses every reader regardless of his community, since everyone holds something that belongs to someone else. Property, a position, a confidence, and a text are all entrusted, and the book's measure is the same for all of them.

The sūrah leaves the reader with the connection between the two halves of the sentence: the fulfilment and the mindfulness belong to one another, and the approval follows from them. What the passage does next, in the following verses, is to describe the conduct of the parties who did the opposite, and the contrast is drawn so that the reader can see both the standard and what departing from it looks like.

---
## Sūrah Āli ʿImrān 3:77

> Indeed, those who trade Allah’s covenant and their oaths for a fleeting gain will have no share in the Hereafter. Allah will neither speak to them, nor look at them, nor purify them on the Day of Judgment. And they will suffer a painful punishment.

**Expanded Commentary**

**A Trade Described in Three Parts**

The verse names a transaction, the price, and the loss. The merchants are those who sell a covenant with God and their own oaths for a small gain, and the consequence is that they will have no share in the Hereafter. The sentence is short and its proportions are deliberate: the thing traded away is a pledge made to God, and the thing received is described by a word that diminishes it.

The Book uses the language of commerce for this kind of exchange repeatedly, and it applies it to several objects. People are said to sell God's signs for a price, to sell the Book, and to sell their oaths; the same vocabulary appears in the sūrah of the Cow's account of those who exchange guidance for error. The consistency of the metaphor tells the reader how the Book assesses such conduct: it is not merely a failure but a purchase, and the assessment of it turns on the value of what was given up against the value of what was received.

**The Covenant and the Oaths**

The two things sold are named separately, and the distinction is worth marking. A covenant with God is the standing obligation of a community that has received a revelation and pledged itself to it; an oath is a particular promise made by a particular person, often in the course of a dispute.

Putting the two together covers both the general and the particular. A community's failure is not usually a single lie; it is a practice of making promises it does not keep, which erodes the general pledge along with each specific one. The Book elsewhere states the requirement in the positive form when it says that those who honour their trusts and are mindful of God are the ones He loves, and the same sūrah has already placed the conduct of the earlier community under that standard. What this verse adds is the mechanism: the pledges are traded, and they are traded for something, which means the person making the exchange has made a calculation about what his word is worth.

**"A Fleeting Gain"**

The price is described by a word that indicates something small and passing, and the Book uses it for the world's goods when they are set against the Hereafter. The same word appears in warnings about those who traded the guidance they had for a brief advantage, and in the charge against the communities that sold their share for a price.

The description is where the verse's argument does its work. The exchange is not condemned because trading is wrong, or because the parties wanted something; it is condemned because the price was inadequate to the thing sold, and the person accepting it had misjudged the value. The Book's ethics of trust therefore rest on a claim about relative worth rather than on a rule about promises; a person breaks his word when he has decided, in a particular case, that what he is being offered matters more than what he has pledged. The verse simply names that decision and states its cost.

**The Three Withholdings**

The second sentence describes the consequence in three negative clauses: God will not speak to them, will not look at them, and will not purify them on the Day of Judgment. The commentators explained the language carefully, since other passages describe God addressing the wicked on that day.

Their conclusion is that the three clauses describe the withdrawal of favour rather than a literal impossibility. In a culture where being addressed, being looked upon with regard, and being treated as clean were the marks of acceptance, the sentence describes a person standing before his Lord in the position of an outcast. The Book does use the language of looking and of speech for divine approval elsewhere, and the sūrah's reader is meant to hear the three clauses as the complete reversal of the welcome that the previous verse promised to the trustworthy.

**The Punishment Named at the End**

The sentence closes with a painful punishment, which is the sūrah's standard formula for the outcome of the conduct it has been describing. The Book often ends an account of wrongdoing with a statement of its consequence, and the effect is to keep the two in view together.

What the reader is being shown, in the passage as a whole, is a community's conduct traced to its end. The verses about mixing truth and falsehood, about the stratagem of morning belief and evening rejection, and about the claim that obligations stop at the community's boundary have each described how a group behaves when it has decided that its position matters more than its word. This verse names the decision in the clearest terms available and states what the Book says follows it, and it does so in one sentence so that the two cannot be separated in the reader's mind.

**A Warning With the Believers in View**

The Book applies this warning to its own community as well, and it does so in more than one place, using the same language of trading a covenant for a small gain. The passage's immediate target is a group among the People of the Book, and the sūrah is not making a prediction about the future of any community.

What the reader is given is a description that he can use to inspect his own practice. The measure is whether one's word holds when keeping it is costly, and the Book leaves that test where the reader can apply it: not in the dispute about which community has the better claim, but in whether the promise made yesterday is still being honoured today. The following verses turn to a different charge, and they concern speech itself.

**Why the Trade Is Named Before the Punishment**

The order of the two sentences in this verse is deliberate. The Book states what was done and what it cost before it says what follows, and the sequence gives the punishment its intelligibility.

A reader who meets only the sentence about the three withholdings is looking at severity without a cause. Meeting it after the account of a pledge sold for a small price, he is looking at a proportion. The Book's habit of arranging verdict and reasoning in this order runs through the sūrah: the earlier passage described the killing of prophets and the killing of those who defend justice before it announced a painful punishment, and the same arrangement appears here in miniature. What is being taught, verse by verse, is that the Book's severity is always a response to something named in the text, and never a display.

---
## Sūrah Āli ʿImrān 3:78

> There are some among them who distort the Book with their tongues to make you think this ˹distortion˺ is from the Book—but it is not what the Book says. They say, “It is from Allah”—but it is not from Allah. And ˹so˺ they attribute lies to Allah knowingly.

**Expanded Commentary**

**A Charge About Speech**

The verse describes a group among the People of the Book as distorting the book with their tongues, in a way that makes what they say sound as though it came from the book, when it does not, and they say of it that it is from God when it is not. The final clause names what they are doing: attributing lies to God while knowing.

The subject is therefore not the copying of a text but the recitation of one. The image is of men reading aloud, bending words as they go, so that a listener without the text in front of him hears something that the text does not contain. The Book's charge concerns the space between what is written and what is said about it, which is a space every religious community occupies whenever it explains its scripture.

**The Tongue as the Instrument**

The phrase about the tongue is exact. A distortion made with the tongue can be a change of wording, a shift of emphasis, or an explanation attached to the reading so that the hearer cannot separate the two. What all three share is that the original remains intact behind the performance, and the person performing knows where the difference lies.

The Book's other account of the same conduct uses the language of writing: woe to those who write the book with their own hands and then say that it is from God, seeking a small gain (2:79). The two verses supply the two channels by which a scripture can be made to say what it does not — the pen and the voice — and the charge in each case is the same deliberate substitution of a community's position for the text it holds. What the Book objects to is not interpretation; it is the presentation of interpretation as revelation.

**"You Think It Is From the Book"**

The clause about the hearers is what makes the offence a public one. The people being addressed are not deceiving themselves; they are managing the impression of a third party, and the verse names the intended effect.

The commentators described several occasions for such conduct, including the presentation of texts to audiences that could not read for themselves and the recitation of passages with the meanings adjusted. What all the accounts have in common is an asymmetry of knowledge: the person reciting knows the book, and the audience does not. The Book treats the possession of that advantage as a trust, and this verse is one of the places where it says what happens when the trust is spent on the speaker's own position.

**The Two Denials in the Sentence**

The verse states the same act in two ways: it is not what the Book says, and it is not from God. The first denial concerns the text, and the second concerns the source, and the Book places them in the order in which a person would check the claim.

A reader who wanted to test such a statement would begin with the book and ask whether it contained what was being attributed to it. If the text did not carry the claim, the question of its origin would be settled, and that is the sequence the verse follows. Both denials are stated without qualification by the one who sent the book down, which is the only authority competent to settle what it contains, and the verdict is delivered without the argument that produced it.

**Attributing Lies "Knowingly"**

The verse's last words return to the phrase that has run through this whole passage. The adverb is what separates the conduct described here from an error of reading.

The Book's consistency on this point is notable. It accuses the communities it criticises of many things, and the charge of ignorance is not among them; the recurring accusation is that of acting against knowledge. A person who has misread a text is to be corrected, and the Book corrects its own readers in passages that ask whether they do not understand. A person who has decided that his community's standing is worth more than the accuracy of what he attributes to God has made a different kind of decision, and the sūrah reserves its sharpest language for that one. The next verses explain what such people are trying to protect, and the answer has to do with a claim about who may be worshipped.

**Reading the Verse Inside a Community That Recites**

The Book addresses this charge to a group within the People of the Book, and then hands the same account to a new community that will recite it for centuries. The sūrah has already warned its readers about the ambitions of the group it describes, and the warning's usefulness depends on the reader's recognising the conduct rather than the people.

The offence named here is available to anyone who speaks about scripture with authority, which means it is available to the community reading the verse. What the Book provides against it is the text itself, preserved and recited in public, along with the repeated instruction not to conceal what one knows. A community that keeps its scripture audible and its explanations of it distinguishable from the text has closed the door this verse describes, and the verse's presence in that community's own book is part of the lock. The Book's own example of the alternative is worth noting as well: it reports the covenant taken from those who were given the Scripture, obliging them to make it known to people and not to hide it (3:187). The obligation to publish stands against the practice of bending, and the two verses describe the same community at the two ends of the same choice.

---
## Sūrah Āli ʿImrān 3:79

> It is not appropriate for someone who Allah has blessed with the Scripture, wisdom, and prophethood to say to people, “Worship me instead of Allah.” Rather, he would say, “Be devoted to the worship of your Lord ˹alone˺”—in accordance with what these prophets read in the Scripture and what they taught.

**Expanded Commentary**

**A Limit Set on the Gifts of God**

The verse is a statement about what is not appropriate for a human being who has been given scripture, wisdom, and prophethood. The list ascends, and the point of the sentence is that the highest accumulation of divine gifts still does not license the invitation to be worshipped.

The Book's method here is to argue from the nature of the office rather than from the character of any individual. A prophet is constituted by the gifts named: he has been given a book, understanding of it, and a mission. Every one of those is a relationship of dependence, and the verse's claim is that the man who has received them cannot turn them into a claim on the worship of others without denying what they are. The grammar of the sentence is impersonal — it is not appropriate for any human being — which makes it a rule rather than an accusation.

**The Three Gifts Named**

The Book mentions scripture, wisdom, and prophethood here in a single list, and it uses the same combination in other places when it speaks of what God bestows on His servants. Scripture is the revealed text; wisdom is the capacity to use it rightly; prophethood is the commission to deliver it.

Each of the three is a trust, and the verse's argument is that a trust cannot be converted into a title. The community that received this verse had a live example in front of it, since the dispute about Jesus concerned precisely the question of what follows from a prophet's extraordinary gifts, and the sūrah had already answered that question with the comparison to Adam. What the sentence adds is the general form of the argument, stated in the abstract so that it applies wherever the gifts appear.

**The Command the Prophet Would Give Instead**
