The second half of the verse supplies the alternative. A person in that position would say: be devoted to the worship of your Lord alone, in accordance with what these prophets read in the scripture and taught.

The phrase about what the prophets read and taught is worth attention. The command being issued is not presented as a new religious instruction; it is what the recipients of the earlier books already had in front of them. The verse's picture of a prophet is therefore of a teacher who directs people back to what has been given, which is the pattern the sūrah has drawn throughout its narrative of the messengers. Noah, Abraham, Moses, and Jesus all come with a message that is recognisable in its content, and the instruction to worship God alone appears in each of their traditions.

**Devotion Instead of Deification**

The Arabic word rendered "be devoted" belongs to the vocabulary of religious instruction and describes a person who gives himself to the service of his Lord. It is the term the Book also uses for those who devote themselves to the study and teaching of religion, and its appearance here in the mouth of a prophet is exact.

The contrast the verse draws is between two invitations: worship me, and serve your Lord. One treats the prophet as the destination and the other treats him as the pointer, and the sūrah's argument is that a man who knows what he has been given would never confuse the two. The alternative in the sentence is not modesty as a personal quality; it is the accurate description of the relation between a messenger and the Lord who sent him, and the verse presents it as the only thing a prophet in that position could say.

**Why the Verse Is in This Passage**

The passage has been describing a community that attributed statements to God which He had not made, and the earlier verses reported their views about obligations and about the credibility of outsiders. This verse turns to the question that lies underneath those manoeuvres, which is the question of who is entitled to be worshipped.

The connection between the two subjects is closer than it looks. A community that has appointed itself the guardian of who may be recognised also tends toward a position in which its teachers occupy the place its religion reserves for God, and the Book names that tendency in other passages when it describes people who took their rabbis and monks as lords apart from God. The verse's refutation is not about procedures; it restores the relation between a servant and his Lord, and it does so by quoting what a prophet would say if he were standing in front of his people.

**The Historical Setting and Its Comfort**

The commentaries connect the verse to questions put to the Prophet about whether he wished to be treated as an object of veneration, and to the wider controversy about how Jesus was regarded among the Christians. In both readings the verse is a categorical denial of any claim on worship by a human being, however exalted.

The sūrah's readers were in a position to profit from the statement in a different way. A community formed around a prophet will always face the question of how far veneration may go, and the answer given here is built into the message itself. The Prophet is presented as a teacher who directs his people to the exclusive worship of God, in accordance with what the previous prophets read and taught, and the verse makes that direction part of the definition of his office.

---
## Sūrah Āli ʿImrān 3:80

> And he would never ask you to take angels and prophets as lords. Would he ask you to disbelieve after you have submitted?

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Second Prohibition**

The verse continues the description of what a prophet would never ask, and it names the objects: angels and prophets as lords. The previous verse excluded the invitation to worship the speaker; this one excludes the invitation to worship other venerable beings, and it does so in the same construction.

The two sentences together cover the whole range of the error. A false teacher may place himself in the position of a deity, or he may direct his followers to intermediaries whose standing is real but whose status is being inflated. The Book closes both routes with one sentence each, and the sūrah's wider argument has already supplied the principle: whatever has been created, including angels and messengers, stands on the servant side of the line.

**Angels and Prophets Named Together**

The choice of these two categories is not arbitrary. They represent the two classes of being that the Book treats as the closest to God, and the communities the sūrah addresses had strong traditions about each.

The angels are described in the Book as servants who carry out God's commands without disobedience, and the prophets as the most honoured of humanity. Naming them together as the objects the prohibition covers removes the possibility of a religion of elevated intermediaries, and it does so without denigrating the beings themselves. The Book elsewhere records a conversation in the Hereafter in which Jesus is asked whether he told people to take him and his mother as gods apart from God, and his answer is a declaration of his own servitude. The verse under discussion is that answer stated in advance as a rule about every prophet and every angel.

**The Rhetorical Question at the End**

The verse closes with a question: would he ask you to disbelieve after you have submitted? The question presents the proposal being rejected as incoherent on its own terms, since the invitation to worship something other than God is an invitation to unbelief, whatever language it is dressed in.

The Book's use of the question form here is different from its use in the earlier passages addressed to the People of the Book. There the questions asked opponents to explain their conduct; this one works inside the argument by showing that the conduct attributed to a prophet would contradict what a prophet is for. The implication is left for the reader to complete: if a man has brought people to submission to God, he will not afterwards turn around and ask them to place their submission elsewhere, and a report that he did so has misdescribed either him or what he said.

**Where the Verse Places the Prophets**

The sentence puts the messengers of God on the receiving end of the same prohibition that protects God's exclusive claim, which is a striking way of honouring them. They are protected from being made into objects of worship by a rule that is stated as a fact about their own conduct.

The Book's treatment of its prophets is consistent in this regard. Their honours are real and the sūrah has enumerated them for Jesus at length: a word from God, honoured in two worlds, brought near, taught writing and wisdom, given signs. What those gifts never become, in the Book's account, is a basis for a share in divinity, and the verse above supplies the reason in the form of what the prophet himself would refuse. The reader who has followed the sūrah's narrative from the family of ʿImrān to this point has seen the gifts and the refusal together, and the two are not in tension.

**The Two Verses as One Argument**

Read with the verse before it, the passage forms a single statement about the limits of loyalty in religion. A prophet directs his people to God and no further; he does not offer himself and he does not offer others, and any teaching that does either is not from the prophets.

The argument's placement in the sūrah is precise. It follows the passage about the community that attributed false statements to God and comes just before the covenant that God made with the prophets, in which the same messengers would be bound to acknowledge a messenger who came after them. The sūrah is constructing a picture of a single continuous mission whose whole purpose is the worship of God alone, and the two prohibitions in these verses are the boundary markers of that mission.

**What the Reader Is Asked to Weigh**

The verse invites its reader to consider a claim about a prophet's message by asking what the prophet himself would do with the loyalty that message produced. The test is available to anyone with a description of the prophet's teaching, and it does not depend on knowing any of the parties in the sūrah's dispute.

That is one of the ways the Book makes its arguments portable. The immediate controversy concerned communities and their doctrines, and the principle set out here concerns the structure of any teaching that claims to come from God.

There is also a warning in the verse's form that any community reading it can use. The two prohibitions deal with what a prophet would never ask, which means a religious practice can be tested by asking where it directs the loyalty it produces. A teacher who accepts veneration for himself, or who has taught his people to depend on intermediaries rather than on God, has moved outside the pattern the verse describes, and the Book's criterion for the messengers is stated here in their own voice. The following verse takes the same argument and gives it the form of a covenant, which turns the whole history of revelation into a single obligation.

---
## Sūrah Āli ʿImrān 3:81

> ˹Remember˺ when Allah made a covenant with the prophets, ˹saying,˺ “Now that I have given you the Book and wisdom, if there comes to you a messenger confirming what you have, you must believe in him and support him.” He added, “Do you affirm this covenant and accept this commitment?” They said, “Yes, we do.” Allah said, “Then bear witness, and I too am a Witness.”

**Expanded Commentary**

**A Covenant Binding Every Prophet**

The verse reports an undertaking that God made with the prophets as a class. They were given a book and wisdom, and when a messenger came to them confirming what they had, they were to believe in him and support him. The covenant is then ratified: God asks whether they agree and take up the obligation, they answer that they do, and God calls them to witness while declaring Himself a witness as well.

The scope of the sentence is what gives it weight. It is not an agreement made with one people at one time; it is a standing obligation attached to the office of prophethood itself, so that every messenger is bound by it as a condition of his mission. The Book states the same idea here in the form of a documented undertaking, complete with offer, acceptance, and witnesses.

**What the Covenant Requires**

The two verbs are believing and supporting, and the pair covers both the inner and the outer response. The messengers are not merely to acknowledge a subsequent prophet; they are to stand with him, which the commentators understood to include helping his cause and making it known.

The addition of support is important, because it explains why the covenant is stated as a mutual obligation rather than a private assent. A prophet has a community behind him, and the covenant binds the mission rather than the individual alone. The commentators took this to mean that the obligation passes to the followers of each prophet, since the prophets themselves would not fail in such a matter; what the covenant establishes is the standing rule of the religious history that revelation describes, in which each messenger's community is answerable for how it receives the message that arrives after them.

**The Confidence of the Report**

The verse reports the exchange as a completed transaction, with the givers of the covenant answering yes and God calling witnesses to the agreement. The Book uses this documentary style in several places for the covenants it records, including the covenant with the Children of Israel and the covenant taken from all of humanity in the primordial testimony that God had them give regarding themselves.

The style does work that a bare statement of obligation could not. A covenant that has been ratified and witnessed cannot be treated as a suggestion, and the parties to it are shown agreeing to its terms before any specific case arrived to test them. The Book's readers are therefore presented with a history of revelation in which the prophets of the past are committed in advance to recognising the prophets of the future, and the verse leaves no room for a reading in which the earlier missions were self-enclosed.

**The Messenger in View**

The commentators held that the messenger to whom this covenant points is the Prophet of this sūrah, and the wording of the sūrah supports the reading, since the formula it uses for a messenger confirming what his predecessors had is the formula the sūrah has applied to the Qur'an itself at its opening.

What the covenant does, in that reading, is to place the mission of the Prophet inside the obligations of all the earlier missions rather than beside them. The communities that held the earlier books are told that their own prophets had promised to acknowledge the one who fulfilled their message, and the argument the sūrah has been conducting about Abraham and about Jesus is thereby given a further dimension. The dispute is not between one community's revelation and another's; it is between a covenant and the conduct of the people who inherited its obligations.

**Why the Report Is Placed Here**

The verse stands after the passage on worship and before the verses that state the consequences of turning back. Its position answers the question a reader might carry from the discussion of Abraham and the People of the Book: on what basis can a new messenger require recognition from communities that already possess scriptures?

The answer given is that the earlier messengers themselves had been bound to this. The obligation the new message imposes is not novel, and it does not represent a demand by the newcomer upon unwilling predecessors. It is the honouring of an agreement whose terms the predecessors had accepted, and the sūrah states it before it states the consequences of refusing, so that the reader meets the obligation before he meets the warning.

**A History of Revelation That Holds Together**

The verse's picture of religious history is of a single successive mission in which each messenger knows he is not the last. That picture differs from a story in which revelation is the property of the communities that received it, and the sūrah has been arguing against the second picture from its opening verses.

The repetition of this theme through the chapter — the books confirming one another, the messengers acknowledging one another, the people of Abraham defined by following rather than by descent — gives the reader a coherent account of what he is reading. What the covenant adds is the mechanism: the confirmation is not an accident of history but a term of the commission, agreed to by every messenger before he began.

**The Last Line of the Verse**

The sentence ends with the witnesses: they bear witness, and God is a witness. The line is short and it closes the transaction, and the sūrah's choice to end on it rather than on the obligation itself is characteristic.

What the reader is left holding is not only what was promised but the fact that it was recorded. The next verse states what becomes of a community that turns back after such an agreement, and the two verses are meant to be read together.

**The Particle That Carries Two Readings**

The construction rendered as by that which I have given and as should a messenger has been read in more than one way. One reading treats the clause as an oath, so that God swears by what He has given the prophets before binding them to the undertaking; al-Ṭabarī recorded that explanation. Another reading treats the clause as a condition, so that the sentence states what the prophets are bound to do if a messenger arrives confirming what they already possess. The two readings arrive at the same substance, and the commentators treated the difference as a matter of grammar rather than of meaning: the Book is making the acceptance of a later messenger part of what the earlier scriptures require.

**Who Is Bound by the Covenant**

The commentators differed over the parties addressed, and al-Rāzī set out the options. On one view the command is given to the prophets themselves, who would be obliged to affirm the messenger if he appeared during their lifetimes. On another, the verse addresses the followers of the prophets, since the messengers themselves would never turn away from what God sent, while their communities might; al-Qurṭūbī and al-Rāzī both recorded this reading. The question that follows, asking whether the parties agree and take up the undertaking, was read by al-Rāzī as spoken by God to the prophets or by the prophets to their followers, while the closing words of the verse, the command to bear witness, were taken by the commentators to be God's own speech. The passage was understood by the community's teachers to refer to the Prophet Muhammad in the first place, whose coming they found announced in the earlier books (7:157), and al-Rāzī acknowledged that the covenant as worded covers any messenger who comes to a prophet in the terms the verse describes.

---
## Sūrah Āli ʿImrān 3:82

> Whoever turns back after this, they will be the rebellious.

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Consequence of the Covenant**

The verse follows directly from the undertaking reported a line earlier, in which the prophets accepted an obligation and God took witnesses to it. Whoever turns back after that agreement, the verse says, belongs among the rebellious.

The sentence is short because its work has been done by the verse before it. The reader has just been shown a ratified covenant with witnesses on both sides; what remains to be stated is what the refusal of a ratified agreement amounts to. The Book's choice of the word for that condition is worth attention, since it is not a word for doubt or error. The term describes a departure from a state of obedience, and it is used throughout the Book for those who leave the way their own undertaking had set out for them.

**What Turning Back Means**

The Arabic describes a turning away and a reversal of course, and the Book uses the same root for apostasy, for the refusal of a summons, and for the conduct of a community that agrees to something and then abandons it.

The word therefore covers conduct rather than a mental state, which fits the verse's setting. The covenant was to believe in and support a messenger; turning back from it is not the failure to reach a conclusion but the abandonment of an undertaking. The Book's legal vocabulary is consistent on this point: an agreement obliges the one who accepted it, and the seriousness of a breach is proportionate to the standing of the party who was given the assurance. A covenant witnessed by God is the most serious kind, and the description of the violator follows from that fact rather than from any additional accusation.

**The Rebels as a Category in the Book**

The Book applies the term to several groups, and its range is instructive. It describes those who refuse what God has sent, those who set aside the obligations they accepted, and those who turn away after having seen the truth.

The consistent element in each case is the presence of something accepted earlier and then left. The Book does not use the word for people who never received a message, and it does not use it for those whose knowledge was too slight to oblige them. That is why the verse's placement matters so much: it comes after a covenant described in detail, with the acceptance and the witnesses reported, so that the rebellion in view is not a departure from an unfamiliar position but the abandonment of one the parties had formally taken up. The reader who has followed the passage from the story of Abraham to this sentence has been shown exactly what the obligation was and how it was contracted.

**Why the Verse Is Not Addressed to the Prophets Alone**

Read strictly, the covenant was made with the prophets, who by the Book's own account would not have turned back. The commentators resolved the apparent difficulty by noting that the obligation passes to the communities that inherit each mission.

The point is not a technical one. The Book treats the religious history it describes as a series of communities bound by what their messengers accepted on their behalf, which is why the sūrah can address the People of the Book about a covenant they themselves did not personally negotiate. A community's identity in the Book is corporate in exactly this sense: it inherits obligations, and it is judged by its fidelity to them. What the verse states is the consequence for the heirs when the terms are abandoned.

**The Severity and Its Source**

The language of the verse is severe, and the severity is drawn from the agreement it follows rather than from the persons of those who break it. That distinction is worth holding onto, because the passage as a whole has been careful to distinguish among the members of the communities it addresses.

The sūrah has already noted that a deposit may be returned faithfully by one member of a community and withheld by another, and it will shortly say in explicit terms that they are not all alike. The verse above states a rule about those who turn back, and the qualification runs through the surrounding verses: the Book names conduct and states its outcome without converting the statement into a verdict on an entire people. The next verse raises the question of what a person leaving such a covenant is actually looking for.

**A Sentence That Looks Forward**

The verse ends with the description of the rebels and leaves the reader at the edge of a question. If a person had a covenant and abandoned it, what destination did he think he was heading toward?

That question is taken up immediately in the following verse, which asks whether such people desire a way other than God's while everything in the heavens and the earth is in submission to Him. The two verses belong together, and the second one provides the scale against which the abandonment in the first is measured. What the reader receives from the pair is a definition of the offence in terms of its object: it is not simply a broken promise between people but a refusal of the arrangement in which everything that exists already participates.

The word chosen for the people who turn back also keeps the Book's account of human conduct consistent. Nobody in this passage is described as having been defeated by an argument; the failure named is a departure from a position that had been taken up with the parties' own agreement and God's testimony. The sūrah has used the vocabulary of turning away several times in the course of its argument with the same communities, and the term chosen here describes the end of that process rather than a single moment within it.

---
## Sūrah Āli ʿImrān 3:83

> Do they desire a way other than Allah’s—knowing that all those in the heavens and the earth submit to His Will, willingly or unwillingly, and to Him they will ˹all˺ be returned?

**Expanded Commentary**

**A Question About Desire**

The verse asks whether the people just described are looking for a way other than God's, and the question is phrased in terms of desire. What is at issue is not only what they do but what they want, and the Book's habit of naming desire as the engine of doctrinal position is on display here.

The question also exposes the impossibility of what is wanted. The sentence continues by stating that everyone in the heavens and the earth submits to God's will, willingly or unwillingly, and that all of them will be returned to Him. A way other than God's is therefore not an alternative route but a contradiction of the only order there is, and the verse's question is designed to be felt as unanswerable rather than answered.

**Submission Willing and Unwilling**

The phrase distinguishes two ways in which submission occurs, and the commentators found it a difficult and fruitful expression. Some read the willing submission as the devout obedience of believers and the angels, and the unwilling submission as the condition of those who must submit to God's decrees in creation, death, and the outcome of events despite refusing His commands.

The Book uses the distinction in more than one place. The sūrah of the Thunder declares that everything in the heavens and the earth prostrates to God, willingly or unwillingly, as do their shadows morning and evening (13:15). In the sūrah of Fussilat, when God addresses the heaven and the earth and calls them to submit, they answer together that they submit willingly (41:11). The sūrah here gives the general case; elsewhere the Book gives the same subject in its particular instances, and the verses about the prostrating sun, moon, mountains, and trees belong to the same theme.

**The Persuasion of an Unavoidable Order**

The verse's argument is not that everyone obeys God's commands, which would be false. Its claim is that nobody escapes God's will, which is a statement about power rather than about piety.

The distinction between being subject to a power and agreeing with it is precisely what the two adverbs are for. The Book elsewhere describes people whose faith appears at the moment of punishment when it can no longer help them, and it states that belief at that point profits no one; the readiness to submit much earlier, while it still counted, is the thing that distinguishes one kind of submission from the other. What this verse establishes is that the universe is not divided between those under God's rule and those outside it. It is divided between those who accept His rule and those who are governed by it against their preference.

**What the Argument Does in This Passage**

The verse stands between the covenant and the passage about the community's inheritance of Abraham, and its placement keeps the sūrah's controversy within a single frame. The disputants had been arguing about which community held the correct position, and the verse reminds them that the question of belonging to God's order is not settled by a community's self-assessment.

The Book's method here is to widen the frame when the discussion has become factional. An argument about who has the correct revelation is set inside a statement about the submission of everything that exists, and the effect is to make the parties' claims look small. The next verse returns to the specifics of the controversy and states the content of the faith that the believers are to profess, and it does so in a form that includes the prophets both sides honoured.

**The Return at the End of the Sentence**

The verse closes with the return to God, which is a favourite ending of the Book either at the end or the beginning of a passage about people who are confident about their standing.

The Book's use of the theme here has a particular force. A person who is looking for a way other than God's will find himself at the end of his road facing the one whose way he was avoiding, and the sentence says this without any elaboration. The verse does not describe punishment, and it does not pronounce a verdict. It states a fact about the destination of all things, and the question with which the verse begins is left lying against it: what does a person who seeks an alternative way imagine that he is seeking, given that everything returns to the same Lord?

**A Note on the Two Adverbs' Comfort**

The passage has a further dimension that the commentators discussed. To submit willingly is the believer's condition, and to submit unwillingly is the condition of the rest of creation; but the two share the same Lord, and the Book states the matter in one sentence so that the difference between them is never obscured by any claim of independence.

A reader who takes the verse seriously learns something about how to think about the world's apparent disorder. The Book's picture is of a creation whose every part is subject to God's will, with human beings given the choice of submitting in the manner of the willing or being carried along in the manner of the unwilling. What distinguishes the two is not the fact of the relationship but the posture of the person within it, which is exactly the distinction the sūrah's next verses set out to describe. The Book returns to the same idea wherever it wants to state the limits of human rebellion, and it states it in the same terms each time: the refusal of a decree does not prevent the decree. What the sūrah's readers are being offered in this verse is not a description of the world as it should be but of the world as it already is, inside which their own decisions take place and by which their weight is measured.

---
## Sūrah Āli ʿImrān 3:84

> Say, ˹O Prophet,˺ “We believe in Allah and what has been revealed to us and what was revealed to Abraham, Ishmael, Isaac, Jacob, and his descendants; and what was given to Moses, Jesus, and other prophets from their Lord—we make no distinction between any of them, and to Him we ˹fully˺ submit.”

**Expanded Commentary**

**A Confession of Faith That Names Its Contents**

The verse instructs the Prophet to state what the community believes, and the statement begins with God and then lists the revelations given to a series of named prophets. The list runs from Abraham through his descendants to Moses and Jesus and the other prophets, and it ends with a declaration that no distinction is made among them and a statement of submission.

What the Book is doing is giving its community a creed in the form of a list. The contents are not abstract propositions; they are the messengers and the books that the sūrah's disputes had been about, named one by one so that the community's position on each is public. The confession is therefore a way of answering the arguments of the preceding verses by means of a statement that includes everything the other parties claimed and refuses to rank it.

**Abraham and His Descendants Named First**

The list begins with Abraham and continues through Ishmael, Isaac, Jacob, and the tribes descended from him. The order follows the Book's habit of naming the patriarchs together, and the inclusion of Ishmael alongside Isaac is significant in a sūrah that has been arguing about who has the better claim to Abraham.

Placing Ishmael in the same sentence as Isaac settles the ancestral dispute in a single stroke. The two sons whose descendants became separate peoples are named as recipients of revelation in one clause, with no hierarchy between them, and the sūrah thereby refuses the competition it has been addressing. The community confessing this creed is not choosing one branch of Abraham's house against another; it is receiving what was given to them all, and the confession's shape makes the choice unnecessary.

**Moses, Jesus, and the Other Prophets**

The second half of the list names Moses and Jesus and then generalises: and the other prophets from their Lord. The two names carry the two books the sūrah has discussed at length, and the general phrase covers the rest of the messengers without requiring an inventory.

The Book's use of this construction, which appears in nearly identical form in the sūrah of the Cow, shows how it handles the history of revelation in a creed. It names the figures its audience knows and divides the whole history under one source, so that the confession has both the specificity of the disputes and the inclusiveness of the whole tradition. What is being recited is not a general principle about prophets; the names are those of the particular messengers whose communities stood in front of the first hearers.

**"We Make No Distinction Between Any of Them"**

This clause is the creed's centre, and it is the Book's standard formula for the relation between the missions. The distinction it forbids is not the recognition of differences in the laws given to different peoples, which the Book acknowledges elsewhere; it is the acceptance of some messengers and the rejection of others.

The same formula appears in the sūrah of the Cow's nearly identical verse and in the passage where the believers are described as accepting God, His angels, His books, and His messengers without distinction. The Book also states the reverse case with equal clarity, describing those who believe in some messengers and disbelieve in others as desiring a compromise that cannot be made. A community that accepts the whole line of prophets has abandoned the option of treating revelation as a set of competing properties, and that is precisely what the sūrah has been pressing toward through its arguments about Abraham and the People of the Book.

**Submission as the Closing Clause**

The sentence ends not with a claim about prophets but with a statement about the speakers: to Him we submit. The confession therefore closes on the same word the sūrah has used repeatedly for the response God requires, and it places the community's own position in the same category as the messengers it has just named.

The arrangement keeps the creed from becoming a list of honoured names. The prophets are named, and then those who name them describe themselves with the word that describes a prophet's own stance before God, which is what prevents the veneration of persons the earlier verses warned against. A community that recites this verse has put itself and the prophets of God in the same position of submission, and the sūrah's statement about worship follows from the grammar of the sentence.

**The Verse as an Answer to the Passage Before It**

The confession arrives after the discussion of the covenant with the prophets, the community that turns back from it, and the submission of everything in creation. Each of those themes appears in the verse: the prophets whose covenant it honours, the refusal of partial acceptance that the covenant bound them to, and the submission that the previous verse described as universal.

The Book's practice of placing a creed after an argument is visible throughout the sūrah, and it serves a purpose that the reader can use. A controversy conducted with an opponent leaves the community holding a set of positions; a creed leaves it holding a statement it can recite, and this one is constructed so that reciting it is itself an answer to the disputes that prompted it. The verses that follow it state the consequences of seeking another way and of abandoning a faith once accepted, and the two statements belong to the same creed: what the community holds is not a private preference among options but the acceptance of what God has sent through all of His messengers.

---
## Sūrah Āli ʿImrān 3:85

> Whoever seeks a way other than Islam, it will never be accepted from them, and in the Hereafter they will be among the losers.

**Expanded Commentary**

**A Statement About the Accepted Way**

The verse declares that whoever seeks a way other than Islam will not have it accepted from him. The word rendered Islam is the same term the sūrah has used since early in its argument, and its meaning in the Book is submission to God rather than membership in a community.

That distinction is not a modern accommodation, and the sūrah itself supplies the evidence for it. The word's participle is applied in the Book to Abraham and Jacob in their advice to their children, to the disciples of Jesus in their answer to him, and to the community that receives this revelation. What the verse is stating, then, is the acceptance of a stance rather than the registration of a name, and the sūrah's earlier treatment of the same word prepares the reader to hear it that way.

**The Wider Sense and the Narrower**

Commentators differed about the verse's scope, and the positions they took are worth setting out. One reading holds that after the coming of the Prophet of this sūrah no religion other than the one he brought will be accepted by God, and this reading is applied by the same authorities to other verses that make the point. A wider reading, emphasised by many classical authorities across the centuries, takes the verse's word to mean submission to God, a state that describes those who conformed to His will in every community that received a messenger.

Both readings rest on the same sentence, and the second has the support of the Book's own usage of the term. What the sūrah does not do is restrict the sentence to the name of a later community at the expense of everything it has said about Abraham, Ishmael, and the disciples, all of whom are described in the Book with the word this verse uses. The reader is best served by holding the two readings together: the way God accepts has always been submission, and it has been given its most complete and final statement in this revelation.

**Where the "In the Hereafter" Is Placed**

The verse ends by saying that the person who seeks another way will be among the losers in the Hereafter, which locates the outcome of the choice after death.

The Book places this theme at the end of several of its arguments with the communities of the Book, and the reason has to do with the nature of the dispute. The parties who disagreed about Abraham and Jesus were not disputing material advantages, at least not only those; the disagreement concerned what would be accepted from them at the end. The verse states the criterion and states the sphere in which it operates, and it leaves the world in which the argument is being conducted as it is. Nothing in the sentence tells the community to enforce the criterion, and nothing in it describes a punishment in this life. It speaks about the accounting that the whole sūrah has been describing since its opening verses.

**The Question of Other Communities**

The verse has been read by some as a denial that any religion other than the one revealed through the final Prophet can be accepted, and that reading has a long history in the tradition. The difficulty it raises, which the classical commentators noted, is that the same Book describes figures from earlier communities with the vocabulary of submission and promises them rewards.

The resolution offered by the commentators who favour the wider reading turns on the sequence of revelation rather than on the standing of the communities. What a community is answerable for depends on what it has received, and the Book makes the point in a verse about the earlier communities when it refers to those who were given a portion of the scripture before this message arrived. The verse above states the rule for the person who has heard what has come and looked for another way; it does not adjudicate the case of anyone who never encountered the question, and the Book's treatment of such people belongs to other passages.

**The Word "Seeks" and Its Implication**

The verb describes a deliberate search, not an unfortunate circumstance of birth or an inherited position. The verse concerns a person who has the option of the way God accepts and goes looking for a substitute.

That is a narrow class, and the narrowness is the point. The Book's arguments in this sūrah have been directed at people who had the message in front of them, argued about the messengers of God, and then turned away from the covenant they had accepted. The verse states the outcome for exactly that conduct, and it does so in the vocabulary of a person making a choice rather than of a person born into the wrong community. Reading it as a verdict on the world's population requires the verb to mean something its sense does not carry, and the surrounding verses continue to address the communities in front of the Prophet as parties who may still respond.

**A Criterion That Has Been Used Against Its Readers**

The verse has a further function in the sūrah's own argument, which is to answer the confidence of communities who took their standing for granted. The people addressed in this passage had a revelation, a history, and a position in the world; the sentence tells them that what will be accepted is not their standing but their submission.

Readers of the verse through the centuries have applied it in the opposite direction, which is a measure of how easily a criterion becomes a possession. The sūrah's own use of the sentence is a warning to anyone who treats the accepted way as a badge rather than as a practice, and the following verses describe what the Book says about those who leave the submission they had accepted.

**How the Verse Stands With Its Neighbours**

The verse sits between a creed that names every prophet without distinction and a passage about people who believed and then turned back. Its position states the relation between the two.

Belief in the whole line of messengers is the content of the submission; the abandonment of that belief is the seeking of another way. The verses that follow pursue the second case in detail and end with a provision for repentance, and the reader is meant to see them as part of one argument rather than as disconnected verdicts on different communities. What the sūrah provides at this point is the standard, and the next lines describe what happens to those who had met it and then left.

---
## Sūrah Āli ʿImrān 3:86

> How will Allah guide a people who chose to disbelieve after they had believed, acknowledged the Messenger to be true, and received clear proofs? For Allah does not guide the wrongdoing people.

**Expanded Commentary**

**A Question About Guidance**

The verse asks how God could guide a people who chose disbelief after believing, acknowledged the messenger as truthful, and received clear proofs. The question is rhetorical in form and precise in content: it names the three things the people had, and their presence is what makes the question unanswerable.

The Book's habitual way of explaining the loss of guidance is visible here. Guidance is not described as something withheld arbitrarily from a person who wanted it; it is described as withdrawn from a course that has been abandoned in the presence of evidence. The three clauses are the evidence, and their sequence moves from the community's initial faith, through its acknowledgement of the message's truthfulness, to the proofs it received. Each step raises the level of responsibility, and the question arrives after the third.

**What the Three Clauses Establish**

The first clause places the community's starting point: they had believed. The second reports an acknowledgement that the messenger was true, which the commentators noted is a conscious act rather than a verbal formula. The third names the proofs, which the Book uses for the signs and evidences that accompanied the message.

Together the three describe a situation in which nothing was lacking except the will to continue. A person who has believed, admitted the truth of the messenger, and seen the proofs has no unanswered question left, and the verse's picture of the refusal is of a decision made with every available means of verification already held. The Book's arguments about the earlier communities follow the same pattern: the accusation is never a shortage of information.

**Who Is Being Described**

The commentators offered two main identifications for the people in view. Some took them as apostates who left the community after having accepted the message, and they connected the verse with a report about a group that departed for Makkah and later returned. Others took the passage as continuing the sūrah's address to the People of the Book, who had received revelations and had then refused the message that confirmed them.

The two readings share the elements the verse names. In both cases the people had believed — the People of the Book had believed in the revelation they received — and in both cases the refusal arrived after knowledge. The Book's terminology here is drawn from its own account of the covenant, and the verses that follow state a consequence in the language of the Day of Judgment, which suits either identification. What matters for the reader is that the verse excludes the sympathetic explanation of ignorance and leaves the refusal standing as a choice.

**Why Guidance Is Related to Conduct**

The sentence says that God does not guide a wrongdoing people, and the clause is the Book's standard way of expressing the connection between a person's conduct and his access to guidance.

The connection runs in both directions in the Book's account, and the sūrah has already stated it in the negative: those who persistently deviated had their hearts caused to deviate, as the Book says of the people of Moses (61:5). The Book's language of guidance describes a process rather than a verdict, and its warnings are addressed to people who still have the ability to turn. What the verse above states is what happens when the turning is unrepented: the guidance that was available is not offered again in the same way, and the condition the verse describes is that of people who have used the means of knowledge to settle their decision.

**The Closing Description**

The verse ends by naming the people wrongdoers, which is the description the Book attaches to conduct that damages both the actor and others. The word is not a synonym for the disbeliever as such; the Book applies it to those whose acts are a wrong done against the truth they have received.

The choice of description fits the passage's argument about the covenant. A person who has accepted an obligation and then set it aside has not merely failed to reach a conclusion; he has acted against something due. The passage will go on to describe the penalty in terms of cursing and lasting punishment, and the reader who has followed the sequence is meant to see the severity as a proportionate response to a wrong that was committed with knowledge and in the presence of proof.

**The Door the Next Verses Leave Open**

The verses that follow state the punishment of the people described, and then the passage provides for those who repent and mend their ways, with a declaration of forgiveness and mercy. The provision is stated in a single sentence and it comes after the severity, which is the Book's usual arrangement.

That arrangement is what keeps the verse above from being a verdict on any person alive. The Book's descriptions of what happens to those who turn away are written to be read by people who have not yet turned away, and the sūrah's own passage will show that the door stays open for anyone who returns. The severity and the offer belong to the same paragraph, and the reader who takes one without the other has misread the passage.

**The Question Form and Its Work**

The verse asks how God could guide such a people, and the form invites the reader to supply the answer himself. The Book uses this method at points where a proposition is so evident to its audience that stating it would be redundant.

What the reader supplies is a conclusion about the connection between knowledge and responsibility. A community that has believed, acknowledged, and seen the proofs is not in a position to plead that it lacked the means of knowing; what it lacks is the willingness to stay. The following verses describe the outcome, and the reader who reaches them has already made the inference the question was designed to produce.

---
## Sūrah Āli ʿImrān 3:87

> Their reward is that they will be condemned by Allah, the angels, and all of humanity.

**Expanded Commentary**

**A Reward That Is a Curse**

The verse states the compensation for the conduct described in the previous lines, and it uses the vocabulary of cursing. The condemned are cursed by God, by the angels, and by all of humanity, and the sentence names the three parties in ascending order of generality.

The Book's language of cursing describes being driven away and removed from mercy rather than the utterance of an insult. The same triple formula appears in the sūrah of the Cow, where the condemned condition of those who disbelieve and die in that state is stated in identical terms. The repetition across sūrahs is a sign that the Book treats the formula as a fixed description of the final condition of a person who has been cut off from mercy, rather than as an expression of anger that varies with circumstance.

**Why Three Parties Are Named**

Naming God, the angels, and humanity as the sources of the curse gives the sentence its scope. The condemnation is not the reaction of one community to another's offence; it comes from the order of things, and the three named parties correspond roughly to the hierarchy the sūrah laid out in its account of the witnesses to God's unity.

The Book uses the same three-tiered structure when it describes the curse attaching to the person who dies in rejection, and it uses a related one when it describes the truth being witnessed by God, the angels, and the people of knowledge. The verse above turns that structure around. What is being described is the whole of creation withdrawing its regard from a person whose conduct has placed him outside the mercy that everything else participates in, and the universality of the statement is the point of the list.

**The Curse in the Book's Wider Usage**

The Book reports curses in several contexts, and its usage clarifies what the term means. Communities that enter the Fire curse one another, and the followers among them blame their leaders; the people of Abraham's community are told that they will disown and curse one another on the Day of Judgment; and the Book describes the curse that rests upon those who conceal the revelations they have been given.

The element common to these passages is a relation that has been severed. Being cursed is being cut off, and the Book's descriptions of the severed relation always include the parties who would otherwise have been connected: allies who blame one another, communities that curse their own predecessors, and those who held a revelation and were cut off from its benefit. The verse above describes the fullest form of that severance, since the parties named on the other side of the cut are God, the angels, and the whole of humanity.

**The Universality of the Statement**

The phrase about all of humanity is the part of the sentence that requires care, since it would make no sense if it meant that every human being individually pronounces a malediction on the person described.

The Book uses this kind of totalizing phrase for the settled judgment of a community, and the commentators explained the verse in terms of what human beings will recognise on the Day of Judgment. The picture is of a verdict that everyone present concurs in, because at that point the truth about what happened is available to all and no interest distorts it. The Book's account of the final gathering repeatedly presents unanimity about facts where unanimity about conduct had been impossible, and this verse's description of universal cursing belongs to that picture.

**What the Verse Achieves in the Passage**

The passage began with a question about how a people who had believed, acknowledged the message, and seen the proofs could be guided after they turned away. This verse states the consequence, and the next verses state that it is permanent and unrelieved.

The Book's arrangement places the cursing before the description of the punishment, which is the reverse of chronology. What the reader receives first is the severance of every relation, and what he receives second is what that severance looks like in the Hereafter. The order keeps the reader's attention on what has been lost rather than on the mechanics of the penalty, and it matches the sūrah's habit of describing the inner reality of a condition before it describes its outward form.

**A Warning That Applies to Whoever Reads**

The formula is stated in absolute terms, and the Book states it in this absolute form at the close of a discussion about a community that possessed a revelation and left it. The reader who recites the verse is included in the process by which the judgment becomes known.

That is the function of such passages in a book that its own community recites. The verses do not describe a class of people foreign to the reader's world; they describe a conduct he is capable of, and the severity of the description is part of what makes the conduct unlikely. The sūrah does not end the passage here, and what follows it, after a statement of the permanence of the condition, is a provision for those who return.

**The Phrase 'A Reward' and the Irony It Carries**

The sentence calls the curse a recompense, using the ordinary word for the return a person receives for his work. The choice is ironic and precise: what is being described is not an arbitrary infliction but the settled outcome of a course of conduct, and the Book insists on describing it as earned.

The same word is used throughout the sūrah for the reward of the believers, and the parallel is deliberate. Both parties are described as receiving what their conduct produced, and the difference lies in what was done rather than in how the accounting was carried out. The reader who has followed the passage from the covenant to this point has been shown the whole sequence — the acceptance, the turning back, the removal of guidance, and now the compensation — and the final word chosen for the outcome is the one that closes the account rather than opening a new charge.

**What the Curse Means**

The condemnation described in this sentence was explained by the commentators as distance from God and removal from His mercy rather than as an act of verbal abuse. The same joint condemnation by God, the angels, and humanity is discussed in the sūrah of the Cow, where the state of those who die in rejection is described in the same terms (2:161). The verse before the reader therefore repeats a formula the Book uses for a condition rather than for an event, and the company of the condemning parties shows how complete the separation is: the created order itself is described as participating in the verdict.

**The Voices of the Hereafter**

The Book describes the people of the Hereafter speaking to one another in ways that belong to this theme. Communities entering the fire are said to curse their sister communities as each arrives (7:38), and those who had followed false leaders are told that on the Day of Resurrection they will disown one another and curse one another (29:25). The sentence before the reader names the outcome without the scene, and the passages that supply the scene show what the curse looks like when it is spoken aloud. The community that recites the verse is being told that a condition entered in secret in this life becomes public speech in the next.

---
## Sūrah Āli ʿImrān 3:88

> They will be in Hell forever. Their punishment will not be lightened, nor will they be delayed ˹from it˺.

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Condition Described as Lasting**

The verse states two things about the people whose conduct the passage has been tracing: their condition will last, and the punishment will neither be eased nor postponed. The two clauses cover duration and intensity, and together they remove the two hopes that a person naturally entertains about a penalty.

The Book's descriptions of the Hereafter often pair a duration with a detail about the experience within it, and the pairing here is unusually bare. Nothing is said about the nature of the punishment, and nothing is said about a possible change in the arrangement. What the reader is given is a sentence about what will not happen: no lightening, no delay. The negative form is the Book's way of stating finality without describing the machinery.

**Duration and the Question It Raises**

The Book uses the language of permanence for the punishment of those who die in rejection, and this verse belongs to that group of statements. A reader who has followed the passage closely will notice that the persons described here are people who had believed and then turned away, and the severity of an unending condition is correspondingly greater.

The sūrah does not leave the difficulty unaddressed, and the verses after this one supply a provision for those who return in this life. What the passage as a whole does is to distinguish between the person whose turning away is final, because his life has ended in that state, and the person whose turning away is a stage he may still leave. The verse above describes the first case, and its absoluteness is what makes the offer that follows it meaningful rather than decorative.

**"Their Punishment Will Not Be Lightened"**

The clause rules out the hope of a sentence that gradually becomes bearable, and the Book states the same negation for the final condition of the rejecters in other passages. Some traditions describe degrees within the punishment and intervals in its intensity, and the Book itself speaks of a Day whose length varies and of punishments that are described in a range of images.

The specific clause in this verse concerns the people whose earlier history included faith and knowledge, and its function is to close off the expectation of relief. A person who expects that a severe penalty will eventually become lighter has a reason to postpone his repentance; the Book removes that reason for the case it is describing, and it does so in the flat language of a statement rather than the ornate language of a scene. What the reader is being told is not how the punishment will feel but that its terms will not be renegotiated.

**"Nor Will They Be Delayed"**

The second negation concerns time, and it removes the other common expectation. A person might accept that a penalty awaits him and still hope that it can be postponed, that some intercession, excuse, or interval might put off the moment.

The Book is consistent in denying this across the descriptions of the Day. It states that no soul can be of help to another, that no ransom will be accepted, and that intercessors will not be heard in the cases it describes. The verse above gives the same denial in two words. The effect is to make the accounting instantaneous in a certain sense: the person arrives and the matter is settled, with no interval between the arrival and the consequence. The Book offers no schedule for the Day, and this verse tells the reader that the arrangements he may imagine for deferring its outcome do not exist.

**Why the Verse Is Placed Here**

The placement of the verse follows the pattern of the Book's treatments of final rejection, where a description of the settled condition is stated before the offer of a way out. The sūrah states the permanence first, and the provision for repentance comes after it.

That order makes the offer of return the reader's destination rather than an interruption. A person reading through the passage meets the sentence about what cannot be lightened, and then the verse that begins with those who change course and mend what they spoiled. The sequence is not a contradiction but a description of two different moments in a life, and the Book's readers are being shown which of the two they are in a position to choose. What the sūrah has done throughout this passage is to state the truth about both outcomes and leave the reader facing the choice, and this verse is the last statement of the first outcome before the door is described.

**A Statement That Stops Rather Than Argues**

The verse contains no argument and no appeal. It does not urge the reader to avoid the condition it describes, and it does not explain why the condition is just. It states what will be and stops.

The Book uses this form where it has already made the case, and the passage has made it at length. The reader has been shown a covenant accepted in the presence of witnesses, a community that turned away after believing and after acknowledging the truth of the messenger, and the guidance that could no longer reach them as before. What remains for the Book to say is what the outcome looks like, and a description of the outcome stated without commentary is what the verse provides. The following verses then describe what happens to those who return.

**The Last Word of the Sentence**

The two negations at the end of the verse leave the reader with nothing to negotiate. This is the Book's characteristic closing move in passages about the final state of the rejecters, and its effect is to concentrate attention on the one variable that remains, which is the conduct of a person still alive.

The verse is the last of the passage's statements about the consequences of abandonment, and the sentences that come after it turn to the offer that the Book makes to everyone in that position. Nothing in the sūrah's treatment suggests that the door remains open after death; what the verse suppresses is any hope within the framework it describes. What the reader takes away is a clear picture of the seriousness of the matter, and the sūrah then supplies the remedy.

---
## Sūrah Āli ʿImrān 3:89

> As for those who repent afterwards and mend their ways, then surely Allah is All-Forgiving, Most Merciful.

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Exception That Interrupts the Passage**

The verse opens with a single word that turns the preceding sentences around. After the description of an unrelieved condition and a punishment that is neither lightened nor delayed, the Book admits an exception, and the exception covers those who repent and make amends.

The interruption is deliberately abrupt. The reader has just been told what cannot be changed, and the next sentence begins with the word for exclusion, so that the severity of the previous verses is measured by the narrowness of the door that opens here. The Book's arrangement is characteristic: it states the rule for those who persist and then states the provision for those who turn. Neither cancels the other, and the two statements are meant to be read together.

**Repentance and Making Amends**

Two conditions are named, and the second is what distinguishes this verse's description from a mere expression of regret. Repentance describes the return; making amends describes the repair of what the return left behind, whether in belief, in conduct, or in the relations a person had cut.

The Book pairs the two terms in several places where it describes the acceptance of those who had gone far astray, and it never leaves the second element out. A person who returns to a position he had abandoned owes something for the damage caused while he was away, and the Book's language treats the repair as part of the return rather than as an optional extra. The verse above does not specify what the amendment consists of, which is appropriate for a sentence that has to cover different kinds of harm; what it does is to name the two things that must be present and stop.

**The Two Names of God at the End**

The verse closes with the declaration that God is Forgiving and Merciful, and the pairing of the two names recurs throughout the Book at the end of sentences about the acceptance of the repentant.

The first name describes the covering and removal of the offence, and the second describes the kindness that accompanies it. The order matters: forgiveness is stated before mercy, so that the reader does not conclude that the return is accepted grudgingly or that its acceptance depends on the person's own adequacy. The Book attaches this pair to statements about the most serious offences it describes, including the offences the previous verses of this passage have just detailed, and its placement here makes the offer apply to exactly the people whose conduct has been described at length.

**The Report the Commentators Attached to the Verse**

The classical commentaries connect this verse with a Companion who had left the community and then wrote to his family asking whether a return was still possible, and they report that the verse was revealed in answer.

[UNVERIFIED: the letter of the Companion who left the community and the occasion of revelation reported for 3:89 in the classical commentaries, whose chains of transmission I have not examined.]

The report, whatever its status, describes the situation the verse is addressed to: a person who knows he has done something serious and wants to know whether the door is shut. The Book's answer is the sentence above, and the answer's form is itself instructive. It does not ask how far the person has gone, and it does not weigh the seriousness of the departure. It names the two conditions and the two divine names and leaves the matter there.

**Why the Exception Comes Here and Not Earlier**

The placement of the exception after the verse about the permanence of the punishment is not careless. Placing it before would have softened the warning while the reader was still reading it; placing it after shows the warning in its full weight and then shows the way out.

The Book uses this order at the points where it wants a reader to feel both the seriousness of the matter and the availability of the remedy. A person who has been told that the condition lasts and that its terms will not be revised has a reason to consider his situation, and the immediate offer supplies the direction to move in. The passage is not an invitation to speculate about the fate of the community described in the previous verses; it shows that the same door stands open to everyone still in a position to walk through it.

**What the Verse Does Not Do**

The sentence does not describe how long the repentant person must wait, what penalty he owes, or what the community's response to him should be. It states God's acceptance of the return and leaves the practical arrangements to other parts of the Book.

The Book deals with the repair of the relations a person has broken in its legal passages and in its instruction about reconciling people with one another, and this verse does not pre-empt those. What it establishes is the underlying fact on which they all rest: the return is accepted, and the amendment is part of it. The verses that follow describe a different case, that of the person who does not return but goes further in the direction he has chosen.

**The Word for Returning and What It Carries**

The Book's term for repentance describes a turning back, and it is the same root the sūrah has used for the reversal of a course in its earlier verses. The vocabulary keeps the two movements in a single frame: the person who left a position is described as turning, and the turning is measured against the distance he has travelled.

That is why the verse's two conditions belong together. A return that leaves the consequences of the departure in place is not a return in the Book's sense, and the sentence names the repair as a separate requirement. The pairing appears throughout the Book wherever it describes the acceptance of those who had gone far in the wrong direction, and its consistency is itself part of the answer the verse gives: the terms of the return are known, and they do not change with the size of the person's offence.

---
## Sūrah Āli ʿImrān 3:90

> Indeed, those who disbelieve after having believed then increase in disbelief, their repentance will never be accepted. It is they who are astray.

**Expanded Commentary**

**A Second Case Stated After the First**

The previous verse admitted the repentance of those who turned back and repaired the damage. This verse names a group whose repentance will not be accepted, and the difference between the two cases is stated in terms of what happens after the return.

These are people who disbelieved after having believed and then increased in their disbelief. The verse's picture is of a movement with a direction: the departure is not a single act that is then reconsidered but a course that continues. The Book states the refusal of their return in direct terms, and the sentence ends by naming them as the ones who are astray.

**"Then Increase in Disbelief"**

The clause describes an intensification rather than a repetition, and commentators explored what the increase consists of. Some explained it as persistence in the state without any return, others as the accumulation of acts that follow from the initial departure, and others as moving from a private refusal to public hostility against the message and its community.

The sūrah's earlier verses make the third reading natural, since the people described in the passage had been arguing, circulating objections, and turning others away from the way. The verse reads as the completion of that conduct: the departure has stopped being a person's own business and has become a campaign. What follows from the description is that the person is not merely in a condition he might leave; he is engaged in making the condition permanent, which is why the sentence treats the refusal of his return as the description of a settled state rather than as a rejection of an enquiry.

**When the Return Is Not Accepted**

The commentators offered a range of explanations for the statement that their repentance will not be accepted. One holds that the sentence refers to the repentance offered at the moment of death, when the Book says elsewhere that no one's return is accepted after the matter has become clear beyond the possibility of choice. Another holds that the return of such a person would not be sincere, since he has already known the truth and turned from it deliberately, and that the sentence describes what he is rather than what God does with him. A third holds that a person who returns and then leaves again has nullified the earlier return, and that the verse describes a state from which the earlier act has been emptied of its effect.

The readings are not mutually exclusive, and each is grounded in the sentence's grammar. What they agree on is that the verse does not describe a person who wants to come back and is refused for no reason. It describes the completion of a determined course, and the Book's treatment of that case is stated in the language of finality.

**The People of the Book and the Muslim Apostates**

Commentators noted that the verse's context suggests the community of this revelation, but that the description also fits the communities of the earlier scriptures who believed in the message they received and then refused the messenger who confirmed it.

The two applications converge on the same conduct. In both cases a person has held a revelation, has known its truth, and has moved from acceptance to a deepening refusal. The sūrah has been addressing exactly this possibility since its early verses, and it addresses it in the plural, as a description of groups rather than of individuals. The passage's warnings are therefore addressed to communities that carry a message, and the community now receiving the sūrah is included among them rather than exempted.

**The Ending That Names Them Astray**

The verse ends by saying that they are the ones who are astray, and the word describes a person who has left a road and does not know how to return to it.

The Book uses the language of straying for the condition in which a person wanders without a route, and it contrasts it with the guidance that consists of knowing where to go. The description is placed at the end of the verse as a summary of everything that preceded it: a person who believed, left, went further from the road, and now cannot find it. What the verse adds to the previous ones is the element of disorientation, which is expressed in the Book's own terms as the loss of the road rather than the loss of the way.

**What the Reader Is to Take From the Sequence**

The passage has now run through the departure, its consequences, the exception for those who return, and the case of those who do not. Each statement has been about a different kind of person rather than about a different verdict on the same person.

That distinction is what keeps the passage coherent. The Book's sentences about the refusal of repentance are not a rule that catches everyone who has ever left the community; they describe the end of a trajectory that the verse itself defines by the word increase. A reader who notices the definition has the key to the whole passage, and the verse that follows adds another dimension by describing what such a person would still be unable to give.

**Why the Sentence Is Addressed in the Plural**

The verse speaks about a group rather than an individual, and the plural is not incidental. The Book's descriptions of the deepening of disbelief are written for communities, since the conduct it describes — arguing against a message, drawing others away from it, and continuing in that work — is a collective activity before it is a personal one.

The same feature appears in the earlier parts of the passage. The people described had received proofs together, discussed the messenger together, and turned away together, so that the warning reaches them as a body. A person reading the verse on his own is therefore not being told that his private doubts have placed him in the category the verse names. What the sentence describes is a public course of action pursued with knowledge, and the severity of the outcome stated in the next verse corresponds to the scale of the undertaking described here.

---
## Sūrah Āli ʿImrān 3:91

> Indeed, if each of those who disbelieve then die as disbelievers were to offer a ransom of enough gold to fill the whole world, it would never be accepted from them. It is they who will suffer a painful punishment, and they will have no helpers.

**Expanded Commentary**

**A Ransom the Size of the World**

The verse describes people who disbelieve and die in that state, and it states that if one of them were to offer, as a ransom, gold enough to fill the whole earth, it would not be accepted from him. The image is built to be impossible, and its function is to state the finality of the matter in terms the reader can picture.

The Book uses ransom language at several points in its descriptions of the Day, and each time it denies the transaction. The sūrah of the Cow states that no ransom will be accepted from those who disbelieve, and the same denial recurs in the accounts of the last gathering. What this verse adds is the measure of the offer: not a sum beyond the reach of most people but a quantity that would suffice to fill the world, which removes the possibility of imagining an amount that would be enough.

**Why the Ransom Cannot Work**

The refusal is not a matter of the price being too low. The Book's account of the final accounting has no mechanism by which a person's standing before God is transferred or purchased, because the relation that would make a purchase meaningful has already lapsed.

The verse's own wording makes the point: those it describes are people who disbelieved and remained in that condition until death. By then the subject of the transaction is gone. The Book's language about the Hereafter consistently places the accounting of a person's life in the life itself, and the descriptions of the Day are accounts of what has already been determined rather than negotiations. The image of the world's gold serves not to set a maximum price but to close the discussion about whether a price exists.

**Dying in the Condition**

The sentence specifies death in the state of disbelief, and the specification limits the verse's scope. The passage has just stated the acceptance of those who repent and make amends, and it stated the case of those who went further in the refusal.

What this verse describes is the third case, which is the end of the trajectory. The Book attaches its statements of final severity to the condition in which a person dies rather than to acts considered in isolation, which is why these verses sit so naturally after the offer of the previous lines. The point of naming the death is to fix the moment at which the offer of return is no longer pending, and the Book's readers are reminded that the moment is not under their control.

**The Painful Punishment and the Absence of Helpers**

The verse ends with two statements: those described will receive a painful punishment, and they will have no helpers. The second statement is the one that deepens the isolation the passage has been building since the cursing was described.

The Book's accounts of the Day repeatedly strip away the supports a person might rely on. Near kindred are named as unable to help, intercession is denied for the cases described, and the entreaties of the condemned are reported as unanswered. The verse above puts the matter in its shortest form: no helpers. From the refusal of a ransom the sentence moves to the absence of anyone who might assist, and the movement is from the resources a person owns to the relationships he has, which are the two things people count on when they imagine their own future.

**The Progression Across the Three Verses**

Read together, the last three verses describe three conditions, and their order is instructive. The first offers acceptance to those who return; the second states that no return is accepted from those who believed, left, and went further; the third describes those who die in the condition.

Each verse mentions something to be offered — repentance, a return, a ransom of gold — and the sequence shows what happens to the offer at each stage. The Book's arrangement is designed for a reader who is still alive, and its logic is the logic of time rather than of rank: what is available now will not be available later, and the verses are placed so that the reader encounters the last one while the first still applies to him.

**What the Book Does Not Say About the Fire**

The verse states that the punishment is painful, and it does not elaborate. The Book's treatments of the final condition vary in detail from passages that describe scenes to passages such as this, which state a fact and stop.

The restraint has a purpose in a passage about an argument with communities who claimed religious standing. An elaborate description would invite the reader to think about the mechanics of the penalty; a single clause about pain and a sentence about the absence of help direct his attention to the seriousness of the state itself. The sūrah turns immediately after this verse to a completely different subject, and the transition is part of the same design: the discussion of the Hereafter has reached its term, and the reader is returned to the world of his conduct.

**The Transition That Follows**

The next verse speaks about the spending of what a person holds dear as the road to righteousness, and the change of subject is the Book's usual way of moving from warning to instruction.

The two halves of the sūrah's method are here in sequence. A passage about the consequences of refusal ends, and a passage about the practice of the believers begins, so that the reader is not left with a warning unaccompanied by a command. What the Book's readers take from the three verses about the Hereafter is a reason to act; what the following passage gives them is what to do.

---
## Sūrah Āli ʿImrān 3:92

> You will never achieve righteousness until you donate some of what you cherish. And whatever you give is certainly well known to Allah.

**Expanded Commentary**

**A Condition Attached to Righteousness**

The verse states that righteousness will not be attained until a person gives away something he values, and it closes by saying that whatever is given, God knows it. The sentence pairs an unqualified demand with an assurance, and the two halves answer the two questions a person asks about charity: how much, and who is watching.

The Book's word here is broader than the English rendering suggests.
