The verse before the reader takes the same material and turns it into a warning for a community that had just been given its own proofs, so that the historical example becomes a mirror rather than a stranger's story.

**Division as a Category in the Book**

The theme recurs in the Book with a fixed vocabulary. One passage states that those who divided their faith and split into sects have nothing to do with the Prophet, and that their affair rests with God, who will inform them of what they did (6:159). Another describes the same people, with each group rejoicing in what it happens to hold (30:32).

Alongside those descriptions stands the command: the Book's charge to uphold the faith and make no divisions in it was given to Noah, Abraham, Moses, and Jesus (42:13). The Book therefore treats unity as a requirement of the religion itself and division as a departure from it, and the passage in this sūrah belongs to that treatment rather than to a general preference for agreement.

**A Warning for the Believers Themselves**

The verse is addressed to the believers, and its position is significant. It follows a reminder of the community's own rescue from enmity and the command to hold together, and it precedes a description of what awaits those who took the other path.

The warning is thus not aimed only at the communities of the past. The believers are being told that the same thing could happen among them, and the Book records the prediction elsewhere in plain terms, saying that the community would divide in the way earlier peoples had. What the verse establishes is the standard by which such a development is to be judged, and it removes any sense that the divisions of a religious community are a neutral feature of its history.

**The Punishment Described as Severe**

The verse closes with the statement that a severe punishment is what awaits those described, and the Book attaches that description to its gravest warnings. The word used for the punishment is the one the sūrah has already used for a reward of a different kind, and the pairing shows what is being weighed.

The punishment is stated without detail, which is the Book's practice at the close of such warnings. What the reader receives is the plain fact that the matter is not small, and the sentence leaves him with the choice the passage has been building toward: a community can hold to what it has been given, or it can reproduce the history it has just been shown. The verses that follow describe the outcome of both courses on the Day when the consequences are shown openly.

**Two Verbs: Splitting and Differing**

The verse uses two words for one development, and they describe different aspects of it. The first names the act of separating, of a body becoming parts; the second names the disagreement that follows and fills the distance between them.

The order matters for how the prohibition works. The Book does not condemn disagreement as such in this sentence; it condemns the breaking apart that makes disagreement into division, and it attaches the warning to the people who produced it. Its standard is the community that keeps its argument inside a shared ground, and the historical example it has just given is of people who stopped sharing one. The distinction is worth keeping, because it explains why the Book can command the community both to refuse the division and to correct one another, and why the presence of different views within a single body is not what the sentence describes.

---
## Sūrah Āli ʿImrān 3:106

> On that Day some faces will be bright while others gloomy. To the gloomy-faced it will be said, “Did you disbelieve after having believed? So taste the punishment for your disbelief.”

**Expanded Commentary**

**A Day That Shows on the Face**

The verse describes the Day of Judgment as the day when some faces become bright and others dark, and it reports what is said to the second group. The image is drawn from everyday experience, where the face carries news of the inner state before any word is spoken.

Arabic uses the darkening of the face for shame, distress, and suppressed anger, and the Book employs the idiom in this world before it applies it to the next. One passage describes a man whose face grows gloomy when he is given news of the daughter he attributes to God, and who suppresses his rage as he does so (43:17). The verse before the reader transfers that familiar reaction to the day when nothing is concealed.

**The Faces That Brighten**

The bright face is the Book's image for joy, relief, and approval, and the spiritual sense the commentators added is that the light on those faces is the light of faith made visible. The Book describes one group of people as receiving the finest reward and even more, and explains that neither gloom nor disgrace will cover their faces (10:26).

The quiet detail in that passage is the two negations. The reward is positive, and the description of what the faces will not carry is what makes the joy concrete, since it names the two things a person dreads most in public: sadness and humiliation. The verse before the reader divides humanity into these two conditions and gives no third category, which is the Book's usual way of describing the final state.

**The Faces That Darken**

The dark face belongs to the people the Book elsewhere describes as liars against God. One passage states that on the Day of Judgment those who lied about God will be seen with their faces gloomy, and then asks whether the Fire is not a fitting home for the arrogant (39:60).

The connection between the face and the accusation is exact. What the dark faces display is the truth that those who lied had denied for a lifetime, and the Book's language of darkening describes the moment when the denial is no longer available. The verse before the reader does not describe the mechanism; it reports the condition, and the sentence that follows supplies the words addressed to the people in it.

**The Implied Words in the Sentence**

The clause about what is said to the dark-faced has no introductory verb in the text, and the commentators supplied it. On their reading, the sentence means that it will be said to them, and the implied words stand before the question that follows.

The grammatical point is small and has an effect on how the verse is heard. What the people receive is not a punishment imposed without explanation but a question, and the question itself is the first part of what they face. The Book's final scenes repeatedly include this element of address: the condemned are spoken to, their conduct is named before them, and the sentence follows. The verse's structure matches that pattern, and it explains why the question comes before the command to taste the punishment.

**"Did You Disbelieve After Having Believed?"**

The question is put to people who had once accepted the message, and the commentators identified them in several ways. The most natural identification, on the sūrah's own argument, is the people the previous verses described as having been warned about being drawn away from their belief, since the warning and the outcome belong to the same passage.

Others read the verse as addressed to those who broke the primordial acknowledgement of God's lordship, the moment the Book describes when humanity testified that God is its Lord (7:172). A further reading applies it to hypocrites, whose attestation of faith was contradicted by their actions. The three readings converge on the phrase the verse uses, which names faith as something the people had and then lost.

**The Punishment Named After the Offence**

The words spoken to the dark-faced tell them to taste the punishment for their disbelief, and the Book's use of the language of tasting describes direct, personal experience of a thing rather than knowledge of it.

The pairing of punishment with the offence is the Book's consistent practice, and the placement of the phrase here gives the passage its logic. The sūrah has described a community that believed and then turned, warned against following those who work to draw others away, and commanded the believers to hold together. The verse shows the end of one of those courses in a single sentence, and the taste it names belongs to the disbelief rather than to an arbitrary decree.

**Where the Verse Sits in the Passage**

The verse follows the warning against imitating communities that divided after receiving proofs, and it supplies the scene in which the consequence of that conduct is displayed. The commands and the warnings have been given; what remains is the outcome.

The passage's movement is characteristic of the sūrah. It describes a duty, gives the history that illustrates it, names the punishment of those who did the opposite, and then names the reward of those who held to the message. The reader reaches this verse with the previous instructions still in view, and the faces he is shown are the picture of what the instructions were protecting him from.

**The Day and the Book's Habit of Speaking of Faces**

The Book describes human beings in the Hereafter through the condition of their faces more often than through any other part of the body, and the choice is not arbitrary. The face is the one part a person cannot hide and the first thing another person reads.

Passages describe faces that are humbled, faces that are radiant, and faces that are turned down, and each of them conveys a state faster than any list of deeds could. In this verse the device carries the whole contrast between the two groups, so that the reader is shown what the two lives produced rather than being told about it. The verse's next sentence then supplies the one piece of speech in the scene, and the words are addressed to the people whose faces have already answered the question.

**The Sects to Which the Phrase Was Applied**

Al-Qurṭūbī and al-Rāzī recorded that the words about disbelieving after belief were applied by some commentators to the groups that formed within the community's later history, among them the Khawārij, who emerged within a generation of the Prophet's death. The identification extends the sentence beyond the first audience without changing its sense, since the pattern it describes is a departure from a position once held. Ibn Kathīr and al-Qurṭūbī also report that the Prophet was shown something of the Hereafter in which people he knew were driven away from him, and that he was told he did not know what they would do after him. The accounts place the sentence within the warnings the community carried about itself, and the sūrah's own context, which speaks of disbelievers and of a community warned about turning back, supports the same reading.

---
## Sūrah Āli ʿImrān 3:107

> As for the bright-faced, they will be in Allah’s mercy, where they will remain forever.

**Expanded Commentary**

**Mercy Described as a Place**

The verse states that the people with bright faces will be in the mercy of God, and the phrasing treats mercy as an environment rather than as a transaction. What they enter is not a payment but a condition in which they remain.

The Book uses this construction in several places to describe the final state of the blessed. The word for mercy in these passages covers the kindness that surrounds a person and the provision that keeps him, so that the verse does not say simply that God was merciful to them once; it places them inside the mercy and leaves them there. The sūrah's earlier verses already used the same vocabulary, when the well-grounded asked for mercy from God's presence while asking that their hearts be kept, and the two passages belong to one body of language.

**The Address to One Group and the Description of the Other**

The previous verse reports words spoken to the people whose faces are dark, and this verse describes the other group without reporting any words at all. The difference in treatment is the verse's quietest feature.

The condemned receive a question and a command, and their state is described in terms of what they are told. The blessed receive no speech in the text; they are simply said to be in mercy. The Book often withholds the description of the reward's content at the points where it wants the reader to understand that the reward is a state of favour rather than a quantity of goods, and the absence of an address in this verse is one of its effects.

**Permanence in the Book's Descriptions of Reward**

The verse states that the people described will remain where they are, and the formula of permanence recurs throughout the Book's descriptions of Paradise. The same sūrah uses it when it describes the reward of those who do good, who receive forgiveness and gardens with rivers flowing beneath them, staying there forever (3:136).

The Book attaches the same word to the punishment of those who persist in rejection, which is why the pairing in this passage is exact and deliberate. Both outcomes are described as lasting, and the sūrah gives both descriptions in the same sequence, so that the reader meets them together. The two verses before and after the one under discussion are constructed as a matched pair by the text itself.

**The Light on the Face and Its Source**

The brightness of the faces has been read by the commentators as the visible sign of the inner light of faith. That reading explains why the two conditions are described with imagery of light and darkness rather than with a list of pleasures and pains.

If the face displays the state of the heart, then the Day of Judgment is the day when the display becomes accurate, and the difference between the two groups is the difference between what they carried within them. The sūrah has been describing hearts that swerve and hearts that are kept, and this verse shows the end of that distinction in the simplest visual terms available to a human being.

**Who Is Described in the Verse**

The people whose faces brighten are those who end their lives in the condition the passage has been urging, and the commentators connected the verse with the believers the sūrah has been addressing since its opening.

The identification matters for the passage's balance. The two preceding verses named a community that received proofs and then split, and the warning was directed at the believers lest they repeat that conduct. This verse states the outcome for those who do not, and it places them inside the divine mercy without describing the details of their deeds. The passage has already set out what those deeds are, in the command to hold together and the instruction to call others to what is good.

**The Two Outcomes Held Together**

The Book does not divide the two groups across separate chapters or present one without the other. Here they stand in consecutive verses, and the reader is given both in a single passage about the community's own life.

The arrangement is a working part of the sūrah's method. A community being warned about division is shown, on one side, what division produced for those who chose it, and on the other, what awaits the people who hold to what they received. The two verses thus complete the argument the passage has been conducting, and the sentences that follow state the truth of the revelation in which both are described.

**Mercy and the Community's Hope**

The verse has served the community as a statement of what it hopes for, and its wording keeps the hope in the right place. What the blessed possess is not a rank they achieved but a mercy they were placed in.

The sūrah returns to mercy repeatedly, in the prayer of the well-grounded, in the account of those who seek forgiveness after wronging themselves, and in the closing verses that describe God as forgiving and merciful. The recurrence is deliberate: a community told to give God His due and to hold together is not left with the impression that its standing depends on the perfection of its performance. What it is shown, at the end of a passage full of warnings, is a mercy that surrounds those who kept faith.

**Why One Group Is Spoken To and the Other Is Not**

The contrast between the two verses is a contrast in treatment, and it carries a claim about the two conditions. Speech in the Book's judgment scenes is often a form of accounting: the condemned are questioned, reminded, and commanded, and their sentences are pronounced in words.

The blessed meet no accusation, and the text grants them no dialogue. What the verse reports about them is a location rather than a verdict. The difference is the difference between a case being made and a case being closed, and the Book states it in the simplest way available, with one group addressed and the other simply described as being where mercy has placed them.

---
## Sūrah Āli ʿImrān 3:108

> These are Allah’s revelations We recite to you ˹O Prophet˺ in truth. And Allah desires no injustice to ˹His˺ creation.

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Revelations Described as Recited**

The verse states that what has been set out in the preceding passage consists of God's revelations recited in truth, and it adds that God desires no injustice for any of His creation. Both sentences are about the message itself and about the one who sent it.

The formula used here appears elsewhere in the Book in nearly identical words. One passage states that these are God's revelations recited in truth and then tells the Prophet that he is truly one of the messengers (2:252). The pairing of the two statements in that verse shows what the formula does: it identifies the material as revelation and locates the one reciting it within the sequence of those sent by God.

**Truth as a Property of the Recitation**

The truth in the verse is not offered as a claim to be tested later. The passage has presented commands, warnings, historical examples, and the descriptions of two outcomes, and the sentence declares the whole of it to be true.

The Book makes this kind of declaration at the close of passages that have answered objections at length, and the effect is to place the reader's response inside a settled frame. The matter has been explained, the objections have been addressed, and the revelation is stated to be what it claims. A reader who has followed the argument from the opening of the sūrah through the disputes about Abraham, the covenant, and the warning about division arrives at a sentence that tells him the account he has been reading is reliable.

**The Omission of the Addressee's Name**

The verse omits the name of the one being addressed, where the parallel passage adds that he is truly one of the messengers. The omission is the kind of variation the Book often uses in repeated formulas.

The reason lies in what the verse is doing at this point. The passage has just described the outcome for two groups, and the attention is on the message and its reliability rather than on the person receiving it. The next sentence states that God does not desire injustice for His creation, and the two sentences together form a statement about the revelation and about its giver, which is where the passage needs the reader to arrive.

**The Statement About Injustice**

The Arabic word translated as injustice describes the placing of something outside its proper place. The verse's sentence denies that God desires such a thing for any of the worlds, and the commentators offered two explanations that fit the wording.

Al-Rāzī read it as a denial that God desires human beings to commit wrong. Ibn Kathīr and al-Qurṭubī connected the sentence with the verse that follows and read it as a statement that God has no need to wrong anyone, since everything belongs to Him and His power is complete. A third explanation, recorded among the commentators, takes the sentence as the plain statement that God does not in fact wrong anyone. Each reading denies injustice; they differ over whether the denial concerns God's will for human acts or the conduct of God himself.

**The Question the Verse Raises in Theology**

The sentence about injustice became one of the points at which the schools of theology worked out their positions on God's relation to good and evil. One school held that wrong is by definition a trespass on what belongs to another, and that since everything belongs to God, nothing He does can be described as wrong. Another held that justice and injustice are objective features of the world that human beings can recognise, and that God is always just by that standard.

The schools agreed about the conclusion the verse states and differed about how to explain it. What neither position loses is the practical point, which is that no person will be treated unjustly on the day the passage has described, and the passage leaves a statement about a person's own case rather than a puzzle about God's.

**The Distinction Between Two Kinds of Divine Command**

Some theologians drew a distinction between what God asks of human beings and what He brings into existence, calling the first the command of obligation and the second the command of creation.

On that distinction, a person can disobey what God has asked of him, and cannot prevent what God has decided to bring about. The verse's denial of injustice fits this account: God's requests to human beings can be refused, and what He wills to be cannot, so that the wrong that occurs in the world belongs to the creature's choice rather than to the creator's desire. The sūrah's passage has been built on exactly this understanding of human responsibility, and this verse states the divine side of it.

**How the Sentence Closes the Passage**

The verse brings the passage to a close by returning to the revelation and its source. The commands, the examples, the two outcomes, and the warning against division are all gathered under the statement that these are God's revelations, recited in truth, from a Lord who does not wish injustice for anyone.

That is the point at which the sūrah's argument reaches its conclusion for this stretch, and what follows returns to a statement about ownership and return. The reader has been shown what he must do and what awaits two kinds of people, and the verse assures him that the account of both is true and that the one who gave it is not unjust.

**The Two Sentences as a Single Answer**

The verse's two statements answer two different anxieties, and the passage needs both. The first answers the question of whether what has been recited can be trusted; the second answers the question of whether the Lord who sent it will deal justly with the people who receive it.

Taken together they close the argument the sūrah has been conducting through this stretch. The community is told that the message is true and that its Lord does not wish injustice to anyone, so that neither doubt about the revelation nor fear about the judge remains available as an excuse. The verse that follows adds the final statement about ownership and the return of all matters, and the three sentences bring the section to its end before the sūrah turns to the community's identity.

**The Ownership That Follows the Denial**

The sentence about injustice is followed immediately by the declaration that whatever is in the heavens and on the earth belongs to God and that all matters are returned to Him, and Ibn Kathīr and al-Qurṭūbī read the two together. What is stated in the second sentence answers the difficulty of the first. The one who judges owns everything he judges and holds everything that the judgment concerns, and the essay on the schools of theology traces how the community's thinkers worked this out: those who held that wrong means taking what belongs to another concluded that nothing God does can be described in that way, while those who held that justice and injustice are features of the world recognizable to human beings concluded that God is always just. The verse itself states the denial of injustice and leaves the argument to those who came after it, and the sentence that follows supplies the fact on which every version of the argument rests.

---
## Sūrah Āli ʿImrān 3:109

> To Allah ˹alone˺ belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth. And to Allah ˹all˺ matters will be returned ˹for judgment˺.

**Expanded Commentary**

**Ownership and the Return of Matters**

The verse states that everything in the heavens and the earth belongs to God, and that all matters will be returned to Him for judgment. The two clauses are a statement of possession followed by a statement of jurisdiction.

The Book pairs them often. One passage states that whatever is in the heavens and the earth belongs to God, and that God is the Self-Sufficient and Praiseworthy (31:26), which makes the point that the ownership of everything carries no benefit for the owner and no limitation on Him. Another passage states that God will certainly gather humanity on a day about which there is no doubt, and then asks whose word could be more truthful than God's (4:87). The verse before the reader stands in that sequence of declarations.

**Why the Formula Settles Disputes**

The sentence about ownership is the Book's standard reply to arguments about authority. Throughout this sūrah, the disputes have concerned lineage, scripture, and standing, with each party claiming a position that the others contested.

The reply is not to adjudicate the claims one by one but to state who owns the terms. If everything belongs to God, then no community owns a claim on Him, and no lineage carries a right against Him. The sūrah has already used the same reasoning when it stated that God is never unaware of what people do and when it described Him as witness over the conduct of the People of the Book, and the sentence here generalises the point to the whole of creation.

**"All Matters Are Returned"**

The clause about matters being returned appears in several contexts in the Book, and one of them is a passage about the battlefield, where the return of matters to God is given as the reason the outcome of a battle was arranged as it was (8:44).

The phrase describes both the final accounting and the disposal of events in this world. Nothing that occurs falls outside the jurisdiction of the one to whom matters return, and the Book uses the same expression for the settling of disputes that ended badly in this life and for the final reckoning. Its function in the verse before the reader is to add time to ownership: the things that belong to God will also come back to Him, and the reckoning is the moment when the ownership becomes visible.

**What the Verse Means for the Parties of This Sūrah**

The communities addressed in this sūrah had claimed Abraham, held scriptures, and disputed about which of them stood where. The verse places all of that inside a statement that leaves nobody outside God's ownership.

A person reading the passage with those arguments in mind receives a different perspective on them. The dispute about who possessed the truth matters, and the sūrah has pursued it at length; what the sentence about ownership supplies is the fact that the dispute itself is subject to a judge whose authority nobody granted and nobody can withdraw from. The communities may argue as long as they like, and the matter will return to its owner.

**The Comfort the Sentence Contains**

The Book states the return of matters to God as a reassurance as often as it states it as a warning, and both uses are present in this sūrah's surroundings. For people who have been wronged and cannot obtain justice, the clause means that no case is lost by being left unresolved in this world.

The sūrah has just described communities that divide after receiving proofs and groups that work to draw the believers away from their faith. Those are wrongs whose consequences are hard to measure, and the sentence that everything returns to God asserts that the measurement will be carried out. The Book's consolations are frequently of this kind, addressed to people who cannot see the outcome they are owed.

**Ownership and Human Trust in This World**

The Book's statements about divine ownership do not remove human responsibility for the world, and it holds the two together elsewhere, where human beings are described as placed on the earth to act within it and as answerable for what they do with what they have been given.

What belongs to God is entrusted to people for a time, and the return of matters is the accounting for the trust. That is the framework in which the sūrah's commands about wealth, about the community's unity, and about calling others to what is good make sense: each of them concerns the use of something that was never owned outright. The verse states the framework in two sentences and leaves the reader to apply it to the instructions he has just been given.

**The Close of a Section**

The verse ends a section of the sūrah that began with the address to the believers about being drawn away from their faith and continued through commands about unity and correction, a warning about division, and the description of two outcomes.

The sentences that follow begin a new movement, and the reader is carried from the terms of the argument to a statement about the community's identity and its place among the nations. The two verses serve as the hinge between those subjects, and both of them do their work by stating a fact about God rather than by praising or blaming any human party.

**A Sentence Repeated at Points of Decision**

The Book places the statement that matters return to God at the moments where human judgment fails or where a dispute cannot be settled in this world. It appears in the account of a battle whose outcome nobody could have predicted and at the close of passages about communities that refused their messengers.

Its recurrence gives the sentence a practical role. A reader who has exhausted what he can do about a wrong is told where the matter goes next, and a community that has been treated unjustly is told that the case is not closed. The verse above belongs to that family of statements, and its position after a passage about division and opposition is a reminder that the sūrah's arguments are conducted in the presence of a judge.

---
## Sūrah Āli ʿImrān 3:110

> You are the best community ever raised for humanity—you encourage good, forbid evil, and believe in Allah. Had the People of the Book believed, it would have been better for them. Some of them are faithful, but most are rebellious.

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Best Community Raised for Humanity**

The verse addresses the believers as the best community brought forth for humanity, and then names the practices that define the description: encouraging what is good, forbidding what is wrong, and believing in God. The rank is stated first and the content of it immediately after.

Some commentators read the verb as describing a destiny settled in advance, so that the community is told what it has been written to be and is then expected to live up to it; others read it as describing what the community becomes by virtue of the practices named. The Book's grammar permits both, since the verb form can carry the sense of the present and of something established. The same title appears in the sūrah of the Cow, where the community is described as made upright so that it may bear witness over humanity (2:143).

**Why the Description Comes Before the Title's Content**

The order of the sentence is worth noting. The practices are named after the title, and the mention of belief comes last, after the enjoining and forbidding.

Ibn Kathīr drew the conclusion that the community is called best because of what it does for others, which is the concern of encouraging good and forbidding wrong, and that the placement of action before belief reflects that emphasis. The three items are not ranked against each other; they are the description of a community that is defined by what it does as much as by what it holds. The sūrah has just commanded the same practices to be carried out by a group within the community, and this verse states the result as the community's identity.

**The Witness the Community Carries**

The role attached to the community in the parallel passage is that of a witness over humanity, with the messenger a witness over it (2:143). That role explains why the description of the community's practices follows its title, since a witness must be visible and its conduct is part of what it witnesses to.

A community that believes in God, calls others to good, and intervenes against wrong is presenting an argument in the form of a life rather than in the form of a claim. The Book's treatment of the community's function toward other peoples matches its treatment of the Book itself, which it describes as a guardian over the earlier scriptures. The role is not a privilege of rank but a responsibility of representation.

**The Conditional Statement About the People of the Book**

The verse turns to the People of the Book and states that if they had believed, it would have been better for them. The sentence is a statement about benefit, not about blame: belief is described as something that would have improved their condition.

What the Book means by belief in this context is the acceptance of the message that had come to the Prophet, since the verse is speaking about a community that already held a scripture. The Book's arguments with them in this sūrah have been precisely about the acknowledgement of that message, and the sentence here states the consequence in the mildest terms available, which gives the following clause its force.

**"Some of Them Are Faithful, Most Are Rebellious"**

The word rendered as rebellious is used in the Book for those who abandon an obligation or step outside a limit, and the commentators noted that it is contrasted here with belief rather than with disbelief.

Al-Rāzī and al-Ṭabarī both read the term as describing the failure of the People of the Book to be faithful to their own scriptures, which, in the Muslim reading, point toward the final message. The choice of the word is exact: it names a breaking of trust with what a person already holds rather than a simple rejection of what he has not held. The verse's description is therefore of a community that had something to be faithful to, and the accusation is that most of it was not.

**Believers Named Among Them**

The verse's statement that some among them are faithful is confirmed elsewhere in the sūrah. A later passage says that they are not all alike and describes an upright group among the People of the Book who recite God's revelations through the night and prostrate themselves (3:113). The same sūrah's closing passages speak of those among them who believe in God, in what has been revealed to the believers, and in what was revealed to them (3:199).

The Book's own categories therefore prevent its readers from converting a judgment about majority conduct into a verdict on a whole people, and the tradition records that individuals of the People of the Book accepted the message and were counted among the community's most respected members.

**How the Passage Continues**

The verses that follow draw out the consequences of the distinction the verse has made. They state what the believers may expect from the opposition they face, and then describe the upright among the People of the Book in more detail.

The passage's method is the one the sūrah has used throughout this stretch of argument. A general statement about a people is qualified by a distinction among them, and the distinction is then developed with specific descriptions of belief and conduct. The reader is left with a picture of two groups within a single community, and with the reminder that his own community's title is attached to practices he has just been commanded to carry out.

---
## Sūrah Āli ʿImrān 3:111

> They can never inflict harm on you, except a little annoyance. But if they meet you in battle, they will flee and they will have no helpers.

**Expanded Commentary**

**What the Opposition Can Actually Do**

The verse tells the believers that the people in question cannot harm them beyond a limited irritation, and that if it comes to fighting they will retreat and find no help. The sentence sets a ceiling on what the community has to fear.

The claim is carefully measured. The Book does not tell the believers that their enemies are harmless, since the same passage has described efforts to turn them away from their faith and has warned them against complying. What it does is name the boundary: what the opposition can produce is annoyance, and what it cannot produce is the destruction of the community that holds to its message.

**The Annoyance the Verse Names**

The word translated as annoyance covers insult, mockery, and the kind of speech that wears a community down without defeating it. The commentators included blasphemous claims about God among the things the term describes.

The sūrah returns to this theme later when it tells the believers that their patience and mindfulness will prevent the schemes of their opponents from harming them at all (3:120). The two verses fit together: one describes the category of harm that remains possible, and the other describes the conduct that neutralises even that. The Book's habit is to name the residual risk rather than to promise absolute immunity, which keeps the exhortation to patience meaningful.

**The Prediction About Fighting**

The second sentence of the verse states that if the opponents meet the believers in battle, they will turn and flee, and that they will have no helpers. The wording is a prediction about armed confrontation, and it matches another passage in the Book that says the same people would certainly flee if they were fought, leaving the disbelievers with no help (59:12).

The sūrah has already described one battle in which the community was outnumbered and the outcome was attributed to divine support, and it will shortly describe another in which the believers were tested. The prediction here is not a promise that every encounter will end in victory, since the sūrah's later passages describe a defeat in detail; it is a statement about the limits of what the opposition can achieve against the message.

**What It Means to Have No Helpers**

The phrase about having no helpers is one of the Book's fixed descriptions for those who are cut off, and it appears in several contexts. It is used of people whose deeds are wasted in this world and the next (3:22), of those subjected to punishment in both lives (3:56), and of those whom God has condemned, for whom no helper exists (4:52).

The recurrence is deliberate. In the Book's vocabulary, having no helpers describes a condition rather than an event, and it is attached to the people who have placed themselves outside the protection that others enjoy. The verse before the reader applies the description to a group that had been trying to draw the believers away from their faith, and the sentence lets them see the end of that effort.

**Why the Verse Is Addressed as Reassurance**

The sentence is framed for the believers, not for their opponents. It tells a community under pressure what the pressure amounts to, and it does so after the previous verse has described that community's rank among the nations.

The pairing matters. A community told that it is the best raised for humanity is immediately told what its opponents can and cannot do to it, so that the rank is not turned into an expectation of ease. The sūrah's pattern is to give the believers both their standing and the limits of their trial, and this verse supplies the second half of that pattern for the present passage.

**The Distinction Between Harm to Persons and Harm to the Message**

The verse's careful limit points to a distinction the Book draws throughout its accounts of persecution. What a hostile group can do to individuals is real and is described plainly, and what it can do to the message is nothing.

That distinction explains the calm of the verse. The community is not told that its people will not suffer; the sūrah's later passage describes the losses at the battle of Uḥud without softening them. What is told is that the opposition cannot make the message fail, and the sentence that they will flee states the outcome of the attempt in the plainest terms.

**The Verse in the Sūrah's Sequence**

The verse follows the description of the community's identity and its qualification of the judgment about the People of the Book, and it precedes a passage about the conditions under which those people live.

Its position keeps the passage's balance. The sūrah has just refused to treat a whole community as one thing, and it now states what the hostile part of it is able to do. The reader is given both facts in sequence: the opposition is real, and it is limited. The verses that follow describe the condition of those who sustain that opposition, and the two statements of this verse provide the frame in which the next description is to be read.

**Annoyance, Patience, and the Long View**

The verse's limit on what the opposition can achieve is not a reason for the community to relax its guard, and the Book does not present it that way. The annoyance it names is real, and the sūrah's response to it is patience rather than confrontation.

That response appears in the passage near the end of this stretch, where the believers are told that patience and mindfulness will leave the schemes of their opponents without effect. The two verses describe one policy: expect the irritation, refuse to be governed by it, and continue. The Book's comfort in such passages is not the promise of an easy life but the assurance that the enemy's capacity is bounded, which is what this verse states at the outset.

---
## Sūrah Āli ʿImrān 3:112

> They will be stricken with disgrace wherever they go, unless they are protected by a covenant with Allah or a treaty with the people. They have invited the displeasure of Allah and have been branded with misery for rejecting Allah’s revelations and murdering ˹His˺ prophets unjustly. This is ˹a fair reward˺ for their disobedience and violations.

**Expanded Commentary**

**A Condition Described as Lasting Abasement**

The verse states that the people in view will be struck with humiliation wherever they are found, unless they are protected by a covenant from God or a treaty with people, and it explains the condition by naming their offences. The sentence is about the circumstances in which such a community lives.

The Book describes the same condition in an earlier passage about the Israelites, where they are said to have been struck with disgrace and misery for rejecting God's signs and unjustly killing the prophets (2:61). The wording of the two verses is close, and the repetition shows that the Book treats the state it describes as the working out of a long-standing pattern rather than as an isolated event.

**The Two Means of Protection**

The exception in the sentence names two things that lift the condition: a covenant from God and a treaty with people. The commentators explained the first as the protection that comes from a divine obligation, whether through accepting the religion or through the pledge that a Muslim ruler grants, and the second as an agreement with a community or a state.

Ibn Kathīr read the same phrase in the command to hold firmly to the rope of God as a reference to a pact, which is the sense it carries here. The sentence therefore acknowledges that a people can live in safety among others, and it locates that safety in a formal relationship rather than in strength.

**The Reading That Connects the Verse With the Tax and Protected Status**

Commentators who lived in later centuries connected the abasement with the indemnity paid by non-Muslim communities under Muslim rule and with the protected status that accompanied it, since the Book's instructions about such agreements appear elsewhere.

Al-Ṭabarī took a different view of the same phrase, arguing that the protection cannot be what removes the abasement, because the abasement and the protection are described as alternatives in the sentence itself. The disagreement is about how a legal institution relates to a scriptural description, and the difference is worth noting because it shows the commentators distinguishing between the text's statement and the arrangements later societies built around it.

**The Offences the Verse Names**

The verse gives two reasons for the condition: rejecting God's signs, and killing the prophets without right. Both are acts committed by communities that had received messengers, and the Book attaches them to the history of the Israelites in particular.

The phrase about killing the prophets without justification is the Book's way of marking a crime that has no excuse available. The prophets were sent to the people as their own, and the Book's account of their rejection includes violence in several cases. The accusation here is not addressed to a foreign enemy; it is addressed to the descendants of those who received the message, and the sūrah's argument with them has been conducted on that footing throughout.

**The Closing Word About Disobedience and Transgression**

The verse ends by describing the outcome as a recompense for disobedience and for going beyond limits. The two words describe the failure to do what was required and the decision to exceed what was permitted, so that the description covers both leaving a duty and invading a prohibition.

The Book uses the pair when it wants to state that a people's condition is earned rather than imposed. That is the point of the sentence in this context: the abasement is not a gratuitous humiliation of one community by another but the result of a course of conduct that the Book has been tracing through the passage. The next verse then prevents the judgment from being applied indiscriminately.

**Why the Verse Does Not Authorise Contempt**

The sentence describes what happens to a people whose conduct has been as described, and it does not instruct the believers to humiliate anyone. The distinction is essential, and the sūrah makes it in the verse that follows by stating that the People of the Book are not all alike.

A community reading this passage is being told how to understand the condition of the people around it, and the explanation offered is moral rather than racial. The Book's own statements elsewhere about believers among the People of the Book and about the faithful remnant prevent the description from hardening into a verdict on a group defined by descent, and the sūrah keeps those statements close to this one.

**The Conditions Under Which a Community Lives Among Others**

The verse's practical content concerns the terms on which communities coexist. It says that safety is available through agreement, and it names the agreement as coming either from the obligations of the religion or from a treaty concluded between peoples.

That is the framework the sūrah's later verses assume when they address the believers about their dealings with others. The Book permits the ordering of relations by contract and by covenant, and it treats the resulting security as real. The sentence before the reader states both sides: the condition of a people that has neither, and the two instruments by which the condition is lifted.

**A Judgment With a Qualifier Attached**

The verse reads differently once the next sentence is in view, and the sūrah's arrangement is deliberate: the judgment comes first, and the qualification follows it immediately. A reader who stops at the abasement has read half of the passage.

The Book uses this pattern at several places where it describes a community's failure. It states what the conduct produced, then names the portion that did not share the conduct, and it does so with enough detail for the distinction to be usable. The purpose is to make the judgment a description of a history rather than a licence for contempt, and the passage in this sūrah carries the point through to the verses that describe the upright group in specific terms.

---
## Sūrah Āli ʿImrān 3:113

> Yet they are not all alike: there are some among the People of the Book who are upright, who recite Allah’s revelations throughout the night, prostrating ˹in prayer˺.

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Qualification That Prevents a Blanket Judgment**

The verse begins by stating that the People of the Book are not all alike, and it then describes one part of them: an upright community that recites God's revelations through the night while prostrating themselves. The sentence follows the previous verse's account of a people struck with humiliation.

The Book's judgment is thus qualified immediately after being stated. Some commentators understood the qualification as a distinction within the People of the Book itself; others read it as a comparison between the believers and the other communities. The two readings agree that the verse forbids the reader to close the account on a whole people, which is the practical point of the sentence.

**What the Word for Upright Carries**

The word describing the group means standing, and it carries the senses of firmness, justice, and the standing posture of prayer. Al-Ṭabarī noted its association with fairness, and others explained the upright as those who maintain the limits God has set and do not distort what they hold.

The word's double sense fits the verse's content, because the same group is then described as praying through the night. What is being described is a portion of a community that remained straight in its conduct and constant in its worship, and the description is offered as the reason the blanket judgment of the previous verse cannot be applied to everyone.

**Night Worship in the Book's Vocabulary**

The Book returns often to the practice of praying in the dark. One passage describes people who abandon their beds to call on their Lord in hope and fear and to give from what they have been provided (32:16). Another places among the righteous those who are patient, truthful, obedient, and who seek forgiveness before dawn (3:17).

This sūrah itself contains the instruction to rise in the last part of the night for additional prayer (17:79), and the command to recite the Book in measured tones comes in the same context. The group described in the verse under discussion is therefore performing a practice the Book commends to its own community, and the passage is acknowledging the practice wherever it is found.

**Why the Night Is Named**

The night carries a significance in these passages beyond the hour. Prayer in the dark is hidden from people, and the Book's descriptions of it repeatedly pair hope with fear, which is the state of a person alone with his Lord.

A practice that no one sees is a practice that cannot be performed for display, and the verse's description of a community reciting the revelation in the small hours is a description of sincerity as much as of devotion. That is why the sūrah's mention of the group at this point in the argument matters: after a passage about communities that fought against the truth and communities that were drawn away from it, the Book names people whose worship was conducted where only God could see it.

**The Reports About the Occasion**

The commentaries record several occasions for the verse's revelation. One describes the believers waiting in the mosque for the Prophet to lead the night prayer, and his telling them that no people from any religion were remembering God at that hour besides them. Other reports name groups from Najrān, from Abyssinia, and from Byzantine territory who followed the religion of Jesus and affirmed the truth of the message. A further report describes a people who prayed between sunset and the end of twilight.

[UNVERIFIED: the several occasions of revelation recorded for 3:113, which the commentaries relate without chains I have examined.]

**How the Verse Sits Between Two Judgments**

The verse stands between the statement that most of the People of the Book were false to what they held and the description of the specific deeds of the upright group. Its position gives the passage its shape.

A reader who has followed the argument from the earlier chapters of this sūrah has heard the community's case against the People of the Book developed at length. This verse interrupts that development to name a part of them that the case does not cover, and the sentences that follow describe that part in detail. The Book's habit of holding both facts in view at once is the reason the passage can be read without producing contempt for a people as such.

**The Standard the Description Sets**

The group is identified by conduct: standing firm, reciting the revelation, and prostrating in worship at night. Nothing in the description depends on lineage or history.

That makes the verse usable as a standard rather than only as a historical note. The community receiving the sūrah is given the marks of the people it is told to respect and recognise among others, and those marks are practices its own revelation commands. The verses that follow add the rest of the description, and the whole picture supplies the answer to the question of what belief looks like when it is found outside the community that holds the final message.

**Recitation and Prostration as One Act**

The verse pairs the recitation of God's revelations with prostration, and the pairing describes a single act of worship rather than two practices that happen to be listed together.

Reading and bowing belong together in the Book's treatment of prayer, where the recitation is the content of the standing and the prostration is its completion. The night prayer that this sūrah commands combines them, and the command to recite in measured tones occurs in the same passage. The group described in the verse is therefore engaged in the practice the receiving community is itself instructed to perform, which is why the description can serve as a standard of recognition rather than only as a report about others.

---
## Sūrah Āli ʿImrān 3:114

> They believe in Allah and the Last Day, encourage good and forbid evil, and race with one another in doing good. They are ˹truly˺ among the righteous.

**Expanded Commentary**

**Four Marks of the Upright Group**

The verse continues the description of the group named in the previous verse and gives four elements: belief in God and the Last Day, encouraging what is good, forbidding what is wrong, and competing with one another in good deeds. It closes by placing them among the righteous.

The list answers the question the previous verse left open about who the upright are. They are identified by what they hold and what they do, and the two halves of the description are as general as the Book's language allows: faith in God and in the final accounting, and conduct directed at both good and evil in the world.

**Why Belief Is Paired With the Last Day**

The pairing of God and the Last Day is the Book's shortest creed and one of its most frequent formulas. When the Book wants to describe belief in a way that covers both the present and the future, it names these two.

The reason is the difference the two make to conduct. Belief in God establishes who is being obeyed; belief in the Last Day establishes that obedience has a destination and that no deed is lost. The Book uses the pair when it speaks about the reward of those who do good, stating that whoever believes in God and the Last Day and acts rightly will have his reward with his Lord, without fear or grief (2:62). A verse in the sūrah of the Table repeats the same formula in the same terms (5:69).

**Practices the Sūrah Has Already Required**

The two practices in the middle of the list are the ones the sūrah commanded the believers to maintain. It told them to have a group that calls others to good, that encourages what is right and forbids what is wrong (3:104), and later it described what this community should be in the same words (3:110).

The vocabulary is not community-specific. The Book applies it to the Muslim community as its own obligation and to the upright among the People of the Book as their description, which shows that the terms name conduct rather than membership. What the sūrah presents here is the recognition of the same conduct in another community, and the recognition is stated as a fact rather than as a concession.

**"Racing With One Another in Doing Good"**

The final element of the description is the language of competition. The Book uses the same verb for the conduct of the righteous in another passage, where it says of Zachariah's family that they used to race one another in good deeds, calling on God in hope and fear and humbling themselves before Him (21:90).

The image is deliberate: two people running toward the same goal is a picture of shared effort rather than rivalry for a prize. The Book uses it to describe a community's internal energy, and it applies it here to the group whose conduct the sūrah has been describing. What the verse adds to the qualities of the upright is motion: the good they do is not a settled possession but an activity that draws them forward.

**What "Among the Righteous" Adds**

The closing phrase places the group among the righteous, using the Book's standard word for those whose conduct is sound and whose account is settled. The phrase is a verdict, and it is given without the qualifications that accompany descriptions of the two other groups in this passage.

The word's placement at the end of the list means that everything the verse has described is gathered into a single outcome. The Book's habit is to conclude such descriptions with a statement of the person's standing, and the sentence that follows this one confirms the same standing by stating that no good they do will be denied.

**The Two Passages That Make the Same Statement**

The sūrah of the Cow and the sūrah of the Table contain statements that are close to this passage in both content and purpose, promising reward to whoever believes in God and the Last Day and does good.

The commentators discussed whether those passages refer to the People of the Book as such or to the believers among them, and they noted the same question in connection with this group of verses. The difference between the readings does not affect the instruction the passage gives: the Book sets out the marks of sound belief and sound conduct and then states their reward, and the community reading it is being taught how to weigh what it sees in others.

**The Verse and the Community That Recites It**

The verse supplies the community with a working standard rather than a slogan. It answers the question of what to look for in a person or a community whose labels do not match one's own, and it answers with belief, practice, and effort.

The sūrah's passage began with the statement that the community is the best raised for humanity, and it has spent three verses describing people outside it who are described as upright. The two facts belong together: a community that is given a rank is also given the criteria by which it must recognise good wherever it occurs, and the criteria here are the ones its own revelation has set.

**Belief, Practice, and Effort in One Sentence**

The verse covers three dimensions of religion in one list, and the sūrah's own instructions run through all three. Belief in God and the Last Day is the doctrine; encouraging good and forbidding wrong is the ethics; racing in good deeds is the effort.

What the list shows is that none of the three is sufficient alone in the Book's account. A person may hold correct beliefs and remain inactive, and the verse pairs the belief with practices that require him to intervene in the world around him. He may act without competing to excel, and the verse adds the motion of racing. The description of the upright group is thus a full picture rather than a partial one, and the passage places it in front of a community that has just been given the same instructions.

**Who These Verses Describe**

The identification of the people praised in this passage depends on two other decisions the commentators had to make. The first is who the upright community of the previous verse is, and the second is how the statement in the earlier verse that some of the People of the Book are believers is to be taken. On the reading that the upright community consists of the People of the Book, the sentence before the reader continues the same description; on the reading that it refers to the Muslims, the passage moves from the community to the group it has been discussing. The content of the passage resembles the earlier statements about those who believe in God and the Last Day and do right (2:62; 5:69), and the same questions about identity arise in each place. What the verse names is a set of qualities rather than a group, and the qualities are those the sūrah has been commending throughout.

**The Reassurance in the Next Verse**

The sentence that follows this one, stating that whatever good such people do will not be denied them, was read by Ibn Kathīr and al-Rāzī as a reassurance given to the former Jews and Christians who had accepted the message and were being told by their former coreligionists that their good deeds before the change had been wasted. Al-Qurṭūbī and al-Ṭabarī recorded a reading of the verb in the second person, which turns the statement into a direct address to the community: what you do will not be denied. On either reading the verse answers a fear, and the fear belongs to people who had left one community for another and were uncertain what had become of the good they had done in their former life. The passage is therefore addressed to the anxiety of converts, and its answer is that God does not discard what people have done well.

---
## Sūrah Āli ʿImrān 3:115

> They will never be denied the reward for any good they have done. And Allah has ˹perfect˺ knowledge of those mindful ˹of Him˺.

**Expanded Commentary**

**A Promise That No Good Is Lost**

The verse states that whatever good such people do will not be denied to them, and it adds that God has full knowledge of those who are mindful of Him. It closes the three-verse description of the upright group with an assurance about their reward.

The assurance is stated in the strongest form the language provides, since the verb of denial carries the sense of refusing something that is due. The Book uses the same idea in other places when it assures people that their charity and their vows are known to God, and that nothing given has gone unrecorded (2:270). The sentence in this verse is the shortest version of that reassurance.

**What the Word for Denial Implies**

The word translated as denied shares its root with the Book's word for ingratitude, which is the refusal to acknowledge a benefit that has been received. Applying that word to the reward means that the good done by such people will not be treated as if it had never happened.

The choice is precise in a passage about people whose standing was doubted by others. The sūrah has just described a group whose worship and conduct the receiving community might have been tempted to discount, and the sentence removes the possibility of discount. What is promised is not a reward of a particular size but the acknowledgement that the deed occurred and belongs to the person who did it.

**The Reassurance for People Who Feared Their Deeds Were Wasted**

Commentators connected the verse with the situation of people from among the People of the Book who had accepted the message and were then taunted by their former coreligionists with the claim that everything they had done before was now worthless.

Ibn Kathīr and al-Rāzī both report this connection, and the verse's wording fits it. The sentence tells such people that the good they performed in their former community is not lost, and it does so without making the reward depend on the label they once carried. Some commentators read the verb in the second person, so that the verse addresses the believers directly and says that they will not be denied what they have done, which produces the same assurance in a different voice.

**God's Knowledge of the Mindful**

The second sentence shifts from the reward to the knowledge of the one who gives it. The Book's statement that God knows those who are mindful of Him explains how the first sentence can be true of deeds that nobody witnessed.

The group described in the preceding verses prayed at night and worked quietly at their good, and the Book has just described practices that are hidden from public view. The sentence about knowledge is what makes the promise about reward coherent: the deeds that no one saw are recorded by the one who saw them, and the standard for the reward is the mindfulness that accompanied the act rather than its visibility.

**Reward as Knowledge Rather Than Arithmetic**

The verse does not describe a scale or a measure, and it places the reward in the same sentence as God's knowledge. The Book's other statements about recompense often multiply or specify, and this one simply says that nothing is refused.

That way of putting the matter suits the passage's purpose, which is to settle a question about standing rather than to publish a tariff. A reader is left with the assurance that what he does is not lost and with the reminder that the one who receives the deed knows the state of the person who performed it. Both halves matter for anyone whose good deeds are not recognised in the world.

**How the Sentence Closes the Description**

The three verses about the upright group end with this promise, and the sequence is worth noticing. The group is described first by their worship, then by their beliefs and practices, and finally by the assurance that their reward is secure.

The order moves from the observable to the promised, which is the Book's usual direction in passages of this kind. Nothing in the description is drawn from claims the group makes about itself; everything is conduct, and the outcome is stated by God. The verse thus completes the portrait that began with the phrase about the People of the Book not being all alike, and it does so by attaching the reward to the conduct rather than to the community.

**The Balance the Passage Has Held**

The stretch of verses that ends here began with an address to the believers about being drawn away from their faith and continued through commands about unity and the warning against division. It then described the community's rank, the limits of what its opponents can do, the condition of those who fight against the message, and the upright minority among the People of the Book.

The passage's balance is the sūrah's method in miniature. Warnings are followed by commands, judgments on communities are followed by qualifications, and descriptions of conduct are closed with statements about reward and knowledge. This verse is the last element in that sequence, and the sentences that follow take up the theme of wealth and children and the fate of those who disbelieve, returning the reader to the contrast with which the sūrah's earlier passage began.

**What the Verse Does Not Measure**

The sentence promises that no good is denied, and it says nothing about how much a good deed is worth. The Book's statements about recompense elsewhere give the impression of abundance rather than of an exact scale, and this verse keeps the emphasis on the fact of the accounting rather than on its size.

The criterion the verse does name is in its final clause, where the reward is connected with mindfulness of God. That is the Book's consistent position on the value of acts: the deed's worth is tied to the state of the person who performs it, and the state is known to God alone. The passage's closing sentence therefore leaves the reader with what the Book considers sufficient, which is the assurance that nothing good is lost and that the one who sees the heart is the one who settles the account.

---
## Sūrah Āli ʿImrān 3:116

> Indeed, neither the wealth nor children of the disbelievers will be of any benefit to them against Allah. It is they who will be the residents of the Fire. They will be there forever.

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Sentence That Comes Back**

The verse restates what the sūrah said near its beginning: that the wealth and children of those who disbelieve will not benefit them against God, and that such people will live in the Fire. The earlier statement was made before the long argument about the covenant, the House of worship, and the People of the Book; this one is made after it.

A repetition in the Book is a structural signal. The reader who has carried the first sentence through the intervening passage now meets it again with everything he has learned in between, and the second occurrence tells him that the intervening material was an explanation of how the condition arises rather than a change of subject.

**What Lies Between the Two Statements**

The distance between the two sentences is filled with the sūrah's discussion of communities that received revelations, disputed about their ancestors, contracted covenants, and then divided. Some of that material concerned the People of the Book and some concerned the believers, and all of it concerned people who possessed things they trusted.

Read with that in mind, the repeated sentence gains a specific sense. The wealth and children it names are not only money and offspring; the passage has been treating standing, lineage, and scripture as possessions of the same kind. What the verse denies is that any of them interposes between a person and his Lord, and the intervening argument has supplied the evidence for the denial.

**The Delusion the Book Describes**

The Book elsewhere gives the psychology of the condition. One passage describes a person who turns away when the revelations are recited to him, and it explains that he does so because he has been given wealth and children (68:14). Another tells the Prophet not to be impressed by the wealth and children of such people, because God's purpose with those gifts is a trial that ends with their death in disbelief (9:85).

The two passages show that the verses before the reader are describing a settled pattern rather than an isolated complaint. What the sūrah denies, the rest of the Book diagnoses: a person who measures his safety by what he holds, and who mistakes the abundance he was given for an endorsement.

**Why Children Are Named With Wealth**

The two items appear together throughout the Book because they cover both of a person's horizons. Wealth is what he has, and children are what continues him, and together they represent the whole of what he might want to secure.

The Book's verdict on the pair is not a condemnation of either. The same Book describes them as the adornment of the present life (18:46) and states that they are a test in which many people are tried (64:15). What is denied is their use as a defence: a person may love his children and possess his wealth and still answer for his conduct, and the sentence treats the belief that these things can stand in his place as the error that ends badly.

**"Against Allah" and the Meaning of Benefit**

The phrase about benefiting against God sets the terms of the denial. Nothing in the verse says that wealth is useless in the ordinary affairs of life; what it says is that wealth cannot be used against the outcome that the passage has been describing.

That is why the verse is placed here rather than at the beginning of the sūrah. The reader has now seen the ending that the passage announces, and the sentence about benefit is a statement about that ending. The Book's habit is to deny the usefulness of a thing precisely at the point where its usefulness has been trusted, and the sūrah has spent a long passage showing what people trust.

**Residents of the Fire, and the Difference From the Earlier Wording**

The earlier statement described such people as the fuel of the Fire, which named what they become. This verse calls them its residents and states that they will remain there, which names where they live and for how long.

The change of image is deliberate and the two belong together. Fuel describes the person's relation to the fire; residence describes his relation to the place. The Book uses the two descriptions in the same sūrah, and it uses them in the order of a claim and its elaboration, so that the reader meets the more vivid image first and the fuller description second.

**Who Is Described, and How the Sūrah Uses the Category**

The verse speaks of those who disbelieve, and the sūrah has used the category carefully throughout. It has distinguished the People of the Book who rejected the message from those among them who believed, and it has refused to treat a whole community as one thing.

The description here is therefore of a condition, not of a birth. What the Book condemns is the state in which a person dies, and the same Book has just described a group within the very community the passage has been criticizing as upright and among the righteous. A reader who applies the verse to a people rather than to a condition has read past the qualification the sūrah placed two verses before this one.

**What the Repetition Tells the Reader**

The sūrah closes the passage's frame by returning to the sentence it opened with, and the return is a way of stating that a verdict has been established rather than merely announced.

The reader is left with a picture of the argument complete: the condition described, the history examined, the community addressed, the opponents measured, the upright recognized, and the verdict repeated. The verses that follow take up the same two possessions and describe what happens to what those people spend in this world, which is the next step in dismantling the securities the passage has named.

---
## Sūrah Āli ʿImrān 3:117

> The good they do in this worldly life is like the harvest of an evil people struck by a bitter wind, destroying it ˹completely˺. Allah never wronged them, but they wronged themselves.

**Expanded Commentary**

**A Parable About Outlay Without Return**

The verse compares what such people spend in this life to a crop destroyed by a bitter wind, and it ends by stating that God did not wrong them and that they wronged themselves. The image is agricultural, and its subject is labour that produces nothing.

The sentence is addressed to people whose generosity was part of their standing, and the parable does not deny that the labour occurred. A harvest is the result of work, and the verse describes the destruction of something that had grown. What it denies is the survival of the result, and the denial is stated with an image that any farmer in the audience would have recognised.

**Wind in the Book's Picture of Effort**

The Book uses wind in several passages to describe the fate of deeds, and the variations on the image carry different emphases. One passage describes a garden with palms, vines, and every kind of fruit, whose owner grows old with young dependents while a fire-laden whirlwind strikes and burns the whole of it (2:266). Another compares the deeds of those who disbelieve to ashes blown away by a fierce wind on a stormy day, so that nothing they earned remains available to them (14:18).

The same Book describes wind elsewhere as the bearer of good news ahead of rain and as a means by which provision reaches people. The two uses belong to a single doctrine: the wind does not discriminate, and what it destroys is destroyed because of where it blew, not because wind is cruel.

**Which Good Deeds Are in View**

The spending named in the verse is the kind that people perform for reputation, obligation, or the maintenance of standing, and the commentators understood the image as applying to such outlays.

The description does not make the acts invisible. It says that their fruit does not reach the place where fruit matters, which is a statement about the relation of the deed to its giver rather than about the deed's size. The Book's treatment of sincere and insincere giving elsewhere takes the same line, and the account of the sūrah in its opening verses, where the disbelievers' wealth is denied any benefit at all, is the same doctrine in another form.

**"A People Who Wronged Themselves"**

The crop in the parable belongs to people who wronged themselves, and the destruction is attached to that condition. The image therefore places the cause inside the owners rather than in the weather.

That is the point the explanation in the same verse makes explicit. A person's losses are not arbitrary, and the Book allows no doctrine of a blind fate; the wind that destroys the harvest is the wind that blows on a field whose people are described as wrongdoers. The Qur'an's parables are generally constructed this way, with the moral stated inside the picture rather than added afterwards.

**The Denial of Divine Injustice**

The verse states directly that God did not wrong them, and it is one of several passages in this sūrah that insist on the point. The sentence before the reader is the same in substance as the statement that God desires no injustice for His creation.

The insistence is needed because of the verse's subject. A person who has worked hard and lost everything is the readiest audience for the idea that he was treated unfairly, and the Book's answer is that what was lost had already been forfeited by the state of the one who planted. The denial of injustice is therefore an explanation rather than a defense: it tells the reader where to look for the cause.

**"They Wronged Themselves"**

The phrase that people wrong themselves runs through the Book, and the sūrah uses it again in the passage about those who remember God after wrongdoing and ask forgiveness. In every case the wrong is described as directed at the self, which is the Book's way of saying that the primary victim of a person's misconduct is his own account.

The formula fits the parable exactly. The field was the owner's, the labour was his, and the wind took what he had. Nothing in the picture suggests that anyone else was deprived, and the sentence about the wrong being self-directed is the explanation of why the destruction is described in those terms rather than as a punishment imposed from outside.

**The Limit of the Parable**

The parable concerns the fate of what a person spends in this present life, and the Book's statements about the reward of the Hereafter are not contradicted by it. The verses immediately before this one promised that the good done by the upright will not be denied, and the two statements stand together in the same passage.

The difference between them is the state of the person who acts. The Book's consistent position is that deeds are weighed with the giver, so that an identical act performed from faith and from display has different results. The parable states one side of that position, and the promise about the upright states the other, and the reader is expected to hold both.

**Why the Verse Follows the Previous One**

The verse before this one denied that wealth and children can stand between a person and God. This verse takes the next step and describes what happens to what such people give away.

The order dismantles the securities in sequence. First the possessions that a person keeps, then the resources he parts with, and in each case the outcome is stated without reference to the amount.
