> Muḥammad is no more than a messenger; other messengers have gone before him. If he were to die or to be killed, would you regress into disbelief? Those who do so will not harm Allah whatsoever. And Allah will reward those who are grateful.

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Name Used in the Sentence**

The verse names the Prophet directly and states that he is nothing more than a messenger, and other messengers had passed away before him. The sūrah uses his name only a few times, and the use of it here is part of the sentence's teaching.

The Book elsewhere insists on the same distinction between the messenger and the message. One passage states that Muhammad is not the father of any of the men among his people but is the messenger of God and the seal of the prophets, and the sentence in this verse works in the same direction by placing him among a line of messengers who came and went.

**Messengers Who Have Passed Away**

The statement that other messengers have gone before him places the Prophet within a sequence, and the Book states the mortality of the messengers in several places. One passage asks whether, if the Prophet were to die, his people would live forever, and another declares that everything is bound to perish except God Himself.

The verses quoted in the comment on this sentence include the declaration that every soul will taste death, and the comment tradition placed it alongside the present verse as a single teaching. The Book prepares its community for the death of the one it loves most, and this verse is the clearest of those preparations, since it asks the question in the community's own voice and answers it in the same breath.

**The Question About Turning Back**

The verse asks whether the community would turn back on its heels if the Prophet died or was killed, and the image describes apostasy in the physical terms of a retreat. Turning around is what a person does when he flees, and the verse uses the picture for the abandonment of the religion.

The question is not rhetorical in the sense of being unanswerable. The sūrah has just described a day when parts of the community did fall back, and the possibility the verse raises had already been demonstrated in a lesser form. The word for turning describes the movement of a person who reverses his direction, and the Book uses it for the abandonment of a commitment rather than for a momentary hesitation. What is being given here is the principle that the day's events made visible.

**To Whom the Harm Would Fall**

The verse states that whoever turns back does not harm God in the least, and the sentence relocates the consequences of apostasy. The loss is entirely on the side of the person who turns, and the cause is unaffected.

The Book repeats this teaching in other passages where it considers the possibility of the community's failure. It states that God has no need of anyone's obedience and that the worlds are not improved by the conduct of those who abandon the truth. The statement in this verse is the same idea applied to a specific crisis, and it removes the last excuse a person might use to justify leaving when the leader is gone.

The verse's final clause states that God will reward the thankful, and the thanksgiving it names is the opposite of turning back. A person who acknowledges what he has been given will not abandon the giver when circumstances change.

The Book connects gratitude with steadfastness throughout, and the ending of the previous verse about the fear of death uses a similar close. The arrangement of the sentence is effective: instead of threatening those who might turn, it directs attention to the people whose response is right, and the reward is stated for them.

**The Rumour at Uḥud**

The comments on this verse record the crisis that occasioned it. During the fighting the Prophet was badly wounded, and word spread that he had been killed, which unsettled parts of the community and raised the morale of its opponents.

The reports describe a companion calling out that if Muhammad had died, the Lord of Muhammad does not die, and urging the people to live and die as he did. They also describe hypocrites among the community taunting the believers with the argument that a true prophet would not have been killed, and pressing them to abandon the religion. The verse answered all of it in a few lines, and the reports that describe the day note how quickly the community's composure was restored once the Prophet was seen alive and the line was held again.

**The Day the Prophet Died**

Years later, when the Prophet did die, the community's response showed what the verse had taught. The reports describe ʿUmar refusing to accept the news and speaking to the assembled people as though the Prophet would not die, and Abū Bakr mounting the pulpit to address them.

Abū Bakr recited this verse, beginning with the statement that whoever had worshipped Muhammad should know that Muhammad had died, and that whoever worshipped God should know that God is alive and does not die (Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī 1241, 1242). ʿUmar later said that it was as though he had never read the verse before that day. The tradition preserved the incident because it shows the verse carrying the community through the moment it had been preparing them for.

**What the Verse Teaches About the Message and the Messenger**

The verse separates the permanence of the message from the mortality of the person who conveys it, and it prepares the community to continue without confusing the two. The Prophet is honored as the messenger, and the mission is what the community is responsible for.

The teaching mattered immediately at Uḥud and again at the Prophet's death, and it has continued to matter in every generation since. A community that identifies its cause with the presence of a particular individual will collapse when that individual is gone. The sūrah provides the correction in advance, and the closing clause about the thankful describes the people who take it.

---
## Sūrah Āli ʿImrān 3:145

> No soul can ever die without Allah’s Will at the destined time. Those who desire worldly gain, We will let them have it, and those who desire heavenly reward, We will grant it to them. And We will reward those who are grateful.

**Expanded Commentary**

**Death and Its Appointed Term**

The verse states that no soul dies except by the permission of God and at a term that has been fixed. It follows the announcement of the Prophet's mortality with the principle that governs every death, and the two verses belong together.

The Book states the same teaching in many places. One passage declares that every soul will taste death, and another declares that everything is bound to perish except God. The sentence in this verse adds the element of appointment: the time of a person's death is set, and no human precaution changes it.

**The Enjoined Term and the Implicit Verb**

Al-Ṭabarī noted that the phrase rendered as an enjoined term works with an implied verb, so that the sense is that God has decreed a term that is fixed. The construction is one of the ways the Book compresses a clause by leaving out what the listener will supply.

The doctrine is stated plainly in the sūrah of the Iron and elsewhere, where the Book tells people that no misfortune befalls them without being written before it happens. The purpose of such statements in the Book is consistently practical: they remove from people's conduct the calculations that fear and greed produce, and the verses that follow in this passage apply that removal to the case of fighting.

**Two Desires and Two Outcomes**

The verse contrasts those who desire the reward of this world with those who desire the reward of the next, and it states that each will be given what he seeks. The Book makes the same contrast in several passages, and the wording there is often more pointed than it is here, with the worldly seekers receiving their portion in this life and having no share in the next.

One passage states that whoever desires the harvest of the Hereafter will have it increased for him, while whoever desires only the harvest of this world will be given some of it but will have no share in the Hereafter. Another states that whoever desires the fading world alone will be hastened toward whatever is willed for him and then consigned to the fire. The contrast in this verse is stated with a similar economy, and it addresses the motives that were in play when the fighting began.

**The Spoils and the Wider Meaning**

Al-Rāzī read the reference to those who desire the reward of this world as pointing to people whose motive in the fighting was spoil, glory, and reputation. Al-Qurṭūbī read the sentence more broadly, as a statement about human motives in general.

The wider reading suits the verse's place in the sūrah. The community had left a position for the sake of what could be gathered on the field, and the clause names the kind of desire that produced that decision without accusing anyone in particular. The sentence's general form is deliberate: it gives the community a way to examine its own motives whenever it takes up a cause.

**Courage, Fear, and What They Change**

Al-Rāzī drew from the verse a lesson about fear and courage, observing that a person's anxiety and his cowardice do not preserve him and that the term of his life is not in his hands. The conclusion he drew is that a person should act for what is good without letting the fear of death govern him.

The argument is precisely the one the verse supports. If the appointment is fixed, then calculation of the risk cannot extend a single life, and the only variable left is the quality of what a person does with the time he has. The Book's commands about fighting are grounded on this reasoning throughout, and the sentence before the reader states the premise in one line.

**The Hypocrites' Argument Silenced**

The commentary tradition noted that the verse also closes an argument that the hypocrites among the community were using. Their claim was that the men who died at Uḥud would not have died if they had stayed home, and they used it to discourage the believers from taking part in further fighting.

The Book answers the argument directly elsewhere by telling the men who said it about their brothers to try to avoid death themselves if what they said was true. The principle in this verse is the deeper answer: the term is fixed, and remaining behind provides no more protection than going out does. The two statements work together to remove the calculation from the community's thinking.

**A Report About Three Men**

The tradition preserves a report that bears on the verse's contrast between motives. Abū Hurayrah related that among the first people whose cases are decided on the Day of Judgment is a man who died as a martyr, who is made to recount the blessings he received and admits them, and who is told that he fought so that it might be said he was brave, and that it was said (Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim 1905a).

The same report describes a man who acquired knowledge and recited the Book, and a man who was given wealth and spent it, and each is told that his motive was the reputation he gained rather than the pleasure of God. The report makes the verse's distinction concrete by showing that the same act can belong to either category according to the intention behind it, and the community's literature has used it for that purpose ever since.

**The Verse's Closing Promise**

The verse ends with the statement that God will reward the thankful, the same clause that closed the sentence about the Prophet's mortality in the verse before it. The repetition ties the two sentences together and identifies the quality that carries a person through both the fear of death and the temptation of gain.

The Book's treatment of gratitude elsewhere describes it as the perception of the source of what one has, and it promises increase to those who give thanks. In this passage the word has a specific force: the people who acknowledge that their lives and their cause belong to God are the ones whose conduct holds steady when the days turn against them, and the sūrah closes the account of the battle on that note.

---
## Sūrah Āli ʿImrān 3:146

> ˹Imagine˺ how many devotees fought along with their prophets and never faltered despite whatever ˹losses˺ they suffered in the cause of Allah, nor did they weaken or give in! Allah loves those who persevere.

**Expanded Commentary**

**A Question That Measures the Community's Case**

The verse opens with the Book's idiom for abundance, asking how many there have been of a certain kind. The construction is not a request for a number; it is a way of saying that the instance before the reader is one of many.

The community at Madinah had just suffered a defeat, and the verse places that experience within a long record. The Book's habit of introducing earlier communities in this way serves a consistent purpose: the listeners are shown that their situation is not unprecedented and that the conduct expected of them has been expected of others before them.

**The Two Readings of the Verb**

The verb in the opening clause can be read as referring to fighting, or as referring to being killed. On the second reading the sentence says that many devoted men stood alongside a prophet who was killed, which is why al-Ṭabarī preferred it: the reading fits the plain sense of the preceding verses about the Prophet's mortality.

Both readings support the same lesson. Whether the prophet fought and his companions fought with him, or the prophet was killed and his companions held their ground, the sentence presents people who continued in their duty while the outcome was in doubt. The difference between the readings concerns which aspect of the earlier history is being held up, and the community's own recent experience answers to both.

**The Word for the Devoted Men**

The noun describing the companions of the prophets has been given several explanations. Some connected it with the word translated as sages in an earlier verse of this sūrah, so that the men are described by their knowledge and their devotion. Others took it as a reference to large groups, and one report gives ten thousand as the number that the singular form of the word denotes.

The variety of explanations reflects the word's rarity, and the sense that emerges from all of them is a body of people marked by seriousness and endurance rather than by any particular office. The verse places such people beside the prophets as the human material of a mission that has always required them.

**Three Things They Did Not Do**

The verse names three responses that the men did not have: they did not falter because of what happened to them, they did not weaken, and they did not demean themselves. The three words describe a single moral posture from different angles.

The first concerns the initial reaction to a shock, the second concerns the exhaustion that follows continued hardship, and the third concerns the submission to humiliation that comes when a person believes the cause has failed. The Book's descriptions of steadfastness usually concentrate on one of these, and this verse covers all three, which is why it is frequently quoted where a community is recovering from a loss.

**What Befell Them in the Way of God**

The phrase about what befell them in the way of God covers injury, loss of property, and death, and it describes these things as taking place within the activities of the religion rather than outside them. The Book uses the phrase to place the cost of a struggle inside the definition of the struggle itself.

The community at Uḥud had lost men who were dear to it, and the sūrah does not present those losses as a sign that the community had been abandoned. It presents them as what befell people in the way of God, which is exactly what the verse says the earlier companions of the prophets endured without faltering.

**The Statement About God's Love**

The verse ends with the declaration that God loves the patient, and the quality named is the one that the three preceding clauses have described in action. The sentence gives the behaviour of those men its meaning, and the same declaration appears in the Book in several places.

The Book's attachment of God's love to particular qualities is one of its ways of teaching its values. Patience, generosity, justice, and trust are each said to attract that love, and the verse before the reader places the endurance of a community under attack in that category. What a community experiences as loss is described here as the occasion of a love that no loss can remove.

**The Verse's Work in the Sūrah's Argument**

The verses immediately before this one asked the community what it had expected and reminded it of what it had asked for. This verse supplies the example that answers both questions: the pattern is not a community that avoids suffering but a community that withstands it.

The Book's method here is to argue from history to the present. The community is told that its position is ancient, that the men who held it are beyond counting, and that the conduct required of it has a record behind it. That combination is more useful to people in the aftermath of a defeat than reassurance alone would be.

**A Model of Steadiness Under Loss**

The verse has been recited by Muslim communities in every generation for the picture it draws of a body of people standing where they are needed while the outcome is unknown. Its subject is not the leaders of the mission but the ordinary people who carry it.

The sūrah presents those people as the reason the mission survives its crises. The prophets deliver the message; the devoted men absorb the losses, hold their positions, and continue. The community that reads this verse is being told which of the two roles its own losses prepare it to fill, and the next verse reports the prayer such people made.

---
## Sūrah Āli ʿImrān 3:147

> And all they said was, “Our Lord! Forgive our sins and excesses, make our steps firm, and grant us victory over the disbelieving people.”

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Restriction in the Sentence**

The verse reports that the only words of these people were a prayer, and the restriction is the point of the sentence. Faced with a defeat, the devoted men did not debate, did not cast blame, and did not announce what the community should have done differently; they asked God for four things.

The Book notices such restraint, and the verse records it as part of the description of the people it praises. The community that had just come through Uḥud is being shown what the right response to a setback looks like in the form of speech, and the model given is short enough to be memorized and repeated by anyone.

**The First Petition and the Two Kinds of Sin**

The prayer begins with a request for forgiveness of sins, and then asks for forgiveness of prodigality in affairs. Al-Qurṭūbī suggested that the first term covers the smaller faults and the second covers the greater ones, so that the two clauses together leave nothing outside the request.

The distinction, if it is accepted, reflects a pastoral concern that runs through the Book. A person who has made a serious mistake and a person who has accumulated minor ones both need to ask, and both need to know that the wording provided covers their case. The prayer teaches the community how to speak about its own failures without either minimising them or treating them as beyond remedy.

**Prodigality in One's Affairs**

The word rendered as prodigality covers waste and excess and also the act of going beyond limits. The Book uses it for the conduct of people who exceed what is due, whether in the use of property or in the pursuit of their appetites.

The verse's phrase attaches it to the whole range of a person's affairs rather than to one department of life. Such excess is not restricted to the obvious crimes; it includes the abandoning of moderation in ordinary matters, and the Book counts it among the things a community should ask to be forgiven. The prayer therefore acknowledges not only particular offences but a general tendency that needs correcting.

**The Request That Steps Be Made Firm**

The third petition asks God to make the community's steps firm, and the request uses the image of standing and walking on the ground. The Book uses the same image when it promises the believers that if they support God's cause, He will support them and steady their footing.

The request has a particular fitness at this point in the sūrah. The community's failure at Uḥud was a failure of footing, and the men whose prayer is recorded here ask for the remedy in the words that describe the problem. The Book presents such prayers as the place where people take the weakness they have seen in themselves and ask for what would correct it.

**Help Against a Named Opponent**

The prayer's final request is for help against the people who deny, and it names the opposition rather than asking for deliverance in general terms. The community that prays it is in a contest, and it asks for support in the contest.

The Book's prayers frequently name the matter at hand, and this one does so without bitterness or the request for anything beyond success in the struggle. The request is for help and not for revenge, and the difference marks the attitude the sūrah commends to a community under attack.

**Prayer in the Middle of Trial**

The verse places the prayer in the middle of the fighting rather than after it. The men described in the previous verse were in the situation the prayer addresses, and their response was to ask rather than to complain.

The Book presents this as the natural conduct of people whose trust is in God. It does not describe hours of preparation or a particular ritual; it records a short supplication made while events were unfolding. The community that recites the passage learns that the correct use of a person's speech in a crisis is to ask God for what he needs.

**Other Prayers Recorded in the Book**

The Book records prayers of this shape in many places, and the community has used them in its own devotions ever since. One passage reports the address of believers who say that they have believed and ask for forgiveness and protection from the punishment of the fire. Another reports the prayer attributed to Adam and his wife in the sūrah of the Heights, where they acknowledge that they have wronged themselves and that without forgiveness and mercy they will be among the losers. A third, longer prayer asks God not to hold the community to account for forgetfulness and error and to grant victory over those who deny.

These passages together form the Book's instruction on how to pray about one's own faults. The verse before the reader is one of the shortest of them, and its compactness has made it one of the most used.

**What the Verse Teaches About Supplication**

The order of the petitions is instructive. Forgiveness comes first, then steadiness, and only then the outcome of the struggle. A community whose own faults have been addressed can stand; a community that is standing can be helped.

The sequence also describes the priorities the Book assumes its people will have. What is asked for at the start is the repairing of the relation with God, and the request for victory comes last. The order teaches the community that its own condition is the first thing to set right when its affairs have gone wrong, and the verse records the teaching in the form of a prayer rather than a list of instructions.

---
## Sūrah Āli ʿImrān 3:148

> So Allah gave them the reward of this world and the excellent reward of the Hereafter. For Allah loves the good-doers.

**Expanded Commentary**

**Both Rewards Given**

The verse reports the result of the conduct and the prayer described in the two verses before it: God gave those people the reward of this world and the best reward of the Hereafter. The Book's promises of this kind appear in several places, and the phrasing here covers the whole of what a person can receive.

The Book does not usually promise both to those who seek only one. It tells those who want the harvest of the next life that it will be increased for them, and it tells those who want only the present one that they will receive some of it while having no share in the next. The sentence in this verse belongs to a different group, and the community at Madinah was being shown what their position could yield.

**The Reward of This World**

Al-Ṭabarī explained the reward of this world as victory, the spoils of war, and stability in the community's affairs. The phrase therefore covers the concrete goods that a community needs in order to continue: success in its engagements, the means to sustain itself, and a settled condition in which its work can go forward.

The Book states elsewhere that with God are the rewards of this world and the next, which places both in His hands rather than in the hands of circumstances. The prayer in the preceding verse asked for steadiness and help, and the answer given here describes what arrives when such a request is granted.

**The Best Reward of the Hereafter**

The second half of the sentence uses the form that marks excellence, and the Hereafter is described as the better of the two, or the most beautiful. The Book uses this comparative language in several places when it places the two lives side by side.

The arrangement does not diminish the first reward; it orders the two. The community is told that what it receives in this world is genuine and worth having, and that what is stored in the next one is better. The Book's consistent teaching about the value of the two lives appears here in a sentence that grants both, and that sentence must have carried particular weight for people who had just lost property and family.

**The Description of the Virtuous**

The verse closes by naming those whom God loves, and the term used covers people who do good and do it well. The same term appears in the Book's praise of people who spend in his way, of those who restrain their anger and pardon, and of those who keep their covenants.

The word's frequency in these contexts suggests that the Book uses it as a broad category for the conduct it commends, and the sūrah has already used it in the passage about the people for whom the garden is prepared. The verse therefore joins the steadfastness of the preceding verses with the generosity and restraint described earlier in the sūrah, and it places the whole range of such conduct under the declaration of God's love.

**The Book's Statements About Whom God Loves**

The Book attaches its love to particular qualities in a set of passages that the commentators gathered. It names the reverent, the patient, the just, and those who act equitably, and it names the virtuous as the group mentioned most often.

The variety is significant. The Book is not describing an attitude that appears in one kind of person but a set of qualities that its people are expected to hold together in their dealings. Each of the passages names a quality that appears in a different setting: worship, endurance, trade, judgment, and the settling of disputes. The sentence in this verse names the broadest of the categories, and the sūrah's readers are meant to see their own conduct inside it.

**The Link With the Verses Before It**

Read as a sequence, the three verses describe a movement: people who stand firm under loss, a prayer that asks for forgiveness and firmness, and a God who gives both the goods of this life and the better things of the next.

The arrangement gives the community a way of reading its own experience. The losses at Uḥud were real, and the sūrah does not promise that the community will recover every loss in the same currency. What it promises is that the conduct it has described is not wasted, and that the reward reaches into the situation the community is in as well as into the one that follows it.

**What the Community Heard in This Sentence**

The first listeners were people who had recently seen their dead carried back from a field they had expected to leave in better order. The verse told them that their endurance had a result and that the result would be given to them in full.

The Book's practice in these passages is to state the outcome before the history has arrived at it. The community would go on to see victories and setbacks in turn, and the sentence here teaches it to read both within a promise that the two rewards belong to the same God, and that the conduct which earns them is the conduct described in the verses immediately before.

**A Pattern for Later Generations**

Later communities have read these verses in their own circumstances, and the pattern they describe has been understood as general. The qualities required are steadiness, an honest reckoning with one's own faults, and the firm hope that God will steady what is unsteady.

The verses present that pattern without tying it to the specific events that occasioned it, which is why they have travelled so well. The battle at Uḥud is the setting for the instruction, and the instruction itself concerns the ordinary life of a community that has to keep going after something has gone badly wrong.

---
## Sūrah Āli ʿImrān 3:149

> O believers! If you yield to the disbelievers, they will drag you back to disbelief—and you will become losers.

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Address and Its Warning**

The verse addresses the believers directly and warns them against obeying those who deny, describing the consequence in physical terms: they would be turned back on their heels and would end up as losers. The warning is stated as a certainty in the form the Book uses for imminent dangers.

The community had come through a period in which advice was plentiful and its sources were mixed. The sūrah has already described a party among the People of the Book who wished to mislead the believers, and it has described the conduct of the hypocrites during the fighting. The verse gathers such advice into a single category and addresses the community's habit of listening to it.

**Who the Warning Concerns**

Al-Ṭabarī recorded that the phrase about those who deny was understood to refer to the enemies of the believers among the various groups of the time: the People of the Book, the hypocrites, and the idolaters. The community was surrounded by people who had reasons of their own for wanting it to change course.

The breadth of the reference is part of the verse's value. The Book is not warning against a single party or a single occasion; it is warning against a habit of mind in which the community takes its direction from those whose interests are opposed to its own. The Book's later passages make the same point about the company a person keeps and the counsel he acts on.

**Obedience and the Loss of Standing**

The obedience named in the verse is not restricted to formal submission. It covers the practical response of a community that follows advice and adopts a course because it has been recommended by people who do not share its commitments.

The Book had already warned the community about such counsel in the earlier passage about the People of the Book, where it described a group who wished the believers would abandon the way they had received. The warning in this verse sharpens the point: the danger is not only that bad advice might be followed once, but that following it repeatedly would move the community back to where it started.

**Turned Back on the Heels**

The image of turning back on the heels is the same one the sūrah used a few verses earlier when it asked whether the community would abandon its religion if the Prophet died. Al-Ṭabarī explained it here as a return to disbelief after faith.

The Book's use of a single image in both places links the two dangers. The possibility of apostasy was raised first as a response to the death of a leader, and it is raised again as a response to the influence of outsiders. Both are treated as the same movement away from the ground on which the community stands, and the second is presented as the more likely of the two in ordinary circumstances.

**The Word for Losing**

The last word of the verse describes people who are lost or ruined, and the Book uses the root for both meanings: to be destroyed and to lose what one has. The two senses run together in a single condition, since the person who abandons the truth loses both his standing with God and what he had built in the world.

The Book uses the word in its descriptions of the people who will regret their conduct on the Day of Judgment, and it uses it in this life as well for those whose efforts come to nothing. The verse places the community under the second use: a community that reverses its course loses the position it was given.

**The Counsel Behind the Warning**

The warning serves the sūrah's larger purpose, which has been the unity and steadiness of the community since the passage about holding fast to God's rope together. A community pulled in several directions by outside advice cannot act with the coherence the mission requires.

The Book's instructions on this point are not presented as a rejection of dealing with people of other faiths; the sūrah contains passages that treat such dealings with fairness and forbearance. The warning concerns direction and authority: the community is to take its course from its own revelation, and the counsel of those who oppose its purpose is not a legitimate source for that course.

**The Continuity With the Previous Verses**

The image of the heels links this verse to the earlier warning about the Prophet's death, and the theme of obedience links it to the community's failure at Uḥud. The verse before the reader draws those threads together.

The sūrah's account of the battle has shown what happens when a community departs from the instructions it has been given. The warning in this verse generalises the lesson by naming the source of such departures as the counsel of those who deny. The community is told, in effect, that the danger it faces after the battle is the same as the danger it faced during it, in a different form.

**What the Verse Asks of the Community**

The verse asks the believers to be careful about whose direction they follow, and it does so by describing where a particular path leads. The command is not stated as a prohibition on speaking with outsiders, nor on hearing what they have to say.

What the community is told is that the point of decision is not the sound of the advice but the identity of the source. The Book's later instruction on consultation inside the community, and its insistence that decisions rest with the believers and their messenger, are the positive form of this warning. The verse before the reader states the negative form, and the sentence that follows gives the community its alternative in a single line.

---
## Sūrah Āli ʿImrān 3:150

> But no! Allah is your Guardian, and He is the best Helper.

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Correction Introduced by the Word of Turning**

The verse begins with the particle that sets aside what has just been said and puts something else in its place. The warning in the previous verse concerned dependence on those who deny; this sentence supplies the alternative.

The construction gives the passage a sharp shape: a danger, and then the remedy stated in one line. The Book often answers a warning with a statement about God in this way, so that the community is left holding a truth rather than only a prohibition.

**The Word for Master**

The noun rendered as master or protector covers several related senses: an owner, a patron, a guardian, and the one who takes charge of a matter on behalf of another. The Book applies it to God in this passage and in others where it describes the relation of the community to its Lord.

One passage states that God is the patron of the believers while those who deny have no patron, and another, in the sūrah of the Pilgrimage, describes God as the guardian of the believers and as an excellent guardian and an excellent helper. The vocabulary of the verse before the reader belongs to that group, and the choice of it says what the community is being offered in place of the counsel of outsiders.

**The Best of Helpers**

The second half of the verse states that God is the best of helpers, and the construction is one the Book uses for the attributes it wants its people to rely on. The comparison is not with other candidates who might help adequately; it states that no helper matches the one named.

The Book states the same in a passage that tells the believers that God knows best who their enemies are and that He is sufficient as a guardian and as a helper. Another passage asks whether the community does not know that the kingdom of the heavens and the earth belongs to God and that it has no guardian or helper besides Him. The sentence in this verse gathers the same teaching into six words.

**Seeking Help From No Other**

Al-Ṭabarī stated the practical contents of the verse: it directs the community to seek refuge with God and teaches it to seek help from no other. The instruction is not limited to the crisis that occasioned it.

The Book's teaching on this point runs through its instructions about prayer, hardship, and fear. The community is told to ask God for what it needs, to rely on Him in what it undertakes, and to expect help from Him. The verse before the reader states the reason: no other source of help has the same claim or the same capacity, and a community that turns to another source for its protection is relying on something that cannot replace what it has left.

**A Short Verse With Weight**

The verse is among the shortest in the passage, and its brevity suits its function. It stands at the end of the section that dealt with the aftermath of Uḥud, and it supplies the conclusion the whole section has been building toward.

The Book uses such sentences as conclusions. After the account of a loss, the warnings about apostasy, and the reminder that death comes at an appointed term, the community is given a sentence it can carry: its master is God, and no helper is better. The sūrah does not add qualifications to the promise, and the brevity is part of what makes it memorable.

**What the Community Needed to Hear**

The believers at Madinah were in a position that invited them to look for support in several directions. They had enemies nearby, allies whose commitment was uncertain, and a group inside the city whose loyalty had been exposed during the fighting.

The verse tells them that the security they were looking for was not going to come from a rearrangement of their alliances. The Book does not forbid the making of treaties, and the sūrah refers elsewhere to covenants the Prophet had with other groups. What the sentence does is establish the order of reliance: the community's protection is from God, and any arrangement it enters into operates within that protection rather than replacing it.

**Guardianship and What It Requires**

The statement that God is the master of the believers carries obligations as well as assurances. A community under a patron is expected to follow the direction that patron gives, and the passage as a whole has been describing what that direction is.

The Book connects its promises of guardianship with the conduct of the people who receive them, and it warns against the assumption that protection continues regardless. The verse before the reader states the relationship at its simplest, and the community that reads it is expected to hear both sides of the sentence: the security offered, and the loyalty it assumes.

**The Passage Closed and the Argument Continued**

The verse closes a movement that began with the reminder that Muhammad was only a messenger and would die. The community was told that its life did not depend on the presence of the Prophet, that death comes at an appointed time, and that those who turn back harm only themselves. The close of the movement places the community under the guardianship of God.

The sūrah does not leave its readers there, and the verses that follow go on to describe the fate of those who oppose the community and the help that God gives. The sentence in this verse supplies the premise for everything that follows, and the sūrah treats it as the ground on which the community's confidence rests in every situation it meets.

---
## Sūrah Āli ʿImrān 3:151

> We will cast horror into the hearts of the disbelievers for associating ˹false gods˺ with Allah—a practice He has never authorized. The Fire will be their home—what an evil place for the wrongdoers to stay!

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Terror Cast Into Hearts**

The verse announces that terror will be thrown into the hearts of those who deny, and the form of the sentence presents the event as settled. The Book describes this casting of horror among the opponents of the prophets in several passages, and the wording is consistent across them.

One passage reports the instruction given to the angels on the day of Badr, in which God states that He will cast horror into the hearts of those who disbelieve. Another describes the expulsion of a group from their homes and the horror placed in their hearts, so that they destroyed their own houses with their own hands. A third describes the same treatment of those who supported an alliance against the community. The sentence in this verse belongs to that family.

**The Reason Given for the Terror**

The verse supplies a reason for what happens to those who deny: they associated partners with God for which no authority had been sent down. The charge is the central one of the sūrah's argument with its opponents, and the wording adds the element of warrant.

The Book's objections to the association of others with God are frequently accompanied by this observation, that the practice rests on no divine authorization. The point is not merely that the practice is wrong but that those who defend it cannot produce the grounds on which it would rest. The verse states the charge in the form of a refusal to accept a claim that had never been supported.

**The Weight of the Word for Authority**

The term rendered as authority covers proof, warrant, and the power that accompanies a legitimate claim. The Book uses it for the evidence that the prophets brought and for the license that rulers possess, and it uses it in its challenges to the opponents of the messengers.

One of the Book's recurring demands is that those who associate partners with God should bring their proof, a demand that the verse before the reader implicitly records. The absence of such authority is presented here as part of the case against the practice, and the punishment announced in the first half of the verse follows from it.

**Their Refuge Is the Fire**

The sentence then states where those who deny will end: their refuge is the Fire. The word describes a place to which a person retreats and in which he remains, and its use here forecloses the hope of escape.

The sūrah uses the same term in the passage about the reward of the reverent, where the garden is described as their refuge. The two destinations are set out in the sūrah with the same vocabulary, so that the reader meets the pair in consecutive contexts and learns to read them as the two ends of the same road.

**The Abode of the Wrongdoers**

The verse closes by declaring that the abode is evil, and it describes its inhabitants as wrongdoers. The Book applies the term to those who deny the truth and to those whose conduct damages the rights of others, and the two usages are connected.

The sūrah has used the word repeatedly in its account of the community's opponents, and it uses it in the passage about the people who fabricate claims about God. The designation in this verse places the opponents of the community, the people who associate partners with God, and those who falsify revelation in a single category, and the sentence about their abode is stated as a conclusion of the whole.

**The Report From the Return to Makkah**

The commentators connect the verse with an event after the fighting at Uḥud. The idolaters, on their way back to Makkah, regretted that they had not finished the community off, and they resolved to return and complete what they had begun. The reports state that God then cast terror into them, and they lost their resolve and continued home.

The report gives the verse a concrete occasion and shows the community what the sentence meant in its own history. The army that had just defeated them was turned back without another engagement, and the sūrah attributes the outcome to the terror placed in their hearts rather than to any change in the community's strength.

**The Book's Realism About Danger**

The verse does not tell the community that its enemies would cease to threaten it, and the sūrah's other passages acknowledge the hostility it continued to face. What the sentence establishes is where the decisive factor lies when the community is defended.

The Book describes the fear of its opponents as one of the means by which the community is protected, and it treats that fear as an arrangement rather than an accident. The community's task in such passages is to hold its position and to keep its own conduct straight, and the removal of the threat is left where the sūrah has placed it, in the hands of the one who casts dread and grants safety.

**What the Verse Establishes for the Community**

The verse follows immediately after the statement that God is the master of the believers and the best of helpers, and it shows what that guardianship had already accomplished. The community was spared a second attack by the same army that had beaten it, and the sūrah records the sparing as the work of its protector.

The placement matters for how the whole passage reads. The community is given a claim about God's protection and then an instance of it from its own recent memory, and the joining of the two leaves the believers with a basis for confidence that does not depend on their own condition after the battle.

---
## Sūrah Āli ʿImrān 3:152

> Indeed, Allah fulfilled His promise to you when you ˹initially˺ swept them away by His Will, then your courage weakened and you disputed about the command and disobeyed, after Allah had brought victory within your reach. Some of you were after worldly gain while others desired a heavenly reward. He denied you victory over them as a test, yet He has pardoned you. And Allah is Gracious to the believers.

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Promise Fulfilled at the Start**

The verse opens by affirming that God was true to the promise made to the community, and it anchors the statement in the first phase of the fighting, when the believers were overcoming their opponents with His permission. The sūrah had described the positioning of the army in the early morning, and the reference in this verse points back to the engagement itself.

The commentators connect the sentence with the early events of the day, when the enemy's standard bearers were killed and the tide seemed to be running entirely in the community's favour. The promise the verse refers to is the help the Book had given the believers, and the testimony here is that the help arrived exactly as stated before the failure set in.

**Three Failures Named in Order**

The verse then lists what happened, and the sequence is precise: the community lost heart, quarrelled among itself about the matter, and disobeyed. The order moves from an inner condition to an open act.

The arrangement describes how a collapse actually proceeds. A weakening of resolve comes first, then a division about what should be done, and then the decision to do something other than what had been ordered. The sūrah does not present the three as separate incidents; it presents them as links in a single chain, and that is how the commentators treat them when they explain the loss of the day.

**The Word for Losing Heart**

The first of the three failures is rendered here as losing heart, and the word describes a slackening of resolve, a collapse of firmness. The same root appeared in the earlier verse of this sūrah that told the believers not to falter after their losses.

The connection between the two verses is instructive. The sūrah first forbids the condition and then records the occasion on which it occurred, and the community that recites the passage hears the instruction and the history in the same sequence. What is described in this verse is not a failure of the sūrah to warn in time; it is the event that the warning had been designed to prevent.

**The Quarrel About the Matter**

The quarrel named in the verse is explained by the commentators as a dispute among the men posted on the high ground. Some of them wished to remain at their positions in accordance with their orders, while others argued for going down to secure a share of what was being gathered on the field.

Al-Ṭabarī reports that the disagreement was between those determined to hold their place and those who pressed to leave it. The episode shows the community's discipline breaking from inside, in a matter where its instructions had been explicit. The verse records the quarrel as one of the three causes of what followed, and the placement of it between the weakening of resolve and the act of disobedience shows how the three belong together.

**Two Desires in One Community**

The verse states that among the community were people who desired this world and people who desired the next, and the distinction is offered as the explanation of the quarrel. The community assembled on the field was not of one mind about what the day was for.

Al-Ṭabarī records a report that Ibn Masʿūd said he had not known, before this verse was sent down, that any of the Prophet's companions could be described as desiring this world. The report conveys the seriousness with which the earliest community received the diagnosis. The verse does not divide the community into two parties of fixed membership; it states that the two motives were present among people who were fighting side by side.

**Turned Aside in Order to Be Tested**

The sentence continues by stating that God turned the community away from its opponents in order to test it. The Book describes the same arrangement in the account of Badr, where it made each army appear small in the eyes of the other for the purpose of establishing what had been decreed.

The verse therefore refuses the reading that has the community losing by accident. The turning aside is presented as an arranged test, and the failure it exposed is precisely what the test was for. The wording keeps the community's responsibility intact while placing the outcome inside a purpose, and the two ideas are held together in a single clause.

**The Pardon Stated in the Same Verse**

The verse then states that God pardoned the community, and the pardon is announced before the passage has finished describing the fault. The commentators note that the pardon followed conduct that was grave, since disobeying an order in the middle of a battle endangers the whole force.

The Book's pattern in these passages is to name the failure and the forgiveness together, and this verse follows the pattern even in the case of a defeat. The community is not left to draw the conclusion that its position has been forfeited; it is told that the offence has been dealt with, and the correction that follows in the next verses concerns its conduct rather than its standing.

**Bounty for the Believers**

The verse closes with the statement that God is possessed of bounty toward the believers. The word covers generosity, favour, and the giving of more than is deserved, and its position at the end of a verse about failure is the point.

The Book's descriptions of God's dealings with the believers frequently end in this way, with the generosity of God named after the account of human weakness. What the community is meant to take from the verse is that its losses did not come from a shortage of divine favour, and that the favour had already produced the pardon announced in the same sentence.

---
## Sūrah Āli ʿImrān 3:153

> ˹Remember˺ when you were running far away ˹in panic˺—not looking at anyone—while the Messenger was calling to you from behind! So Allah rewarded your disobedience with distress upon distress. Now, do not grieve over the victory you were denied or the injury you suffered. And Allah is All-Aware of what you do.

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Scene Reconstructed**

The verse describes the battlefield in the hour of the collapse: the believers moving away, refusing to look at anyone, while the Messenger of God called to them from behind. The picture is assembled from three details, and each of them adds to the account.

The community's flight is presented without softening, and the sūrah reports it as a fact of its own history. The Book's willingness to describe the conduct of the believers at their weakest moment is part of what gives the passage its authority, and the verse is addressed to the people who had lived through the day.

**The Verb and the Terrain**

The verb describing the movement has the basic sense of going up, and al-Ṭabarī records a difference of opinion about what it denotes in this form. Some held that the form used here means to travel along level ground, which would fit the account of the men coming down from the high ground to the field. Others took it as describing flight up the slopes of the mountain.

Both readings describe the same disorder. On the first, the community is depicted streaming across open ground with the enemy behind it; on the second, it is scattered up the hillside. The disagreement is a reminder that the commentators were working with detailed reports of the terrain and the positions, and that they cared about getting the picture right before drawing lessons from it.

**Casting a Glance to No One**

The phrase about not looking at anyone describes a person so absorbed in his own flight that he has no attention left for those around him. The commentators explain it as not caring about anyone else.

The image is the opposite of the solidarity the sūrah has been urging on the community since its commands about holding fast together. The men on the field were not looking to one another, and the verse lets the picture carry the point without adding a reproach. What the community is shown is what its division looks like from the outside, at the moment when it mattered most.

**The Call From Behind**

The reports describe the Prophet calling after the retreating men, and the words attributed to him in the accounts are an address to the servants of God, repeated, with the call to come back to him. The verse records the call as coming from the rear, which is where the Messenger had remained with those who stood firm.

The detail is among the most affecting in the sūrah. The person the community had come out to defend was calling it back while it fled, and the reports place him among a small group holding the position. The verse mentions the call in a subordinate clause and leaves the image to do its work, and the sorrow the next sentence announces is placed in relation to it.

**Sorrow Upon Sorrow and Its Explanations**

The verse states that God recompensed the community with one sorrow upon another, and the commentators offer several accounts of what the two sorrows were. On one reading, the first was the grief of having caused the Prophet grief, and the second was the loss they suffered afterward. On another, the sorrows were the loss of the battle and the loss of the spoils, followed by the enemy's rejoicing. A further reading holds that the first was the defeat and the second the fear that the enemy would return to finish what it had begun.

Al-Rāzī adds that the retreat itself was a form of sorrow, since a person who runs away feels his own weakness. The variety of explanations reflects the density of the experience, and the verse's phrase holds all of them: the day delivered one grief after another, and the community was made to feel the weight of the whole.

**The Purpose Stated in the Sentence**

The verse attaches a purpose to the sorrow: so that the community would not grieve over what escaped it or what befell it. The teaching is that the loss of advantage and the loss of life are both to be held in a scale that does not make them the measure of everything.

Al-Rāzī explained the clause as a means of loosening the community's attachment to the goods of this world, so that it would neither be saddened by losing them nor gladdened by gaining them. Read this way, the sorrow of the day was itself an instruction, and the community's education in detachment came through the experience of losing what it had hoped to keep.

**The Discipline of Fear**

The verse's account of the collapse also treats the fear that produced it as a condition to be governed. The Book's commands about courage in this sūrah rest on the same ground as its commands about patience: the person who knows that the outcome is in the hands of God is not ruled by the prospect of loss.

The community at Uḥud had been given a demonstration of what fear does to a body of people, and the sūrah preserves the record so that later generations could learn from it. The lesson is not that the believers were cowards but that a failure of steadiness in one place spreads through everything that depends on it, and the verse supplies the sequence in which that happened.

**The Closing Statement About Awareness**

The verse ends by stating that God is aware of everything the community does. The sentence is not a threat appended to a narrative; it is the ground of the account that has just been given.

The Book knows what happened on the field, and it knows what was in the people who ran and in the Messenger who called. The community that recites this verse is told that its conduct is seen by the one who pardoned it, and the next verse continues the account by describing what came down upon the believers after the sorrow had done its work.

---
## Sūrah Āli ʿImrān 3:154

> Then after distress, He sent down serenity in the form of drowsiness overcoming some of you, while others were disturbed by evil thoughts about Allah—the thoughts of ˹pre-Islamic˺ ignorance. They ask, “Do we have a say in the matter?” Say, ˹O Prophet,˺ “All matters are destined by Allah.” They conceal in their hearts what they do not reveal to you. They say ˹to themselves˺, “If we had any say in the matter, none of us would have come to die here.” Say, ˹O Prophet,˺ “Even if you were to remain in your homes, those among you who were destined to be killed would have met the same fate.” Through this, Allah tests what is within you and purifies what is in your hearts. And Allah knows best what is ˹hidden˺ in the heart.

**Expanded Commentary**

**Security Sent Down After Sorrow**

The verse reports that after the sorrow, God sent down security in the form of a sleepiness that settled over one company of the believers. The Book describes similar gifts in its accounts of the community's earlier battles, and the parallel is exact in one of them.

The passage about Badr describes drowsiness overcoming the believers as a gift of serenity, together with rain sent down to purify them and steady their feet. The Book treats the ability to rest in the middle of a crisis as a sign of trust, and the account of Uḥud records the same gift arriving after the worst of the day had passed.

**What the Sleep Signified**

Al-Rāzī discusses the phenomenon at length and reads the sleep as evidence that God was with the community. He reports a statement attributed to Ibn Masʿūd that sleeping during battle indicates trust in God and detachment from the world, while sleeping during the prayer indicates the opposite, because the community's situation in each case is different.

The reports about the field describe believers falling asleep where they stood, with weapons slipping from their hands, and the state was so remarkable that the tradition preserved the detail. What the verse presents is a physical mercy with a moral edge: the people whose nerves had been broken by the day were given rest, and the rest was sent by the same God whose help they had doubted.

**The Company That Remained Anxious**

Beside the sleeping group, the verse sets another company that was anxious about itself and could not rest. The two groups lay on the same field under the same conditions, and the difference between them is the subject of the sentence.

The verse does not name the second group directly, but the description that follows identifies it. These were people who were worrying about their own safety and about the outcome of a decision they had opposed, and their anxiety expressed itself in the way they spoke about God. The pairing of the two companies is the sūrah's way of distinguishing the community's members by what the crisis brought out of them.

**Thinking About God What Is Not True**

The verse describes the anxious company as thinking about God thoughts that were not true, and it calls this the thinking of the Age of Ignorance. The Book uses that name for the period before the message arrived, and the comparison is severe.

The commentators explain the thought as the belief that if the community had really been on the side of God, it would not have met with such a setback. Al-Rāzī develops the point at length, warning against judging the will of God by a person's own assessment of what is pleasant or painful. The verse identifies the error as a way of thinking about God rather than as a simple mistake about tactics.

**The Question About the Decision**

The anxious company is reported asking whether they had any decision in the matter, and the sūrah's answer is that the decision belongs entirely to God. The commentators differ about who spoke the question, with one view assigning it to the hypocrites and another holding that sincere believers might have asked it in their bewilderment.

However the question is assigned, the answer stands on its own. The community is told that the outcome of the expedition was never within its own control, and the sentence removes the basis for the complaint that had begun to circulate. The answer's brevity matches the sūrah's method of dealing with the community's arguments: it states the truth that resolves the difficulty and leaves the reader to draw the conclusion.

**Al-Rāzī on Providence**

Al-Rāzī's comment on this verse includes a discussion of providence in which he argues that people should not claim to deduce the will of God from their own evaluations. His reasoning is that human beings do not possess all the measures needed to judge whether a particular event is good or harmful, and success or failure on a battlefield is one of the clearest examples.

The argument supports the verse's own structure, which contrasts the community's anxious speculation with the statement that the decision belongs to God. The Book's teaching here is that a person's limited view of the consequences of an event disqualifies him from reading the event as a verdict, and the lesson applies beyond the case of the battle.

**The Claim Made in Secret and the Answer Given**

The verse reports that the anxious group kept to themselves a claim they did not disclose openly: that if the decision had been theirs, they would not have been killed where they stood. The answer comes in a sentence that removes the premise: had the community stayed in its houses, those who were destined to be slain would have gone out to the places where they were to die.

The sentence is one of the sūrah's clearest statements of the fixed term, and it matches the verse that declares that no soul dies except by God's permission at an appointed time. The Book denies the calculation of safety on the grounds that the location of a person's death is not the variable that determines it.

**The Purpose of the Test**

The verse closes by stating that the events were arranged so that God might test what was in the community's hearts and bring it to the surface. The test is not for the purpose of gaining information but of making the truth visible.

The Book knows what a person conceals, and the Book states that God knows what lies within the breasts. The events at Uḥud made the contents of those breasts visible to the community itself, and the sūrah treats that exposure as one of the day's purposes. What follows in the passage is the community's opportunity to act on what it has been shown about itself.

---
## Sūrah Āli ʿImrān 3:155

> Indeed, those ˹believers˺ who fled on the day when the two armies met were made to slip by Satan because of their misdeeds. But Allah has pardoned them. Surely Allah is All-Forgiving, Most Forbearing.

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Day the Two Hosts Met**

The verse refers to the day the two armies met, which the commentators identify as Uḥud, and it addresses those who turned away during the fighting. The reference places the sentence within the same narrative the previous verses have been unfolding.

The retreat described here followed the departure of the archers from the high ground, when the enemy's cavalry was able to work around the community's position. The verse does not repeat the details; it names the participants and then states what the sūrah wants the community to understand about what they did and about how God dealt with them.

**Satan Made Them Slip**

The verse attributes the turning away to a slip caused by Satan, and the Book uses the same image of slipping in its account of the first human failure. In the story of Adam and his wife, Satan caused them to slip from the state they were in, and in another passage the Book warns that if people slip after the clear proofs have come to them, God is mighty and wise.

The image describes a loss of footing rather than an intention to abandon the faith, and the verse's use of it keeps the offence in its proper scale. The act was real and had consequences, and the community had been warned against exactly this. At the same time the sentence identifies the agent that caused the slip, and it does so in a way that leaves room for the pardon stated at the end.

**The Question of What Caused the Slip**

The clause about the cause of the slip has been read in two ways. One reading takes it to mean that Satan caused them to slip in part of what they had committed, meaning that the failure was confined to certain matters rather than being general. The other treats the phrase as stating that they slipped because of what they had previously done, so that the earlier offence opened the way to this one.

Al-Rāzī records both and draws the lesson that one error tends to lead to another. The two readings describe different aspects of the same event, and both agree that the community's own conduct had prepared the ground on which the slip occurred.

**Who Turned Away**

The commentators were not unanimous about the identity of those described. Al-Ṭabarī records several views: that they were believers who ran from the fighting, that they were people who had remained behind in the city, and that the group includes both those who fled toward the town and those who climbed the mountain. Another report names specific individuals among the community, and the reasons given for their flight include fear and the rumour that the Prophet had been killed.

The absence of agreement on the question of identity is itself instructive. The verse addresses a class of conduct rather than a list of names, and it describes what happened in terms that apply to anyone who does the same thing.

**Why the Reports About Individuals Matter**

The reports that name particular people, including men of standing in the community, have been read by the commentators as evidence of the scope of God's forgiveness. The people who turned away on that day were pardoned, and the pardon is stated in the same verse that records their failure.

The commentators connect the case with the Book's account of Adam, whose repentance was accepted after his error (2:37). The comparison supports the sūrah's larger purpose in this passage, which is to teach a community recovering from failure that its mistakes do not have to define it, and that the remedy has been provided.

**The Pardon Stated Without Delay**

The verse states that God pardoned them, and the pardon is mentioned in the same sentence as the sin. The sūrah does not create a period in which the community is left to wonder whether it has been forgiven.

The arrangement matches the pattern of the passage. The verses have described the disobedience, the quarrel, the flight, and the secrecy of the anxious group, and each description has been accompanied by a statement that God pardoned. The effect is to keep the community's attention on the correction that follows rather than on a debt it cannot discharge.

**The Two Names That Close the Verse**

The verse ends with two names of God: the Forgiving and the Clement. The first describes the readiness to forgive, and the second describes the quality of patience that does not rush to punish.

The pairing is used elsewhere in the Book when it describes God's dealings with communities that have failed. Clement also means forbearing and unhurried, and the name describes the way the pardon is granted: not as an immediate reaction to a fault but as the settled disposition of the one who forgives. The community that had fled from a battle is told that it has to do with a Lord whose forbearance gave it time to return.

**What the Community Learned From the Verse**

The verse teaches that a failure after faith can be pardoned, and it teaches the same thing without removing the seriousness of the failure. The community is not told that its flight was trivial; it is told what caused it, and it is told how God responded.

That combination is the heart of the sūrah's treatment of Uḥud. The community had to be able to continue after a day that exposed its weaknesses, and the Book gives it both the diagnosis and the pardon. The verses that follow turn from the battle to the lessons the community was to carry out of it, and the passage keeps the two movements in that order.

---
## Sūrah Āli ʿImrān 3:156

> O believers! Do not be like the unfaithful who say about their brothers who travel throughout the land or engage in battle, “If they had stayed with us, they would not have died or been killed.” Allah makes such thinking a cause of agony in their hearts. It is Allah who gives life and causes death. And Allah is All-Seeing of what you do.

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Prohibition and the Model Rejected**

The verse addresses the believers and forbids them to resemble those who deny in what they say about their dead. The comparison is the point of the sentence: the community is shown a way of speaking about loss and told that it does not belong to people of faith.

The Book often teaches by means of such contrasts, and the instruction here is about speech rather than about belief. What the community is told not to imitate is a habit of recording outcomes as though human decisions had controlled them, and the habit is presented as characteristic of the people who have not accepted the message.

The commentators identified the speakers of the sentence in several ways. Some held that the words came from the disbelievers in general, some that they came from the hypocrites, and one view assigns them to a particular leader among the hypocrites who is mentioned earlier in the sūrah's narrative.

The verse does not settle the question, and its wording covers the conduct rather than the names. The community is taught to recognise the sentiment wherever it appears, which is why the commentators could differ about the occasion without disagreeing about the lesson.

**The Claim About Staying Behind**

The claim the verse reports is that had the dead stayed at home they would not have died or been killed. The sentence presents death as the consequence of a decision to travel or to go out on campaign, and it treats the decision as the thing that could have been made differently.

The Book's answer is that the arrangement belongs elsewhere. Al-Rāzī put the point by saying that the verse restates what the earlier passage already established: human beings should never forget that God, not human agency, determines life and death. The claim in the verse is not merely mistaken; it takes away the one fact that gives a person security when he risks his life in a good cause.

**What the Words Were Spoken About**

Al-Zamakhsharī noted that the phrase about the brothers of the speakers carries the sense of speaking on account of them, so that the words were said because of what had happened to those men. The grief was real, and the remark was the shape it took.

That reading makes the verse a lesson about how grief expresses itself. The Book does not reproach the sorrow; it reproaches the analysis that turns the dead into victims of their own decision. The community is being taught to hold its losses without adopting a framework in which caution would have preserved anyone.

**Regret Made in the Hearts**

The verse states that God made this a source of regret in their hearts, and the commentators offered several explanations. One holds that the regret belongs to those who spoke, and that it is a fitting recompense for words that were meant to discourage others. Al-Rāzī noted that the regret may also come on the Day of Judgment for having said such things at all.

Another reading holds that the purpose was to create doubt in the hearts of weaker believers, so that the community's faith would be tested by the remarks it heard. The verse leaves room for both, and the difference between them concerns who is being corrected rather than what the correction is about.

**God Gives Life and Causes Death**

The sentence that answers the claim is a statement of divine authority over life and death, and it is the same statement that the passage has made twice already. The community was told that no soul dies except by God's permission at an appointed term, and it was told that those destined for death would have gone out to the places where they were to die.

The repetition is deliberate. The community had just heard the fatalistic argument, and the Book answers it by returning to the fact it had already established. What changes between the two statements is the context: what was first a reminder about a fixed term becomes here a response to a claim about the dead.

**The Spiritual Reading of the Sentence**

Al-Rāzī records a further explanation of the statement, according to which God gives life to the hearts of those close to Him and causes the hearts of His enemies to die. On this reading the sentence is about spiritual life and death as well as bodily.

The reading widens the verse's application without displacing its plain sense. The community is told that the one who controls the physical outcome also controls the inner outcome, and that the two are governed by a single authority. The claim made by the speakers in the verse was a claim about that authority, and the answer given restores it to its owner.

**The Closing Statement About Seeing**

The verse ends by stating that God sees what the community does. The sentence returns to the theme that appeared at the end of the passage about the retreat, and it places the community's conduct under the same observation.

The Book's statements about its knowledge are frequently placed at the end of an instruction, and the placement gives them a practical force. The community's speech about its dead, its conduct on the battlefield, and its treatment of the people who failed are all seen by the same God, and the sentence reminds the readers of the verse that no part of their behaviour is outside the account.

---
## Sūrah Āli ʿImrān 3:157

> Should you be martyred or die in the cause of Allah, then His forgiveness and mercy are far better than whatever ˹wealth˺ those ˹who stay behind˺ accumulate.

**Expanded Commentary**

**A Preference Stated in Plain Terms**

The verse states that if the believers are killed or die in the way of God, forgiveness and mercy from God are better than anything their opponents amass. The comparison is between two collections, and the sentence asks the community to weigh them.

The Book uses this comparative form when it wants to place two things side by side in the reader's mind. The wealth that the community's enemies were gathering at that time was the visible measure of success in the world, and the verse puts the forgiveness and mercy of God against it and states that the second is greater. The sentence does not deny the existence of the first; it denies its weight.

**The Two Ways of Dying**

The verse names both dying in battle and dying in the ordinary course of events, and the pairing is repeated in the following verse. The community had just watched men die at the hands of an enemy, and it had also lost people in ways that had nothing to do with the fighting.

The Book's phrasing removes the distinction between the two in terms of the promise. What qualifies a death for the mercy described here is not the manner of it but the cause in which the person was engaged, and the community is taught to stop grading its losses by how much violence attended them.

**The Qualifier "In the Way of God"**

The promise attaches to a person who dies in the way of God, and the qualifier is the important element of the sentence. The Book uses the phrase for conduct undertaken for God's sake, and it uses it in the same way in its instructions about wealth and fighting.

The community that had lost people on the field at Uḥud was engaged in precisely that cause, and the verse tells it what the deaths of those men amounted to. The claim is not that death is good; it is that the cause in which a person dies determines what his death has earned, and the reward named here is forgiveness and mercy rather than the spoils that the sermon writers of later ages placed beside it.

**What Their Opponents Amassed**

The phrase about what they amass has been explained as referring to their wealth, and also more broadly to their collecting of the vanities of this world. Ibn Kathīr took it in the second sense, which widens the contrast the verse draws.

The sūrah had earlier described the wealth that the community's opponents were gathering and had warned the believers against the love of it. The comparison in this verse therefore connects with the surrounding passages: what the enemies of the community accumulate is what their lives are aimed at, and the sentence states that the mercy that attends a death in God's cause is worth more than all of it.

**Forgiveness Named Before Mercy**

The two nouns are placed in an order, with forgiveness first and mercy second. The arrangement reflects the movement a person makes from his own record to his final state: the faults are forgiven, and the mercy follows.

The Book pairs the two often, and the pairing appears in the sūrah's earlier passages about the people whose reward is forgiveness from their Lord. The community that reads this verse in the aftermath of a defeat hears the two words attached to the men it had lost, and the sentence gives it a way to speak about them that does not depend on the fortunes of the day.

**The Book's Descriptions of the Martyrs**
