The Book expands the promise in the verses that follow this one, where it tells the community not to consider those killed in the way of God as dead, since they are alive with their Lord and well provided for. Another passage states that those who have believed and emigrated and struggled with their wealth and their lives are greater in rank with God, and that these are the ones who will triumph.

A further passage says of a certain kind of person that he would dedicate his life to seeking the pleasure of God. Taken together, these sentences describe a death that is not a subtraction from the person who suffers it, and the verse before the reader is the compact statement of what the others explain at greater length.

**The Verse as a Reply to the Talk About Staying Home**

The verse answers the argument reported in the preceding sentence, in which the death of a person was attributed to his decision to go out. The reply is not that the decision was insignificant, but that the outcome of a life consecrated to God is not on that scale.

The community was being offered a way of thinking in which caution was the highest value, and the verse replaces it with a comparison that has a different unit entirely. What is at stake is not whether a person returns safely but whether what he has done for God is met with forgiveness and mercy, and the sentence states that the second is worth more than everything the other side gathers.

**What the Community Is Asked to Weigh**

The verse asks the believers to compare two things whose value cannot be measured in the same currency. That is the nature of the instruction, and it is why the Book states it as a comparison rather than as a command.

The community that recites the passage is expected to hold the sentence in view when its own losses come. The comparison is not a consolation offered after the fact; it is a judgement about value that the community is asked to adopt in advance, so that the losses it meets do not shake the estimate on which its conduct depends.

**What the Word for Amassing Covers**

The sentence closes with a comparison between what God gives and what people gather, and Ibn Kathīr read the word for what is gathered as covering wealth and, more broadly, the accumulation of the world's vanities. The comparison is stated as a fact rather than as a recommendation: the believer is not told to despise what others collect, only to measure it against what is promised to those who die in God's cause. The verse's own subject is the death of the community's members, and the sentence answers the fear that those deaths were a loss. The fuller account of the state of the slain is given a dozen verses later, where the Book states that they are alive with their Lord and provided for (3:169), and the two passages are read together as a single answer to the same anxiety.

---
## Sūrah Āli ʿImrān 3:158

> Whether you die or are martyred—all of you will be gathered before Allah.

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Gathering That Follows Death**

The verse states that whether the believers are killed or die, they will be gathered to God. The sentence takes the two ways of dying that the previous verse named and gives both of them a single destination.

The Book uses the image of gathering and return for death in many places, and the choice of that vocabulary shapes how the community thinks about what happens at the end of a life. A person who is returned to someone is not simply extinguished; he moves into the presence of the one who sent him, and the sentence treats the two kinds of death as the same departure.

**The Book's Recurring Statement**

The Book repeats the sentence about the return to God in passages that speak about death. One states that every soul will taste death, that humanity is tested with good and with evil, and that all will be returned to God. Another states the same sequence in fewer words: every soul will taste death, and then to God all will be returned.

The sūrah of the Family of ʿImrān makes the same teaching in its own way in a later verse, where it states that every soul will taste death and that the full reward will be given on the Day of Judgment. The claim in this verse therefore belongs to the Book's basic instruction about human destiny, and the sūrah restates it at the point where the community needed to hear it most clearly.

**Why the Sentence Repeats the Earlier One**

The verse begins in almost the same words as the verse before it, and the repetition is one of the sūrah's methods. The community had heard that forgiveness and mercy are better than what the enemies of God amass; it is now told where the departed have gone.

The Book's repetitions are not idle. Each of them rests on the same truth and draws a different consequence from it, and this one supplies the fact that makes the comparison in the previous sentence reasonable. Mercy and forgiveness can be compared with wealth only if the person who dies has not simply ceased to exist.

The Book's language for death includes returning, being gathered, and going to meet God, and each of these expressions carries the sense of movement toward a person rather than movement into nothing. The vocabulary shapes the community's attitude at funerals and in grief.

The sūrah's own account of the battle uses the same orientation. The community had seen its dead carried away, and the verse tells it where those men were going. The sentence does not describe what awaits them in detail; the following verses supply more, and the community's confidence rests on the direction of the movement rather than on a picture of its stages.

**The Earlier Warning About the Appointed Term**

The sūrah has already stated that no soul dies except by God's permission at a term that has been decreed. The verse before the reader complements that statement by naming what follows the appointed end.

The two sentences together leave no room for the fatalistic argument that the community had been hearing. The first removes the possibility that human decisions control the timing of a death, and the second states that the timing is not the end of the matter. The Book's treatment of death in this passage therefore answers the argument from both directions.

**The Reward That Awaits**

The Book describes the state of those who die in the way of God in several places, and the descriptions are consistently of life rather than of loss. One passage tells the believers that those killed in God's cause should not be thought of as dead, since they are alive with their Lord and provided for.

Another passage promises that whoever leaves his home for the cause of God and dies in the course of it has his reward secured with God. A third speaks of a person who dedicates his life to seeking God's pleasure. Read with the verse before the reader, these sentences form a single teaching: the departure is real and the destination is known.

**A Sentence the Community Carries**

The verse is short enough to be held in memory, and the community has used it in its burial practices and its consolations. Brevity of this kind is deliberate in the Book, since a sentence that will be spoken at the graveside needs to be carried easily.

What the sentence provides is a fact rather than a sentiment. It does not tell the mourner how to feel; it tells him where the person has gone. The community's grief is not denied by the verse, and the sentence gives it a direction to face, which is what a grieving community most needs from its revelation, since a direction is more useful than an argument.

**The Place of the Two Verses in the Passage**

The two verses shift the passage's attention from the failures of the battle to the destiny of those who die in God's cause. The community had been given an account of its own conduct, and it now receives a statement about the men it had lost.

That shift is part of the sūrah's pastoral work. A community that has been shown its faults also needs to know that its dead are not casualties of those faults, and the Book supplies the assurance before it resumes its instructions. The verses that follow turn to the Prophet's own gentleness and to the community's practice of consultation, and the passage closes with a statement about where reliance belongs.

---
## Sūrah Āli ʿImrān 3:159

> It is out of Allah’s mercy that you ˹O Prophet˺ have been lenient with them. Had you been cruel or hard-hearted, they would have certainly abandoned you. So pardon them, ask Allah’s forgiveness for them, and consult with them in ˹conducting˺ matters. Once you make a decision, put your trust in Allah. Surely Allah loves those who trust in Him.

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Gentleness Attributed to Mercy**

The verse states that it was by a mercy from God that the Prophet was gentle with the community, and the sentence places his treatment of the men who had disobeyed within the working of divine mercy. The Prophet had every ground for harshness after the events of the day, and the verse names the quality that he showed instead.

Al-Ṭabarī identified the people concerned as the Prophet's companions and followers who had fallen short in their conduct during the battle. The sentence is therefore not a general observation about his character, though it is that too; it is a statement about how he dealt with the specific failure that the sūrah has just described.

**What Would Have Happened Otherwise**

The verse states that had the Prophet been severe and hard-hearted, the community would have scattered from around him. The word for severity describes a manner that is harsh in its treatment of people, and the hardness of heart describes a person who is not moved by their condition.

The observation is a piece of practical wisdom about leadership, and it is stated as a counterfactual. If the man who had been disobeyed had responded with contempt, the community would have broken apart at the moment when it needed to hold together. The verse gives the alternative its full weight, and then records what actually happened.

**Three Instructions in One Sentence**

The verse then issues three instructions: pardon them, ask forgiveness for them, and consult them in the matter. The sequence moves from the wrongs committed against the Prophet to the wrongs committed against God and then to the business the community shared.

Al-Rāzī explained the division by saying that the first instruction concerns what the people had done to the Prophet himself, and the second concerns what they had done against God. The third instruction reaches beyond the question of fault altogether and returns the community to the work it had been assembled for, which is a mark of how completely the failure was to be left behind.

**Consultation in the Battle's Own History**

The instruction to consult arrives after the community's most conspicuous failure, and the sūrah had described the consultation that preceded the battle. The Prophet had asked the Muslims of Madinah whether to remain in the city or to march out, and the decision to go out had prevailed.

The commentators note that the outcome of the fighting did not lead to the abandonment of the practice. The verse instructs the Prophet to seek the community's judgment in the very kind of matter that had just gone wrong, which teaches the community that a defeat is not a reason to abandon a sound method.

**The Scope of the Consultation**

The commentators restricted the command to matters of war and the ordinary affairs of the community, since revelation governed the rest. Al-Qurṭūbī and others record the view that consultation on the Prophet's part was superfluous because he received revelation, and they record the rejection of that view, noting that he consulted his contemporaries, men and women alike, on many matters.

One report quoted in the tradition has the Prophet saying that the people knew more about the affairs of this world than he did. On that basis the consultation was substantive rather than a formality. Al-Rāzī suggested that the Prophet's practice was intended to establish consultation as a settled practice of the community after him.

**Consultation as a Practice of the Believers**

The Book names consultation among the marks of the believers in another passage, where it describes people who respond to their Lord, establish the prayer, conduct their affairs by mutual consultation, and give from what they have been provided.

The instruction in this verse therefore belongs to a wider teaching. The community is not to be governed by the impulse of a single person, however well placed he may be, and the Book presents the practice as one of the qualities it praises. The sūrah places the command in the middle of the passage about the battle, which gives it a particular weight: the consultative practice survived the test of the day that exposed everything else.

**Resolve and Trust**

The verse's final instruction concerns what happens after the consultation has ended. Once the Prophet has decided, he is told to place his trust in God, and the commentators read the sentence as describing a reliance that does not rest on the quality of the deliberation.

Al-Qurṭūbī explained the sequence as a decision made after consultation followed by trust in God rather than in the process. The Book states elsewhere that whoever places his trust in God will find that God is sufficient for him, and other passages repeat the instruction in the same words. The verse is among the Book's clearest statements of the combination: the human process and the reliance that accompanies it.

**The Closing Declaration**

The verse ends with the statement that God loves those who place their trust in him, and the declaration gives the instruction its motivation. Trust is not merely a practical attitude; it is one of the qualities the Book attaches to divine love.

The sentence follows a series of instructions that reach back to the beginning of the sūrah's account of the battle. The community had been told to obey, to stand firm, to consult, and to rely, and the passage closes with the statement that the last of these qualities brings a person under the love of God. The next verse states the same teaching about help and reliance in the form of a declaration, and the passage ends there.

---
## Sūrah Āli ʿImrān 3:160

> If Allah helps you, none can defeat you. But if He denies you help, then who else can help you? So in Allah let the believers put their trust.

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Two Conditions Stated Together**

The verse sets the help of God against His withholding of help, and it states the consequence of each. If God helps the community, nothing can overcome it, and if He abandons it, no one else can take His place.

The second clause of the sentence is the one that carries the weight. The community at that moment was calculating its strength in terms of numbers, allies, and the quality of its position, and the verse reduces the calculation to a single term. The help it needed was not the kind that could be secured by arrangement.

**The Truth of the First Clause**

The first clause is stated as an absolute: when God helps, none can overcome. The Book's promises of this kind are always connected in the surrounding passages to the community's own conduct, and this verse does not suspend the connection.

The community had been helped at Badr with everything the two clauses describe, and it had been shown at Uḥud what happens when the connection is broken. The sentence does not promise that every engagement will end in victory; it states who controls the outcome, and it leaves the community's responsibilities where the earlier verses placed them.

**The Reading That Sees the Two Battles**

The commentators frequently read the two clauses of this verse as a description of the community's recent history: God helped the believers at Badr, and He withheld His help at Uḥud. The verse would then be a statement of the difference between the two days rather than a conditional promise.

The reading gives the sentence a particular force for its first listeners, who had lived through both days within a year. The sūrah had already explained the change in terms of the community's own conduct, and this verse states the result in terms of help received or withheld, without adding any qualification that would soften the contrast.

**The Second Reading of the Closing Phrase**

The phrase rendered as after Him, or thereafter, can be read in two ways. Some take it as referring to time, so that the question is who could help after God has withheld His help. Others take the pronoun as referring to God Himself, so that the sense is who could help apart from Him.

Al-Rāzī records the second reading, which harmonises the verse with the sentence in the sūrah that declares God to be the master of the believers and the best of helpers. On either reading the question in the verse is unanswerable, and the function of the sentence is to leave the community with no alternative to reliance on God.

**Who Else Could Help**

The Book states the same thought in several places. One passage asks whether the idols that people invoke besides God could undo a harm if God willed it, or withhold a mercy if He willed that, and concludes that God is sufficient and that the faithful place their trust in Him.

Another passage reports the declaration of the believers that nothing will befall them except what God has destined, that He is their protector, and that in Him the believers put their trust. The verse before the reader states the same principle in the form of questions, and the community is left to answer them.

**The Command to Trust**

The verse closes by instructing the believers to place their trust in God, and the instruction is the practical conclusion of the two questions. Trust in the Book's usage is not the abandonment of effort; the sūrah has just commanded consultation, preparation, and firmness.

Trust, in the passages that explain it, is what accompanies a person's work once he has done what he can. The Book names it among the marks of the believers in a passage that describes hearts trembling at the remembrance of God and faith increasing when His revelations are recited. The community's task, on this understanding, is to act and then to leave the outcome with the one who holds it.

**A Verse Recited Throughout Life**

The sentence has been carried by Muslims in every generation as a statement of where reliance belongs, and it is used in circumstances far removed from a battlefield. Its usefulness in ordinary life comes from its structure: it disposes of the question of who controls outcomes before any particular difficulty is described.

The Book states the same teaching in other passages with different images, and the community's teachers have placed this verse at the head of their instructions about trust. The reason is that it gives the doctrine in a form that can be recited in a single breath, which is what a person needs in a moment of fear.

**The Close of the Passage's Movement**

The verse brings the passage that began with the rumour of the Prophet's death to a close. The community had been told that the messenger would die, that death comes at an appointed time, that the failures of the day had been pardoned, and that its dead had been gathered to God. It is now told where help comes from.

The sequence is one of the sūrah's characteristic movements, from a crisis to its lessons and then to a statement about God that reorders the community's understanding of its position. The verses that follow move on to new material about the fate of those who deny and the signs God has given, and the sentence about help and trust stands as the ground on which the community is expected to read everything that comes next.

---
## Sūrah Āli ʿImrān 3:161

> It is not appropriate for a prophet to illegally withhold spoils of war. And whoever does so, it will be held against them on the Day of Judgment. Then every soul will be paid in full for what it has done, and none will be wronged.

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Statement About the Prophet**

The verse declares that it is not for any prophet to defraud, and the sentence is a defence of the Prophet's integrity in a matter where it had been questioned. The sūrah addresses the subject in the aftermath of a battle, when property had changed hands and accusations were circulating.

The commentators connect the verse with the distribution of the spoils of war and with reports that an item of value had gone missing, after which some people suggested that the Prophet himself might have taken it. Al-Ṭabarī's preferred reading is that the verse was revealed simply to inform people that such a thing does not happen with a prophet.

**What the Verb Covers**

The verb rendered as defraud is used specifically for taking part of what should be shared out, and the commentators treated the verse as dealing with the spoils above all. Some held that it concerned a valuable piece of cloth lost after one of the battles, and others that it concerned the failure to distribute spoils equitably.

The discussions show how seriously the community treated the smallest misappropriation of common property. The verse's scope was then extended by the commentators to cover every kind of embezzlement and every misuse of a trust, since the principle in a sentence forbidding a prophet to take what is not his must apply even more plainly to anyone lower in station.

**The Different Occasions Reported**

Beyond the reports about the spoils, some commentators connected the verse with the archers who left their positions and were given no share of the spoils they had been trying to secure. Others linked it to expeditions whose spoils had been distributed before the fighters returned. Al-Ṭabarī records a further view that the verse has nothing to do with spoils at all, and that it forbids the Prophet to withhold any part of the revelation entrusted to him.

The variety of these reports does not affect the verse's meaning, since each of them concerns a trust and the taking of what is not one's own. The fact that so many occasions were proposed is a sign of how directly the sentence spoke to the community's situation and of how many of its problems touched the same principle.

**What the Fraudster Brings on the Day of Judgement**

The verse states that whoever defrauds will bring what he took on the Day of Resurrection. The image is a concrete one: the misappropriated thing accompanies the person who took it into the presence of God.

The commentators quote reports that describe people arriving on that day with the objects they had wrongfully taken hanging from their necks, and the description matches the sūrah's later verse about those who were miserly, who will be collared on the Day of Resurrection by what they hoarded. The Book's imagery in such passages gives property a weight that follows its possessor, and the sentence is designed to make a person think about what he will be carrying.

**The Payment Made in Full**

The verse then states that every soul will be paid what it has earned in full and will not be wronged. The sentence widens the view from the specific offence to the general settlement.

The Book uses this formula at the close of its instructions about property, and it does so because the fear of loss and the desire for gain shape more of human conduct than most people admit. The community is told that the account will be accurate and complete, and the phrase about no one being wronged answers the anxiety that a person might lose what he deserves.

**The Reports About Public Trusts**

The commentators connect this verse with reports about officials collecting alms who returned and said that part of the property was the community's and part had been given to them as a gift. The Prophet's response, according to those reports, was to ask whether the man's gift would have come to him had he stayed in his father's or his mother's house.

The question exposes the practice as a concealed payment for a public office. The verse's principle reaches such cases directly, and the tradition has used it as the ground for its rules about gifts to officials, just as it has used it against the taking of anything that belongs to the common fund.

**The Generalization Beyond the Spoil**

Though the occasion of the verse concerned the spoils of war, the commentators generalised it, and their generalisation has governed the community's treatment of the subject ever since. Any mishandling of public property falls under the sentence, and the tradition classifies the taking of spoils before distribution among the serious offences.

The verse's placement in the sūrah supports the wider reading. It comes after a long passage about the community's conduct in battle and before verses that discuss the difference between those who seek the contentment of God and those who earn His anger. The subject of trust follows naturally from the account of a community that had just been tested in a matter involving property.

**What the Verse Teaches About Leadership**

The sentence begins with the word for any prophet, and the point is that the office itself excludes such conduct. The person who conveys God's message is entrusted with the message and with the community's affairs, and the verse removes him from any suspicion of serving his own interest.

The community that hears the sentence is being told what it should expect from its leaders and what it should refuse to believe of them without grounds. The sūrah corrects a rumour and establishes a principle at the same time, and the next verse contrasts two figures so that the principle can be seen in human terms.

---
## Sūrah Āli ʿImrān 3:162

> Are those who seek Allah’s pleasure like those who deserve Allah’s wrath? Hell is their home. What an evil destination!

**Expanded Commentary**

**A Question That Places Two Figures Side by Side**

The verse asks whether a person who pursues the contentment of God is like a person who earns a burden of anger from God and whose refuge is the fire. The question expects a negative answer, and the whole sentence is built to make the difference visible.

The Book uses such comparisons in several places, and the commentators gathered the passages where the righteous and the wicked are set against each other in the same form. The sentences are not arguments in the technical sense; they present two conditions and leave the reader to judge whether they could possibly be the same.

**The One Who Pursues Contentment**

The phrase about pursuing God's contentment describes a person whose aim is the pleasure of God, and the Book attaches this aim to specific forms of conduct: keeping a trust, speaking the truth, spending from what one has, and holding to an agreement.

The verb carries the sense of seeking and following after what is desired, and its use in this verse makes the pursuit continuous rather than a single decision. The person described is not one who happens to have pleased God on an occasion but one who is in the business of seeking that pleasure, and the sūrah has just described what such conduct looked like on the field where the community's trust was tested.

**The One Who Earns a Burden of Anger**

The second figure is described as one who returns with anger from God laid upon him, and the word for what he earns describes something borne, a load that a person carries away with him. The Book uses the same expression in the passage about those who earned anger among the earlier communities.

The pairing of the two descriptions is exact in structure and total in contrast. One person is going toward something he seeks, and the other is coming away with something he has brought upon himself. The verse places the two directions in one sentence without adding any argument for the difference, and the question's answer is left to the reader's own judgement.

**The Refuge That Is Named**

The verse states that the man's refuge is the fire and calls it an evil journey's end. The word for refuge describes the place a person ends up in and settles into, and the word for the journey's end describes what an undertaking finally produces.

The two terms together describe a movement that has been completed. The person who spends his life in pursuit of what is other than God arrives somewhere, and the verse names the destination in the imagery the sūrah has used through this passage. The exclamation with which the sentence closes is one of the Book's standard ways of marking a matter as beyond dispute.

**The Contrast as the Book's Method**

The Book's method of teaching by contrast appears throughout this sūrah. The verses about the two companies on the field, the two desires in the community, and the two faces on the Day of Resurrection have prepared the reader for a sentence as direct as this one, and the verse gathers their various contrasts into a single question.

The method is effective for a community that had just seen both kinds of people among its own members. The comparison in this verse is not between the community and its enemies alone; it is between two possible directions for a human life, and the sūrah has shown both of them at close range within the space of a few days.

**The Anger of God in the Book's Language**

The Book refers to anger from God in several passages, and it uses the expression for those who have incurred punishment after the truth has come to them. The phrase in an earlier sūrah describes the state of a people on whom anger was placed, and the same term appears in the sūrah's own description of the People of the Book.

The vocabulary adds weight to the verse's contrast. The person seeking God's contentment is working toward an aim that can be achieved; the person who has earned anger carries an outcome that follows from what he has done. The book presents the two not as two feelings of God but as two results that differ as much as the destinations named in the verse.

**What the Question Leaves Undecided**

The verse states the contrast and stops, and the decision it implies is left to the reader. The Book often ends its arguments in this way, presenting the two paths and letting the plain sense of the comparison do the work.

The next verse states that the two groups are ranked in degrees with God, which answers the question's premise directly: they are not equal in rank. The sūrah's treatment of its themes in consecutive sentences is one of its features, and the answer supplied in the following verse tells the community what to conclude from the question it has just been asked.

**The Aim as a Way of Life**

The verse describes a life in terms of what it is pursuing, and the description applies to the ordinary conduct of a person as much as to a decisive choice. The Book's word for contentment covers the approval that a person seeks in what he does, and the pursuit of it gives shape to the ordinary details of a person's dealings.

The community at Madinah had just been through an examination of exactly this kind. The spoils, the positions on the hill, and the question of who took what were all part of an afternoon in which the community's aims had shown themselves, and the verse that sets the two aims side by side is written for people who had seen them both at work.

---
## Sūrah Āli ʿImrān 3:163

> They ˹each˺ have varying degrees in the sight of Allah. And Allah is All-Seeing of what they do.

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Statement of Rank**

The verse states that the two groups are ranked in degrees with God, and it closes with the statement that God sees what they do. The sentence answers the question posed in the verse before it by denying the equality the question had proposed.

The commentators read the ranking in two ways. Al-Ṭabarī observed that the two groups are at different levels in this world, since their conduct and the conditions it produces differ. Al-Rāzī read the verse as a statement about the next life, where those who are punished occupy different levels of suffering just as those who enter the garden occupy different levels of delight.

**Ranks and the Book's Teaching About Reward**

The Book states repeatedly that people will be dealt with according to what they have done, and the language of degrees is one of its ways of expressing the principle. One passage states that each will be assigned ranks according to his deeds, and another states that God will pay every soul in full for what it has earned.

The verse before the reader takes its place in that group. The sentence does not describe the rewards and punishments in detail; it states that they are graded, and the grading itself teaches the community that conduct has a weight which the settlement will reflect. The Book's readers are expected to see the point and to draw the consequence for how they live.

**Why Degrees Rather Than a Single Division**

The Book's descriptions of the Hereafter include levels for the people of the garden and levels for those who are punished, and the tradition of interpretation discussed the differences at length. The verse in this sūrah supports the picture by stating that both groups are ranked.

The idea has a practical dimension for the community that recites it. If the outcome were a single division, a person who had already secured his place would have no reason to improve it, and a person who had made one mistake would have no reason to recover. The statement that the ranks differ maintains both incentives, and it matches the Book's frequent exhortation to compete in good works.

The phrase that the ranks are with God places the scale of measurement outside the community's own estimates. The Book uses the same construction when it commends those who strive with their wealth and their lives and describes them as greater in rank in the sight of God.

The phrase matters because human communities tend to construct their own hierarchies from wealth, descent, and reputation. The verse states that the ranking that counts is held elsewhere, and the sūrah has been demonstrating the difference between the two scales throughout its account of the community's history.

**The Statement That God Sees What They Do**

The verse closes with a sentence the sūrah has used at several points, and the repetition connects the passage's theme of divine observation to the subject of ranks. The God who ranks the two groups is the God who sees what each of them does.

The Book's statements about its own knowledge are frequently attached to instructions and warnings in this way, and the effect is to make the sentence a matter of practical consequence rather than abstract doctrine. The community is told that no conduct is invisible and that the scale of ranks is applied by the one who has full information about the lives it is applied to.

**The Contrast With Human Judgement**

The sūrah's account of the battle included the community's own arguments about who had acted correctly and who had not. The verse places the assessment of conduct in the hands of God and does not invite the community to settle the question for itself.

The Book's consistent teaching about the ranking of people is that the judgement belongs to God, and the community is warned elsewhere against claiming purity for itself. The sentence in this verse gives the same warning in the form of a statement, and it leaves the community free to attend to its own conduct rather than to compare itself with others.

**The Doctrine as a General Principle**

The verse's closing statement that ranks exist with God can also be read as a general affirmation that reality is arranged in levels. The commentators noted this reading and connected the sentence with the Book's descriptions of the gradations among the creatures.

Read in that way, the verse teaches the community to think of the world as orderly rather than flat, with differences of degree that reflect the wisdom of the one who made it. The reading does not displace the verse's primary application to the two groups, and it gives the sentence a range that extends beyond the immediate contrast, since a claim about the order of creation is also a claim about the one who ordered it.

**What the Sentence Contributes to the Passage**

The verse is short and stands between the comparison of the two figures and the reminder of the favour God has shown the believers. Its brevity suits its function, which is to close the comparison without elaborating it.

The passage as a whole moves from the question about trust and defrauding to the two destinies and then to the favour of the message itself. The sentence in this verse marks the end of the contrast and prepares for the shift to gratitude, and the community that reads the sequence is given a reminder of the scale on which its conduct will be weighed, which is a matter the sūrah has raised repeatedly in its account of the battle.

---
## Sūrah Āli ʿImrān 3:164

> Indeed, Allah has done the believers a ˹great˺ favour by raising a messenger from among them—reciting to them His revelations, purifying them, and teaching them the Book and wisdom. For indeed they had previously been clearly astray.

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Favour Named at the Outset**

The verse states that God conferred a favour on the believers by sending them a messenger from among themselves, and the sentence places the coming of the Prophet at the head of everything the community had received. The word for favour covers a gift and an act of kindness, and the Book uses it for the blessings that carry the greatest weight.

The choice of the term matters after the passage that has just ended. The community had been shown its failures in detail, and the verse now directs its attention to the gift that made its position what it was. What follows in the sentence describes the work the messenger did among them.

**A Messenger From Among Themselves**

The phrase describing the messenger as one of the community's own was the point that the community's opponents found hardest to accept. The Book reports the objections of those who asked whether they should follow a human being like themselves, and the reasoning behind their refusal is recorded in several passages.

The verse presents the very fact they objected to as the favour. A messenger drawn from the community could speak its language, know its conditions, and share its life, and the Book elsewhere describes the Prophet as concerned for the suffering of the believers and merciful toward them. The gift consisted partly in the closeness of the messenger to the people he was sent to.

**Reciting the Signs**

The first of the messenger's works named in the verse is the recitation of God's signs to the community. The phrase describes the delivery of the revelation in the form in which it was received, and the community's first relationship with the message was through hearing it.

The Book's descriptions of the Prophet's mission consistently begin with recitation, and the sūrah of the Congregation uses the same sequence in describing the messenger raised among the unlettered people. The recitation comes first because everything else rests on it: the purification and the teaching described in the same sentence both depend on the community's hearing of what was sent down.

**Purification and Teaching**

The verse then names purification and instruction in the Book and in wisdom. The word for purification describes the cleansing of a person from what defiles him in conduct and in character, and the word for wisdom describes the understanding that accompanies knowledge.

The order of the two is instructive. The Book's arrival changes the people it addresses before it informs them, and the tradition of interpretation reads the sequence as a description of the moral and intellectual formation that the message produced in a community that had not possessed either. The sūrah's own account of the community's transformation presumes exactly this work.

**The Book and Wisdom Together**

The pairing of the Book and wisdom in the verse appears in several passages about the messenger's task. One describes the prayer of Abraham for a messenger who would recite the signs, teach the Book and wisdom, and purify the people. Another, in the sūrah of the Cow, describes the sending of the messenger in nearly the same words.

The recurrence of the wording links the mission of the Prophet with the supplication of the patriarch from whom the community traced its descent. The Book presents the coming of Muhammad as an answer to a prayer recorded in its own earlier passages, and the verse before the reader states the fulfilment of that request as a favour to the believers.

The verse closes by describing the community's condition before the messenger came: it had been in clear error. The Book uses the word for straying and for a state of confusion from which a person cannot find his way without help.

The description is not a reproach but a measure of the change. The sūrah had already referred to the community's history before the coming of the message, and the sentence gives the contrast its full extent. The community's standing, whatever its lapses, was the result of a transformation that it had not produced for itself, and the verse names the source.

**The Objections the Verse Answers**

The Book records the objections that the message was brought by a human being rather than by an angel or accompanied by treasure, and it records the answers given in several passages. Some of those answers point to the ordinary working of God's arrangements for human guidance.

The verse before the reader supplies another kind of answer by treating the human messenger as the content of the favour rather than an obstacle to it. The community is told that the form of the gift suited its need, and the sentence makes the cause of the opponents' objection into the reason for the believers' gratitude.

**What the Verse Asks of the Community**

The verse's opening words about favour set the tone for the community's response, which the sūrah develops in the verses that follow. Gratitude for the message and obedience to the messenger are the same thing in the Book's presentation, and the sentence establishes the ground on which the community's obligations rest.

The passage around this verse has dealt with the community's failures, its losses, and the conduct required of it. The sentence about the messenger's coming places the whole of the account within a benefit that the community had received, and the effect is to make the obligations that follow read as the natural response to a gift rather than as burdens imposed on a failing people. The favour is stated in the past tense, as something already given, and the community's task is to live in a way that answers it.

---
## Sūrah Āli ʿImrān 3:165

> Why is it when you suffered casualties ˹at Uḥud˺—although you had made your enemy suffer twice as much ˹at Badr˺—you protested, “How could this be?”? Say, ˹O Prophet,˺ “It is because of your disobedience.” Surely Allah is Most Capable of everything.

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Question Asked After the Defeat**

The verse addresses the community about the affliction that had befallen it and notes that the community had already inflicted a wound twice as large on its opponents. The question that follows is the one people were asking: where had this come from?

The Book reports the question and then supplies the answer in its own words. The members of the community who asked it were trying to reconcile their losses with the promise of help they had received, and the verse takes up their difficulty directly rather than leaving it unanswered. The answer it gives is addressed to the whole community and not to a faction within it.

**The Comparison Between Badr and Uḥud**

The commentators worked out the arithmetic behind the reference to a double wound. Al-Ṭabarī reports that the believers lost seventy men at Uḥud, while at Badr they killed about seventy of the idolaters and took seventy more as prisoners, which amounts to twice the number in the sense that the prisoners could have been executed.

Other explanations were offered as well: that the community had routed its opponents twice, once at Badr and once in the early part of the fighting at Uḥud, while it had been routed only once. The differences among these readings concern how the accounting is done, and the verse's point survives all of them: the community's losses were smaller than those it had inflicted.

**The Answer Given in the Verse**

The answer to the question is that the affliction came from the community itself, and the sentence is stated as a command to the Prophet to say it. The Book repeats the principle in another passage, where it states that whatever good befalls a person is from God and whatever evil befalls him is from himself.

The sentence is one of the most direct statements of responsibility in the Book, and it follows a passage in which the community's failures have been described in detail. The verse does not attribute the defeat to the enemy's strength or to fate; it attributes it to the conduct of the people who suffered it.

**The Conduct That Brought the Loss**

The commentators identify the conduct in various ways that all point to the same events. Some held that the community was afflicted because it had ransomed the prisoners of Badr rather than putting them to death, obtaining worldly wealth in exchange for a military advantage. Others held that the cause was the disobedience of the archers, whether by leaving their positions, pursuing the spoils, or fleeing later in the day.

Al-Rāzī and al-Ṭabarī record these views without settling on one. What the explanations share is that the loss followed from decisions the community had made, and the verse's answer holds all of them: the affliction came from the community's own side.

**The Question as It Was Actually Asked**

The reports explain the question of whence this came as arising from the rout during the battle, and the commentators note that it was sometimes phrased in a way that carried an implication: if this is a true prophet, why did the defeat take place?

The verse treats the question as a serious difficulty and answers it without impugning the questioner. The Book's manner in such passages is to give the community the explanation it needs, and the sentence here does so in four words before going on to state the underlying truth about God's power.

**Why the Answer Was Necessary for the Community**

A community that had been promised help and had then been defeated had two ways of explaining what had happened. It could conclude that the promise had failed, or it could conclude that the community had failed, and the verse states the second.

The first conclusion would have destroyed the community's confidence in its message. The second preserved the message and directed the community's attention to its own conduct, which is the only one of the two factors it could do something about. The sūrah's whole treatment of the battle follows this line, and this verse states it in the plainest available terms.

The verse closes by stating that God is powerful over all things, and the sentence places the community's conduct and its consequences within the scope of that power. The Book uses the declaration at the end of passages about both mercy and punishment.

The phrase prepares for the verses that follow, which will describe what happened to those who stood firm and what happened to those who fell. The community's losses and its victories alike are held inside the same power, and the declaration that closes this verse prevents either of them from being read as an accident.

**The Lesson the Community Drew**

The verse has been read by later generations as a statement of a general principle: that a community's setbacks cannot be blamed on its enemies alone, and that the Book directs it to examine its own conduct first.

That reading is supported by the Book's treatment of the matter elsewhere and by the uses to which this verse has been put in the community's teaching. The question the community asked after the battle is one that every generation asks after its own losses, and the answer supplied in this verse is the one the sūrah has been preparing from the beginning of its account, with its descriptions of the quarrel, the pursuit of spoils, and the failure to hold the position that had been assigned.

---
## Sūrah Āli ʿImrān 3:166

> So what you suffered on the day the two armies met was by Allah’s Will, so that He might distinguish the ˹true˺ believers

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Wound Attributed to God's Permission**

The verse states that what befell the community on the day the two hosts met happened by God's permission, and it adds that the event served the purpose of making the believers known. The sentence is the sūrah's summary of the battle's place in the divine arrangement.

The wording sits beside the answer given a verse earlier, where the community was told that the affliction came from itself. The two statements are not in competition; the Book holds them together, and the commentators treat the pair as the complete account of what happened on the field. The community's conduct produced the loss, and the loss occurred within a permission that God had granted. The sentence also guards the community against reading its defeat as abandonment, since what happened took place within a permission rather than outside the knowledge of God.

**Reconciling Permission With Responsibility**

The Book states in another passage that whatever good comes to a person is from God and that whatever evil comes to him is from himself, and it uses the same division in this sūrah. The two halves of the statement describe different aspects of a single event: the good is granted, and the harm is the consequence of conduct.

The commentators applied the distinction carefully, since a community that hears only the first half drifts toward fatalism and one that hears only the second drifts toward despair. The verse before the reader supplies the first half for a community that had already been given the second, and the pairing is the Book's usual way of teaching its people to hold both truths at once.

**What Permission Means in the Sentence**

The term rendered as permission describes the granting of leave, and its use here states that the event happened within the scope of God's will rather than outside it. The Book uses the term for many kinds of event, from the arrival of rain to the delivery of a message.

One passage states that no calamity or blessing occurs on the earth or in a person's own self without being recorded before it is brought into being. The verse before the reader makes the same claim about the day of fighting. The community is told that its losses were not an interruption of the arrangement but a part of it, and that the permission under which they occurred was not withdrawn afterward.

**The Purpose Stated in the Sentence**

The clause about knowing the believers uses the same expression that the sūrah applied to the events of the battle in an earlier passage, and the commentators explained it in the same way. The knowledge described is the kind that becomes evident rather than the kind that is acquired.

The community had learned from the day who among its members would hold a position under fire and who would not. The verse states that this disclosure was one of the purposes the event served. What the community received, along with its losses, was a clearer understanding of itself, and the sūrah treats the understanding as part of what the day was for.

**The Day the Two Hosts Met**

The phrase naming the two hosts is the sūrah's standard way of referring to Uḥud, and it appears in the passage about those who turned away. The wording keeps both sides of the engagement in view and presents the battle as a meeting of two bodies rather than as a disaster that struck the community alone.

The Book's naming of the event in this way keeps its readers from reading the day as an isolated misfortune. What happened was a battle between two gathered forces, and the fact that one of them suffered more than it expected is stated in the same passage that explains why.

**The Wound as a Means of Disclosure**

The verse's arrangement of the two clauses makes the disclosure a purpose of the wound rather than an incidental result. The community was tested, and the test was intended to show what it contained.

The Book describes trials in this language throughout, and the sūrah had already used it in its account of the alternation of days. The community that understood the sentence would stop reading its losses as evidence that it had been abandoned and start reading them as information about itself, which is the reading the rest of the passage supports.

**The Consolation in the Statement**

The sentence is not a reproach. The verse immediately before it had told the community where its affliction came from, and this sentence places the same event within a purpose that God had willed.

That combination is the sūrah's method of consolation after the battle. The community is not allowed to excuse itself, and it is not allowed to conclude that the loss was meaningless. The next verse completes the sentence by naming the other group the day had exposed, and the community is thus given the full picture of what its wounds had accomplished.

**The Sentence's Place in the Sequence**

The verse stands at the head of a short passage that runs through the statements about the hypocrites, the challenge to those who claimed the dead could have been saved, and the declaration about the martyrs. It supplies the frame for all three.

The passage as a whole answers the questions the community was asking after the battle, and it does so in an order that moves from the general arrangement to the particular conduct. The community's loss, its enemies' intentions, and the state of its dead are each placed within the sentence's scope, and the verse that follows names the first of the groups the day had exposed.

---
## Sūrah Āli ʿImrān 3:167

> and expose the hypocrites. When it was said to them, “Come fight in the cause of Allah or ˹at least˺ defend yourselves,” they replied, “If we had known there was fighting, we would have definitely gone with you.” They were closer to disbelief than to belief on that day—for saying with their mouths what was not in their hearts. Allah is All-Knowing of what they hide.

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Second Group Named**

The verse continues the purpose stated in the verse before it and names the hypocrites as the other group that the day had exposed. The construction treats the two groups as outcomes of the same event, and the sūrah has been distinguishing them since its account of the march began.

The pairing is the sūrah's way of showing what a trial does in a community. The same hardship that showed who among the believers would stand also showed who among them had never been committed, and the verse states both results in consecutive sentences without softening either.

**The Call to Come and Fight**

The verse reports the appeal made to the group: come, fight in the way of God or defend. The commentators explain the second alternative in several ways. Some read it as a call to fight in self-defence if they would not fight for God's cause, so that they would at least not be counted among the cowards.

Al-Ṭabarī understood it as a call to remain on the field and form ranks, even if no fighting followed, so that the community's numbers would appear greater to the enemy. All of the readings describe the same intention behind the appeal: the community needed bodies in its line, and the group was being asked for the minimum.

**The Excuse They Offered**

The group's answer is recorded in the verse: had they known there would be fighting, they would have followed. The commentators connect the exchange with the withdrawal of a leader of the hypocrites and about three hundred others before the fighting began, which the sūrah mentioned in its account of the army's departure.

The excuse's content is a claim about their own judgement rather than about their loyalty. They presented their departure as a correct assessment of the situation, and the verse records the claim so that the community could see the reasoning for what it was. [UNVERIFIED: the number of three hundred men in the withdrawal, which the commentaries give without a chain I have examined.]

**How Their Answer Has Been Read**

Al-Rāzī considered two ways of taking the group's statement. On one reading they genuinely believed that no fighting would take place and expected only a standoff. On the other, they expected that if anything happened it would not be a battle but a massacre, and their departure was prompted by the certainty of defeat.

Both readings, al-Rāzī observes, describe an attitude that the verse calls hypocritical rather than sincere. The group had joined the expedition and then left it on the basis of a private calculation, and the sūrah places that calculation among the things the day had brought to light.

**Closer to Disbelief Than to Belief**

The verse states that on that day they were closer to disbelief than to belief. Al-Rāzī draws a careful lesson from the wording: the Book does not call a person who has pronounced the testimony of faith a disbeliever, since even here it describes the group as nearer to one than the other rather than assigning them to disbelief outright.

Other commentators took the sentence to mean that the group's outward conduct was nearer to disbelief while their inward state was disbelief altogether. The two readings differ over how the sentence should be applied, and the discipline the first of them recommends has been influential in the community's treatment of those who profess the faith while falling short of it.

**Saying With Their Mouths What Was Not in Their Hearts**

The verse describes the group as saying with their mouths what was not in their hearts, and the phrase is the Book's standard description of hypocrisy. It appears in this sūrah's warning against taking confidants from outside the community, and it appears in the sūrahs that deal with the groups in Madinah who watched the community's fortunes before committing themselves.

The Book's descriptions of such people are consistent: they speak the language of the community while their loyalties remain available to whoever seems to be winning. The verse before the reader places the conduct of the group at Uḥud in that category, and the report of their answer provides the evidence.

**God Knows What They Conceal**

The verse closes with the statement that God knows best what they conceal, and the sentence returns to the theme that runs through the passage. The community could see the withdrawal and hear the excuse; the verse states that the full contents of the matter were known to God.

The Book attaches this reminder to its descriptions of hypocrites in many places, and the effect is to remove the possibility that a person might manage his appearance while keeping his conduct out of account. The community is told that the assessment of the day's events is not limited to what was visible on the field, and the sentence about concealment ends the verse on that note.

**What the Verse Teaches the Community**

The verse shows a community being asked to look at itself after a crisis, and it shows that the crisis divided its members by what it brought out of them rather than by what they had claimed beforehand.

The sūrah's treatment of the conduct it describes is severe, and it is also explanatory: the group's reasoning is set out so that the community could recognise it in future. The verses that follow turn to the claim they made about the dead, and the sūrah answers it in terms that the whole community could apply to itself.

---
## Sūrah Āli ʿImrān 3:168

> Those who sat at home, saying about their brothers, “Had they listened to us, they would not have been killed.” Say, ˹O Prophet,˺ “Try not to die if what you say is true!”

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Argument Restated**

The verse reports a group saying of their brothers, while they themselves sat at home, that had those brothers obeyed them they would not have been killed. The claim is the same one the sūrah answered earlier in its account of the people who spoke about those who had travelled or campaigned.

The repetition is deliberate. The community had been told not to resemble the speakers of that sentence, and the verse before the reader now reports the claim a second time and answers it with a challenge. The Book's repetitions of this kind mark the matters that needed the most attention, and the argument about the dead was evidently one of them.

**The Description of the Speakers**

The verse describes the speakers as sitting at home while they spoke about their brothers, and the participle marks their position throughout. They were not among those who had gone out.

The commentators identified them as the hypocrites, and some connected the verse with the leader of that group and his companions. The comment on this passage also notes that the brothers in question could be blood relatives as well as brothers in the faith, and the grief of the community at Uḥud touched many households. The claim the verse reports was therefore being made about people who were close to the speakers as well as about fellow believers.

**Why the Counterfactual Fails**

Al-Rāzī's comment on this verse explains the logical problem with the claim. The speakers asserted what would have happened under circumstances that had not occurred, which in effect claims knowledge of what God would have done had things been otherwise.

The sūrah had already given the answer to such claims when it stated that those who were destined to be killed would have gone out to the places where they were to die even if the community had stayed in its houses. The claim that obedience to the speakers' advice would have preserved the dead assumes that the appointed term can be moved, and the Book denies that assumption on grounds that were explained earlier in the passage.

**The Challenge Issued in Reply**

The verse's answer takes the form of a challenge: then ward off death from yourselves, if what you say is true. The Book uses this form when it wants a claim to be recognised for what it is, and the challenge here is addressed to people who were sitting safely at home.

The demand is impossible, and its impossibility is the argument. The men who claimed that a different decision would have saved their brothers were being told to demonstrate their power over death in their own case first. The Book's method in such sentences is to make the implication of a position visible, and the group's claim collapses as soon as it is stated in the challenge's terms.

**The Persons and the Address**

The challenge is addressed to the speakers as a body, and the Book reports their words before answering them so that both parts of the exchange are preserved. The community that recites the passage hears the claim and the answer together.

The sūrah's practice in the whole passage is to leave its readers with the exchange rather than with a conclusion. The listeners are expected to recognise the form of the argument when they meet it again, whether in their own speech or in the talk of others, and the verse supplies them with the reply in a form short enough to remember.

**The Connection With the Earlier Warning**

The passage that forbade the believers to imitate those who spoke in this way had already stated that God gives life and causes death. The verse before the reader returns to the same subject from the other side, addressing the people whose words the community had been told not to adopt.

The connection gives the passage its unity. The first statement warned the community about the sentiment; this verse shows the sentiment being answered directly; and the verses that follow give the community the truth about the state of those who had died. The three movements follow one another in the sūrah's usual order, from instruction to argument to consolation.

**The Book's Teaching About Death in the Passage**

The sūrah has stated several times that death comes at an appointed term and by the permission of God, and it has denied that human arrangements can change the time. The verse before the reader treats the community's losses as falling under that teaching rather than outside it.

The claim that the group was making would have required the appointed term to depend on a decision about whether to march or stay, and the Book's statements about the term exclude that. The community's dead had died when they died because the term had arrived, and the sūrah's answer to the claim rests entirely on that fact.

**The Verse's Function in the Sequence**

The verse prepares the ground for the declaration about the martyrs that follows it. The community had been hearing arguments about whether the dead had died needlessly, and the answer to those arguments is given first in the form of a challenge and then in the form of a statement about where the dead now are.

The order is effective for people in grief. The Book refutes the claim before it consoles, and the refutation removes the framework in which the community's losses would have looked like a waste. What remains, when the argument has been dealt with, is the sentence about the living, and the community is given it in the next verse.

---
## Sūrah Āli ʿImrān 3:169

> Never think of those martyred in the cause of Allah as dead. In fact, they are alive with their Lord, well provided for—

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Prohibition of Thinking Them Dead**

The verse forbids the believers to regard those who were killed in the way of God as dead, and it states what they are instead. The instruction addresses the community's grief directly, and it also answers the arguments that the preceding verses reported.

The wording is a prohibition rather than a description, and the commentators read it as directed at the way the community was speaking about its losses. The people who had died on the field were being discussed in the terms the hypocrites had supplied, and the verse replaces those terms with its own account of their state.

**The Word for Those Who Were Killed**

The verse uses the verb for being killed, which describes a death by violence, and it applies the phrase about the way of God to it. The community had just buried men who had died in exactly that manner, and the verse does not avoid the word for what happened to them.

The Book's willingness to name the violence is part of the consolation's honesty. The sentence does not tell the community that the men had not been killed; it tells them not to consider those killed in God's cause as dead. The distinction between the manner of the death and the state of the dead is the whole content of the instruction.

**The Statement That They Are Alive**

The verse states that they are alive with their Lord, and the commentators discussed what kind of life is meant. The Book's language is used in the passage about the martyrs in another sūrah, where the believers are told not to say that those killed in God's cause are dead, since they are alive, though the community does not perceive it.

The two verses together give the teaching its shape. The life is real and it is not perceptible to the community that remains, and the phrase about being with their Lord locates it in a state that the Book describes without setting out its stages. The community is not told how to picture the state; it is told the fact that governs how it should speak.

The verse adds that they are provided for, and the word describes the supply that sustains a living thing. The participle's form indicates a condition that continues rather than an act completed.

The Book uses the same term for the provision it gives in this life, and the commentators read the sentence as a statement that the men who died in God's cause have been given something better than what they left. The community at Madinah had lost men who had been supporting households, and the verse tells it that the dead have not been left without provision.

**The Book's Other Statements About the Martyrs**

The Book returns to the state of those who die in God's cause in several places. One passage promises that those who emigrate for God's cause and are then killed or die will be given a good provision, and it names God as the best of providers. Another promises that those killed in God's cause will not have their deeds rendered void.

A third passage describes the company of the prophets, the truthful, the martyrs, and the righteous as those with whom the obedient will be gathered. The verse before the reader is the shortest of these statements, and the others fill in its content.

The verse in the sūrah of the Cow adds the observation that the community does not perceive the state of the martyrs. That clause explains why the instruction in this sūrah is phrased as a prohibition: the community's senses reported only the burial.

The Book's teaching here concerns the limits of what people can observe, and it asks them to speak on the basis of what they have been told rather than on the basis of what they can see. The community that had watched the fighting and the burials is told that its observation did not extend to the matter it was now discussing.

**What the Verse Says About Death**

The sentence is one of the Book's clearest statements that death is not the end of a person's existence. It describes a transition from one state to another rather than a cancellation, and it places the dead in the care of their Lord.

The Book's treatment of death in the passages about the martyrs is the sharpest form of a teaching it states in general terms elsewhere, where it describes every soul as tasting death and returning to God. The verse before the reader applies the general teaching to a particular case that the community was grieving, and it gives the community language for it that does not depend on what the community could see with its own eyes on the day of the burial.

**Why the Statement Follows the Argument**

The declaration about the martyrs comes after the sūrah has dealt with the claim that the dead could have been saved, and its placement is part of its meaning. The community had been told to stop making the argument about whether the men should have gone out, and it is now told where they are.

The passage thus moves from a refusal of the wrong question to the statement of the right fact. The community's losses are not explained away, and the status of the dead is not left to the estimation of the survivors. The next verse continues the description of their state and adds the detail that they are aware of those who remain behind.

**The Requests of the Slain**

The Book's account of those who died in God's cause includes the report that they ask to be sent back to the world so that they may die again in His way, a report that al-Rāzī and al-Ṭabarī record from the traditions attached to this passage. The request is the clearest evidence of the state the verse describes, since a person content with what he has received would not ask to exchange it for a repetition of the experience that brought him there. What the next verse adds, that they rejoice in those who have not yet joined them, belongs to the same picture. The community in this world is told that its dead are aware of it, and the warning about the bars between the living and the dead is answered by the two sentences rather than by any claim about how the awareness works.

**Where the Dead Are**

Al-Rāzī considered the reading that the verse means the slain will be alive later, in the Hereafter, and rejected it. His argument is that everyone will be alive in the Hereafter, so the sentence would say nothing distinctive, whereas the Book's statement that the slain are provided for and rejoicing in those who have not yet joined them shows that something is being said about their state now. On his reading the phrase means that they are alive at that moment, in proximity to their Lord, and that God knows them as such. The verse and its companion in the sūrah of the Cow were used extensively in the community's theology for the position that souls are alive between physical death and the resurrection, against those who taught otherwise. The traditions describe the state of souls at that stage in several ways, and the Book's verses leave the question of where the dead are unanswered, which is why the commentators described the matter with caution and left the detail to God.

---
## Sūrah Āli ʿImrān 3:170

> rejoicing in Allah’s bounties and being delighted for those yet to join them. There will be no fear for them, nor will they grieve.

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Joy Attributed to the Martyrs**

The verse continues the description of the men who were killed in the way of God and states that they are exulting in what God has given them from His bounty. The participle carries on from the previous verse's sentence, so that the reader is given a picture of an ongoing condition.

The Book's descriptions of the Hereafter often include the joy of those who have arrived, and the joy is always presented as a response to what God has given rather than as a possession. The men described in this verse are not said to be enjoying what they earned; they are said to be rejoicing over what has come to them from another's generosity.

**The Word for Bounty**

The noun rendered as bounty describes favour and generosity, and it appears in this sūrah at the end of the passage about the battle, where God is described as possessed of bounty toward the believers. The word's recurrence ties the reward of the martyrs to the same generosity that the sūrah had named for the community as a whole.

The choice of the term keeps the description from becoming a calculation. The Book does not present the state of the dead as the payment of a wage that they had coming; it presents them as recipients of a gift, and the joy the verse describes is the joy of people who have received far more than their deeds could have secured.

**The Second Joy in the Sentence**

The verse adds that they rejoice in those who have not yet joined them from among the believers who remain behind. The commentators explained this in a range of ways: that they are glad at the prospect of their brothers arriving where they are, that they are glad for the safety of those still alive, and that they take pleasure in knowing that the survivors will not be harmed by what frightened them.

The explanations differ in detail, and they agree about the direction of the joy. The men who have died are not described as absorbed in their own condition; their attention extends to the community they left, and the verse makes their concern for those behind them part of their state.

**The Pair About Fear and Grief**

The verse closes with the statement that no fear shall come upon them and no grief shall be theirs. The pair of terms appears throughout the Book as the description of the condition of those who are secure with God, and it answers the two anxieties that the community at Madinah was living with.

The Book repeats the promise to the believers, to those who follow guidance, and to those who do good in several passages. The two terms cover the future and the past: fear is the apprehension of what is coming, and grief is the weight of what has already happened. The verse announces that the men in question have been delivered from both.

**To Whom the Closing Statement Belongs**

The commentators discussed whether the clause about fear and grief applies to the martyrs or to the believers who are still alive. Some read it as belonging to the martyrs, whose state is described as wholly free of both. Others read it as describing the condition that the surviving believers are promised if they follow the same path.

The two readings are not far apart. The sentence's position at the end of a verse about the martyrs favors the first, and the community that heard it would have taken the second as well. The Book's promises in such passages are frequently read by the tradition in both directions, and the practice is consistent with the way the Book's language works.

**The Book's Uses of the Pair**

The promise that no fear will come upon a group and that they will not grieve appears in the Book's descriptions of the believers, of those who follow the guidance of God, and of the people of the earlier scriptures who believed and did good. The pairing is one of the Book's standard forms of assurance.

Its frequency means that the community reciting this passage had met the phrase before. The verse before the reader applies it to the men who had died at Uḥud, and the application is the point: what the Book promises to the believers in general is stated here for the particular people whose deaths the community was mourning.

**What the Passage Achieves**

The whole passage, from the direction of the day in the divine permission to this description of the dead, is arranged to answer the questions a community asks after a loss. The verses deny that the dead had died by mistake, refuse the argument that different conduct would have saved them, and then state where they are.

The consolation the Book offers is not a denial of the loss. The community had lost men it could not replace, and the verses do not say otherwise. What they give is a description of the state of the dead that makes the loss bearable without making it smaller, and the community is expected to carry both the grief and the description.

**The State of the Martyrs in the Sūrah's Teaching**

The sūrah's statements about those killed in God's cause make up a short body of teaching: they are alive, they are with their Lord, they are provided for, they are glad, they are free of fear and grief, and they are aware of those who remain. The Book assembles these statements in its passages on the subject, and the community's teaching has used them ever since.

The verses that follow this one return to the condition of the believers who are still alive and to the warning against the attitudes the battle had exposed. The account of the martyrs stands between, and it supplies the community with the fact it needed in order to continue its work.

---
## Sūrah Āli ʿImrān 3:171

> They are joyful for receiving Allah’s grace and bounty, and that Allah does not deny the reward of the believers.

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Continuation of the Description**

The verse continues the sentence about those who were killed in the way of God, and it adds a further element to the state described in the two verses before it. The men are said to be rejoicing in a blessing and a bounty from God, and the sentence closes with a statement about the reward of the believers in general.

The passage has been building a single picture across three verses: alive with their Lord, provided for, glad, aware of those who remain, and free of fear and grief. The verse before the reader supplies the ground of their joy and the assurance that the reward of such people is not lost.

**Blessing and Bounty Distinguished**

The two words in the sentence are not synonyms. The first describes a good condition that a person is given, and the second describes favour that goes beyond what is due, the generosity of a giver who is not paying a debt.
