The pair is used in the Book at the close of several passages about divine giving, and the sūrah had already used the second term when it described God as possessed of bounty toward the believers. The men who died are said to rejoice in both, and the sentence therefore presents their state as one that combines a settled condition with an ongoing generosity.

**The Negation of Loss**

The sentence states that God neglects not the reward of the believers, and the wording denies the possibility that the reward is either lost or reduced. The Book uses the same formula elsewhere: one passage declares that God does not discount the reward of those who do good, and the sūrah about the Repentance repeats the phrasing at the end of a list of the hardships the believers endure.

The community needed the sentence. The arguments it had been hearing suggested that the men who died had thrown their lives away, and the verse answers the suggestion by denying the premise of any wasted deed. The reward is stated to be in the keeping of a God who does not allow it to disappear.

**Why the Assurance Is Placed Here**

The assurance stands at the end of the account of the martyrs because the sūrah has been dealing with a community that had reason to feel its sacrifices were lost. The Book does not require the community to treat the loss as insignificant; it requires it to trust the account that will be settled later. The dead had left households behind, and the survivors had been told by their own critics that the losses had been avoidable.

The Book's answer does not dispute the losses; it asserts the accounting. The sentence places the reward in a register that the community could not see, and it tells the believers that nothing they had given in the way described in the passage had been forgotten.

**The State Between Death and Resurrection**

The passage's description of men who are alive, glad, and aware of those still living gave the community's teachers a great deal of material, and the tradition used these verses in its teaching about the state of the soul after death and before the resurrection. The Book provides the fact in a few words and leaves the stages unstated.

The sūrah of the Cow states that those killed in God's cause are alive, adding that the community does not perceive it. The two passages together establish the reality of a state that the living cannot observe, and the tradition's discussions of the subject begin from them.

**The Report About the Slain of Badr**

The commentary tradition records that after the battle of Badr the Prophet addressed the enemy's dead and asked whether they had found what their Lord had promised them to be true, and that when he was asked why he spoke to the dead, he replied that they could not hear him any better than the dead could.

The report is part of the tradition's evidence for the awareness of the departed, and it is placed alongside these verses in the commentaries. What the verse before the reader establishes is the state of the believers who died in God's cause, and the reports belong to the same subject in the community's teaching.

**Reflections on Time and the Departed**

The commentators noticed that the passage describes the people who have died as aware of those who have not yet joined them, and they discussed how such awareness relates to the sequence of events as the living experience it. Time as measured by the living may not be the measure of the state the verses describe.

The Book does not settle such questions, and the tradition's discussions of them have remained the work of scholars rather than a matter of doctrine. The verses state what the community needed to know, and they leave the rest, which is a pattern that the Book follows consistently in its descriptions of the unseen.

**What the Verse Establishes for the Believers**

The sentence's last clause speaks of the believers in general, and it draws the community reading the passage into the same assurance that has been given about its dead. What is not neglected for the martyrs is not neglected for anyone who follows their path.

The community is thus given a statement it can rely on in every situation in which its efforts seem to have produced nothing. The verses that follow describe the community's answer to a call made while its wounds were still fresh, and the assurance stated here is part of the ground on which that answer was given. The verse does not promise visible results; it promises an account that will be complete, and the sūrah's next verses show the community what response it was expected to make after the fighting had ended.

---
## Sūrah Āli ʿImrān 3:172

> ˹As for˺ those who responded to the call of Allah and His Messenger after their injury, those of them who did good and were mindful ˹of Allah˺ will have a great reward.

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Summons After the Wounds**

The verse describes those who responded to God and the Messenger after they had been wounded, and it promises a great reward to those among them who acted well and remained mindful of God. The phrase places the response after the suffering, and the order is the point of the sentence.

The incident is well known in the sūrah's history. On the day after the fighting, with the community's wounded still being tended and its dead not yet counted, the Prophet called the men who had marched the previous day to set out with him in pursuit of the Makkan army.

**The Call and the Place of Assembly**

The reports describe the community assembling despite its condition, with the Prophet himself among the wounded, and marching a few miles from Madinah to a place called Ḥamrāʾ al-Asad. The force was smaller than the one that had fought the day before and in worse condition. The reports note that the men who answered the call included those who had been injured the day before, and that the place they reached lay several miles out on the road the enemy army had taken.

The verse's phrase about responding after being wounded therefore describes something quite specific. The community was not summoned at a time when enthusiasm was easy; it was summoned when the cost of the previous engagement was visible to everyone, and the verse records that the call was answered. The sūrah mentions the wounds before it mentions the response, and that order has shaped the way the passage has been read ever since.

**The Arrangement That Prevented Another Battle**

The reports describe the steps the Prophet took to prevent the Makkans from turning back toward Madinah. A man from a tribe with which the Prophet had a treaty was sent to tell the Makkans that the Madinans were pursuing them in far greater numbers than before, now including all those who had stayed behind during the fighting.

The community also lit a great many campfires at night within sight of the Makkan camp, so that the enemy would judge its numbers from the fires. The Makkans abandoned their intention to return, and the sūrah reports the outcome in the verse that follows this one. The arrangement shows how much of the affair turned on what each side believed about the other, and the community's own uncertainty was answered by the success of the ruse.

**What the Phrase About Responding Means**

The phrase about responding to God and the Messenger identifies the merit of the people described, and it does so by naming the two directions of the summons. The community's response was not to a leader's preference but to a call that carried divine authority.

The sūrah has used this vocabulary throughout its account of the campaign, and it uses it here for the group that answered when the answer was difficult. The Book's descriptions of merit are frequently attached to the difficulty of the act rather than to its scale, and the verse before the reader places a march of a few miles in that category because of the condition of the men who made it.

**The Reading That Points to the Lesser Badr**

A minority of commentators connected these verses with the appointment for a return engagement that the two sides are said to have made after Uḥud, with the meeting set a year later at the site of Badr. On that account the believers went out at the appointed time, found no enemy there, and bought goods at a market before returning home.

The reading changes the occasion but not the lesson. Whether the community marched in pursuit of the army that had beaten it or out to a meeting that its opponents failed to keep, the verses praise people who answered a summons when their own condition made compliance costly.

**The Condition Attached to the Reward**

The verse promises a great reward to those among them who were virtuous and mindful of God, and the qualifier distinguishes within the group that went out. The sūrah has already shown that the community's ranks included people whose aims varied, and the sentence keeps the distinction in view.

The requirement is the combination the sūrah has named repeatedly: good conduct and the awareness of God. The men who answered the call were not all alike in their motives, and the reward named in this verse belongs to those whose action was accompanied by the quality the sūrah has been teaching throughout the passage. The conditional form keeps the community from supposing that the march itself, apart from its motive, secured the promise.

**The Encouragement the Book Gives to Pursuit**

The Book addresses the same situation in another passage, where it tells the believers not to falter in the pursuit of the enemy and reminds them that their opponents were also suffering, while the community had hopes that the others did not have.

The encouragement in that verse and the account in this one belong together. The Book treats the decision to keep pressing an opponent as a matter that follows from the community's hope, and the men described in this verse made that decision while their wounds were still fresh. The difference in prospects between the two sides is presented in that passage as a practical advantage, and not merely as a consolation for the hardships of the march.

**The Model the Verse Supplies**

The verse offers the community a picture of what recovery from a defeat looks like: the fighting ends, the losses are counted, and then the community answers the next call. The Book presents that response as something more than a military decision.

The sūrah's readers have been given an extended account of a failure followed by correction, and this verse begins the account of what the corrected community did. What the Book shows is a body of people who had been told the cause of their loss and who then acted in accordance with the correction rather than with their fear. The next verses describe the report that reached them on the road and the reply they made to it, and the passage closes with a sentence about the source of the fear they were being asked to feel.

---
## Sūrah Āli ʿImrān 3:173

> Those who were warned, “Your enemies have mobilized their forces against you, so fear them,” the warning only made them grow stronger in faith and they replied, “Allah ˹alone˺ is sufficient ˹as an aid˺ for us and ˹He˺ is the best Protector.”

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Warning That Reached Them**

The verse reports what people said to the community on the road: that a force had gathered against them, and that they should be afraid. The commentators identify the speakers in two ways, either travellers who had passed the Makkan contingent and carried the news on to Madinah, or the hypocrites who had been discouraging the community from fighting all along.

The content of the message is a report of the enemy's strength. The men receiving it were wounded, fewer in number than before, and in no condition to meet a renewed attack, and the report was designed to produce the reaction the verse's next clause denies.

**The Reply Recorded in the Verse**

The community's reply was that God is enough for them and that He is an excellent guardian. The phrase has remained one of the prayers most used by Muslims in danger, and the Book uses the same declaration in other passages: in the sūrah about Repentance the Prophet is told to say that God is sufficient for him, and in the sūrah of the Crowds the faithful are described as saying that God is sufficient for them.

The reply's structure is the exact answer to the warning. The report said that a force had gathered; the response named the one on whom the community relied. The sentence does not deny the report and does not discuss the numbers.

**The Effect of the Warning**

The verse states that the warning increased the community in faith, and the statement reverses what the report was meant to achieve. Warnings of this kind work by narrowing a person's attention to the danger; in this case the effect was to turn the community's attention to its reliance.

The Book describes similar reactions in other passages, where the believers are said to have grown firmer when they were tested. The sentence is a statement about the community's responsiveness, and the Book's praise of it is praise of the way the report was received rather than of the report itself. The sentence is one of the Book's regular teachings about the way faith works: the same event can produce fear in one person and confidence in another according to what each of them trusts.

**The Disposition Behind the Reply**

The sentence describes the community's reaction as an increase in faith rather than as a display of courage, and the distinction matters. The men who went out had been told what they would find, and their reply indicates where their judgement of the situation rested.

The Book does not present their confidence as a calculation about the enemy's willingness to fight. The Makkans had been eager to return, and the community knew it; its security rested on something other than an assessment of the balance of forces, and the verse's wording reflects that. The men who spoke this reply had been asked to be afraid, and their answer shows what they had already decided to rely on before the question was put to them.

**The Deterrent and Its Results**

The reports describe how the threat was turned back. The message carried to the Makkans was that the Madinans were pursuing them in far greater numbers than before, and the many campfires lit within sight of the enemy's camp supported the claim.

The Makkans concluded that another engagement would be unwise and abandoned their plan, and the believers returned without a battle. The enemy turned back toward its own city, and the community came home without further losses, which is the outcome the next verse describes in the language of blessing and bounty. The verse before the reader records the community's reply at the moment of the warning, and the fruits of that reply are described in the verse that follows.

**The Prayer in the Community's Practice**

The declaration that God suffices and is an excellent guardian has been used by Muslims at the outset of difficulties, and the Book contains it in more than one place. The sūrah of the Prophets and the sūrah about Repentance both use the same formula in different situations.

Its frequent repetition in the Book has made it one of the most recognisable sentences of prayer in the community's life. The verse before the reader places it on the lips of a wounded company on the road from Uḥud, and the tradition's use of it has been shaped by that setting ever since.

**A Reading of the Verse's Wider Application**

One reading of the passage draws a wider lesson from it: that a person whose concern is with God should not be discouraged when people devoted to worldly interests unite to oppose him, since their opposition is a sign of the difference between the two orientations rather than of the man's error.

The reading is applied to the interior life rather than to the battlefield, and the commentators who offered it did so without displacing the verse's plain sense. The Book's sentences about trust have been used in this way throughout the community's teaching, and the verse's wording supports the extension.

**What the Verse Teaches About Fear**

The verse closes the exchange without adding a threat of its own, and the next verse states the command that follows from it. The community had been asked to be afraid and had answered with a statement about sufficiency, and the sūrah treats that answer as the correct one.

The teaching is taken up in the verse that follows, where the source of the fear is identified and the community is directed to the fear that belongs to its faith. The passage thus moves from a report of danger to a discipline about what a person should be afraid of, and the sūrah's dealings with the community's insecurity reach their sharpest expression in the sentence about Satan and his friends.

---
## Sūrah Āli ʿImrān 3:174

> So they returned with Allah’s favours and grace, suffering no harm. For they sought to please Allah. And surely Allah is ˹the˺ Lord of infinite bounty.

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Return Described**

The verse states that the community returned with blessing and bounty from God and that no harm had touched it, and it adds that the men had pursued the contentment of God. The sentence describes the outcome of the expedition that the previous verses introduced.

Al-Ṭabarī explains that the community came back unharmed by the enemy, since no second battle took place. The sentence supplies the outcome of the decision reported in the previous verse, and it does so in the language of gift rather than of achievement. On the reading that connects the passage with the appointment at Badr a year later, the return was from that meeting, where no fighting occurred at all. Both readings describe a homecoming without losses.

**Blessing and Bounty Distinguished**

Al-Rāzī drew a distinction between the two words: the blessing may refer to goods of this world, such as the safety and the provisions of the journey, while the bounty refers to the good of the Hereafter. The sentence therefore covers both portions of what the Book promises to those who obey.

The pair had appeared in the earlier description of the martyrs, and the repetition links the two groups. Those who died in God's cause and those who came back safely from the pursuit are described with the same vocabulary of divine generosity, and the passage presents both outcomes as gifts.

**Pursuing the Contentment of God**

The phrase about pursuing God's contentment appears earlier in the sūrah, where the verse contrasts the person who seeks it with the one who earns anger, and the two verses are connected by the same words. The men who went out after Uḥud are described by their aim, and the aim is the one the sūrah has named as the mark of the righteous.

The Book's use of the same phrase in both places gives the passage a symmetry. The community that had been instructed about trust and reward is shown in action, pursuing the same contentment that the earlier verse described as the object of a good life.

**The Book's Promises to Those Who Obey**

The Book attaches both kinds of good to the obedience it commends. In one passage it tells the believers that God will give them help and a victory that is near, describing the gift as something they long for. In another it tells them not to falter in pursuing the enemy and reminds them that they have hopes their opponents do not share.

The verse before the reader fits this pattern. The community's decision to march was answered with safety and with generosity, and the sūrah records both as a single outcome of a single decision. The promises in the two passages come from different moments in the community's history, and the Book states them with the same confidence that obedience and gift belong together.

**What "Untouched by Evil" Covers**

The phrase covers safety from the harm that had been feared, and the commentators read it as a statement about the community's condition rather than only about its bodies. The men had gone out wounded and returned without further losses, and the sūrah notes the fact without elaborating it.

The detail matters in the passage's economy. The community had been told that it would be tested and that its conduct would determine the outcome, and the expedition after Uḥud was the first occasion on which it could apply what it had learned. The verse records that the application went well.

**The Name That Closes the Verse**

The sentence ends with the declaration that God is possessed of tremendous bounty, and the phrase echoes the close of the earlier verse about the pardon the community had received. The same generosity that covered the failure at Uḥud is named here for the success of the pursuit.

The repetition gives the two moments the same ground. The community's pardon and its reward both come from a giver whose generosity is not measured by the merit of the recipients, and the sūrah's readers are expected to hold both statements together when they consider what the community had been through.

**The Confidence That Was Restored**

The two expeditions stand side by side in the sūrah: the march that ended in defeat, and the march that ended in safety and gain. The community had lost confidence in the first, and the second restored it.

The Book uses the pair to show that a community's condition is not fixed by a single day. The sūrah had explained the first outcome in terms of the community's conduct and had promised pardon; the second outcome follows the corrected conduct and is presented as what such conduct produces. The reports describe the men setting out with their wounds still fresh only days after the defeat, and the safe return gave the community a second memory to place beside the first.

**The Pattern the Passage Teaches**

Read with the verses before it, this sentence describes a community that had been told its losses came from its own hands, that had accepted the correction, that had answered a call while still wounded, and that had returned with what the Book calls blessing and bounty.

The sequence is the sūrah's answer to the frustration of the earlier passage. It shows that the community's position with God had not been forfeited by the defeat, and it gives the readers of the sūrah a model of recovery that does not depend on the specifics of the campaign. The next verses leave the fighting behind and take up the sūrah's wider arguments, and the account of the expedition stands as the community's working example of what it had been taught.

---
## Sūrah Āli ʿImrān 3:175

> That ˹warning˺ was only ˹from˺ Satan, trying to prompt you to fear his followers. So do not fear them; fear Me if you are ˹true˺ believers.

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Warning Traced to Its Source**

The verse identifies the fear that had been stirred up in the community as the work of Satan, who frightens his friends. The report that reached the community on the road was presented as information about the enemy, and the verse states what was behind it.

The commentators read the sentence as a statement about how the warning worked rather than only about who delivered it. Al-Qurṭūbī and al-Ṭabarī explain that Satan inspires the disbelievers to frighten the believers, so that the community's resolve would fail before its opponents had done anything. Naming the source is the Book's way of reducing a threat to its true size, and the sentence does this by identifying the influence behind the report rather than by disputing the details of the report itself.

**Satan's Friends**

The phrase describing the friends of Satan identifies those whose cause the fear serves. The Book uses the expression in its description of the people who follow their impulses and forget the remembrance of God, and it describes them as a party that is bound to lose.

The verse before the reader attaches the party to the fear it was promoting. The community is told that the people whose threats it was dreading were acting as agents of an influence that had no claim on the outcome, and the sentence reduces the threat to a single source. The phrase also shows who the community's fear would have served, since the threats came from people whose cause the Book had already described as lost.

**The Word Applied to Human Beings**

The commentators note that the Book uses the term for human beings as well as for the unseen creature, and this allows the verse to be read as applying to the disbelievers and hypocrites themselves. The sūrah's earlier passage about the community's confidants describes men whose speech carries the same suggestion.

The Book's usage of this kind is deliberate, and it teaches its readers to judge conduct by its character rather than by the nature of the actor. The verse before the reader describes an influence that works through human speech, and the sentence does not require the community to identify who was whispering in order to resist it.

**The Command Not to Fear Them**

The verse forbids the community to be afraid of the group whose threats had been reported. The command's object is the fear itself rather than the danger, and the Book's instructions about fear are usually phrased in this way.

The community's situation gave the fear a foothold. Its men were wounded, its ranks thinned, and its opponents known to be eager for a second engagement, and the Book does not tell the community that the danger was imaginary. It tells it that the fear of the enemy is not the fear it should be governed by, and the next clause supplies the alternative.

**The Command to Fear God**

The alternative is the fear of God, and the Book uses the same instruction in other passages. One states that God is more deserving of the community's fear if its members are believers. Another tells the people who were entrusted with the scripture not to fear the people and to fear God instead. A third instructs the community to be mindful of God as it is due.

The command places the two fears side by side, and the Book's teaching in all of these passages is that a person cannot be governed by both. What the community is told to fear is the one whose judgement matters and whose protection is effective, and the sentence treats the fear of anything else as a misplacement of the same instinct.

**The Condition Attached to the Command**

The verse closes with the phrase that the community's faith depends on its answer to this command, and the conditional form gives the sentence its weight. The Book attaches such conditions to its instructions when it wants to describe what a person's claim of faith amounts to in practice.

The clause does not suggest that the community's faith was in doubt. It sets out the practical content of the claim: a person who fears his enemies more than he fears God has given his fear to something other than the one he professes to worship, and the sentence states the matter in that direct form.

**Fear as a Discipline of the Community**

The Book treats the fear of God as one of the governors of conduct, and it uses the term alongside mindfulness and reverence in its instructions. The community is told in another passage that God warns it about Himself, which places the awareness of God's judgement at the centre of its self-understanding.

The instruction in this verse belongs to that body of teaching. The community had just been shown how fear had nearly governed its decision about marching, and the sentence supplies the correction. The Book's remedy is not the removal of fear but the redirection of it, and the sūrah has used the vocabulary of mindfulness since its opening verses, where the Book is described as a guidance for those who guard themselves against what they fear.

**The Affair of Uḥud Closed**

The verse brings the sūrah's account of the battle and its aftermath to an end, and the passage closes with the community's fear placed where the Book believes it belongs. The remaining verses of the sūrah turn to their opponents among the People of the Book and to the arguments of the community's own doubters.

The placement of the sentence at this point is deliberate. The community had been tested by wounds, by rumours, by the loss of its men, and by the fear of a second attack, and the sūrah leaves it with a command about what it should be afraid of. The lessons of the campaign are gathered in that sentence, and the readers of the sūrah carry it as the conclusion of the whole account.

---
## Sūrah Āli ʿImrān 3:176

> ˹O Prophet!˺ Do not grieve for those who race to disbelieve—surely they will not harm Allah in the least. It is Allah’s Will to disallow them a share in the Hereafter, and they will suffer a tremendous punishment.

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Consolation Addressed to the Prophet**

The verse tells the Prophet not to let those who rush toward disbelief cause him grief, and it then states that their conduct does not harm God in the least. The instruction follows a long passage about the community's own failures, and it turns the Prophet's attention to another group whose opposition was personal to him.

The Book addresses the Prophet's distress at the disbelief of others in several places, and the commentators gathered the passages together. One sūrah tells him not to let the conduct of those who deny cause him grief, another tells him not to let their speech cause him sorrow, and a third asks whether he will consume himself in regret over people who will not believe. The verses form a body of consolation addressed to the same experience.

**Who the Verse Concerns**

The commentators identified the group in more than one way. Al-Rāzī read the phrase as referring to the idolaters of Makkah, who were the Prophet's own kin and who worked hardest against him. Al-Qurṭūbī included the People of the Book, who had a scripture of their own and were expected to recognise what came after it, and the hypocrites, who claimed adherence while working against the community.

The three groups had little in common except the conduct described in the verse, and the sentence covers all of them. The Book's manner in such passages is to state the matter in terms that apply wherever the conduct is found.

**The Word for Hastening**

The verse describes the group as hastening toward disbelief, and the verb carries the sense of moving quickly and eagerly. The phrase describes people who did not drift into their position but pressed toward it.

The distinction is worth keeping when the sentence is read in a community's own situation. The Book distinguishes between people who fall into an error and people who rush to embrace it, and the phrasing in this verse places the group in the second category. The Prophet is told not to be grieved by what they do, and the wording of the verse describes the act rather than the persons.

**The Statement That They Harm No One**

The verse states that the group will not harm God in the least, and the same formula appears earlier in the sūrah when it tells the community that whoever turns back on his heels does not harm God at all. The Book uses the sentence to place the consequences of defection where they fall.

The harm, in the Book's account, belongs to the person who commits the act. The community that hears the sentence is being taught that its message does not depend on the number of its adherents, and the Prophet is told that the loss of any follower is not a subtraction from the cause he was sent to convey.

**What It Means to Have No Share in the Hereafter**

The verse states that God desires to give the group no share in the Hereafter, and the commentators explained the phrase as referring to a share in its good and its blessing rather than to the mere experience of the next life. The Book describes its enemies as present in the Hereafter and receiving their treatment there.

The sentence is therefore a statement about what the group has lost rather than about the annihilation of their existence. The Book's descriptions of the Hereafter consistently distinguish between being in it and having a portion in it, and the verse before the reader uses the second of those ideas.

**The Balance of the Sentence**

The verse gives the Prophet a command and then supplies the reasons for it, and the two statements that follow are arranged to relieve a burden rather than to increase it. The grief the verse prohibits is the grief of a person who feels responsible for what others choose.

The Book relieves that burden by stating what the disbelief does not affect and what the group forfeits by it. The Prophet is not told that the matter is unimportant; he is told that his own standing is not diminished by it, and the sentence lets him set down a weight he had been carrying. The Book's comfort in such passages is always the same in kind, and it is offered to the Prophet as a release from a responsibility that was never his to bear.

**The Book's Habit of Comforting the Messenger**

The repetition of this instruction across several sūrahs shows how persistent the experience was. The Prophet's distress at the refusal of his people is a recurring subject of revelation, and the Book answers it repeatedly rather than once.

The pattern is instructive for the community that reads these verses. Whatever grief a person feels over the rejection of the message by those he cares about, the Book treats the feeling as natural and supplies the same remedy: the cause belongs to God, and its outcome does not depend on the response it receives.

The verse's application extends beyond the Prophet. Any believer who invests himself in the response of others faces the same disappointment, and the sentence offers the same release from it.

The passage around this verse has been concerned with a community that had been tested and had lost members to apostasy and hypocrisy. The sentence tells the believers what such losses mean for the cause they carry, and it prepares the reader for the verse that follows, which restates the same principle in the language of trade. A community that has lost members to defection can measure the loss against what the sentence says was never at stake.

---
## Sūrah Āli ʿImrān 3:177

> Those who trade belief for disbelief will never harm Allah in the least, and they will suffer a painful punishment.

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Image of a Trade**

The verse describes those who have purchased disbelief at the price of belief, and it states that they will not harm God and that a painful punishment awaits them. The commercial image is one the Book uses frequently for moral choice.

The commentators drew attention to the pattern. One sūrah describes people who trade guidance for misguidance and observes that the trade is profitless. Another describes the same exchange and adds that the traders are persistent in pursuing the fire. A third, on the same image, describes those who purchase the present life at the price of the next. The Book's use of the market as a picture of a person's decisions is one of its characteristic ways of explaining consequences.

The verse's exchange is between belief and disbelief, and the order of the words is important. What the group had is named as belief, and what they took in its place is named as disbelief.

The Book's descriptions of the same transaction usually mention what was given up in the process: guidance, forgiveness, the next life. The sentence in this verse is brief, and the brevity makes the loss clear without adding anything. What was given up was the more valuable of the two, and the sentence assumes that any reader knows which is which.

**The Profitlessness of the Exchange**

The Book repeatedly states that the trade does not profit those who make it, and the earlier sūrah says as much in a single phrase. The verse before the reader does not use the word for profit, but the sentence about their punishment states the same outcome in a different register.

The commercial language matters because it treats belief as something a person possesses and may dispose of badly. The Book does not present faith as an external label that can be worn or set aside without cost; it presents it as property whose exchange has consequences, and the market image gives the reader a familiar way to weigh what happened.

**Who the Traders Were**

The commentators applied the verse to the People of the Book who knew the truth and turned from it, and to the groups who had received clear evidence and preferred something else. The sūrah about the Repentance uses the same image and speaks of those who chose a fleeting gain over God's revelations.

The hypocrites and the Makkan idolaters are included in the same category by the commentators, since all of them gave up a claim for an advantage they thought would last. The verse's list of punishments is stated in general terms, which allows it to be applied wherever the exchange occurs. The sūrah's own audience had seen the pattern in individuals who had been close to the message and had turned away from it.

**The Repetition About Harm**

The verse states again that the group does not harm God, and the repetition in consecutive verses gives the point its weight. The sentence is not a description of the group's power but a statement about the limits of what any created being can affect.

The Book uses the same construction in the sūrah's earlier passage about those who turn on their heels, and it states in the sūrah of the Repentance that whoever withholds from giving harms only himself. The community that recites these sentences is being taught where the damage from a person's defection lands, and the answer is always the same.

**The Punishment Named**

The verse describes the outcome for the group as a painful punishment, and the term is the one the Book applies to those who knowingly exchange the greater for the smaller. The sūrah of the Bees makes the exception of a person who is compelled to disbelieve while his heart remains firm in faith, and that exception marks how deliberate the conduct in this verse is.

The word describes the pain of the outcome rather than its duration, and the Book uses it in passages that deal with conduct chosen with knowledge. The verse before the reader therefore places the group in the class of those who acted deliberately, and the punishment named suits that description.

**The Fleeting Gain in the Book's Language**

The Book describes the advantage that people take in exchange for their faith with the word for something passing, and it uses the phrase in its warnings about the traders. The gain is described as brief in itself, and the reader is left to compare the two parties to the exchange.

The sūrah's readers had watched the community's own members make calculations of this kind during the campaign. The verse states the accounting in plain terms, and its placement after the instruction not to grieve gives the Prophet the confirmation that the conduct of the traders carried its own cost. The gain they took is described in the Book as fleeting in the passages that use this image, and the description leaves the reader to compare the two sides of the exchange.

**The Verse's Place After the Consolation**

The verse restates the sentence that preceded it and adds the punishment, and the repetition is the Book's way of confirming a matter for a person who is grieving. The instruction not to grieve is followed by an explanation of why the grief was unnecessary.

The community that reads the two verses together is given the same lesson twice, once in the vocabulary of harm and once in the vocabulary of trade. The next verse turns to the question that the sight of unpunished deniers raises, and the sūrah answers it by describing what a long life can be for those who use it badly.

---
## Sūrah Āli ʿImrān 3:178

> Those who disbelieve should not think that living longer is good for them. They are only given more time to increase in sin, and they will suffer a humiliating punishment.

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Respite and the Misreading**

The verse warns those who deny not to suppose that the delay they are granted is good for them, and it states that the delay allows them to increase in sin. The sentence addresses a conclusion that people naturally draw when they observe the prosperous among the wicked.

The community had watched its opponents return home in good order while its own dead were being buried, and the sight raised the question the verse answers. The verse explains what such survival amounts to, and it does so in terms that remove the advantage a person might read into it.

The commentators explain the respite as the granting of more life, in place of dying or being killed. The Makkans who had escaped the fighting were given additional years, and the sentence treats those years as the subject of the warning.

The Book uses the same idea in other passages, and it consistently refuses to treat long life as evidence of divine approval. The verse before the reader takes the observation the community had made about its enemies and states what the observation actually means.

**Two Ways of Reading the Sentence**

The warning can be understood in two ways. On one reading, since the people in question are deniers, a longer life can only be worse for them, because every additional year is spent in a state that leads away from God. On the other, the delay is itself part of the punishment: God answers their disbelief by increasing it in them, so that the state of denial is a suffering in its own right rather than only the cause of a later one.

The two readings are recorded in the commentaries, and they agree about the substance. The person who receives the respite is not being favored, and the verse says so in the plainest terms.

**The Alternative Reading of the Verb**

One commentator read the verb as an imperative rather than as a prohibition addressed to the deniers, which changes the sentence's addressee rather than its content. On that reading the verse tells the reader not to suppose that the respite granted to those who deny is good for them.

The reading makes the sentence a warning to the community against the same misreading, and it fits the verse's place in a passage that keeps addressing the believers. The difference between the two readings concerns whom the Book is correcting, and the correction is identical in both.

**The Debate Recorded by al-Rāzī**

Al-Rāzī reports a debate over whether God may be said to want some people to increase in sin. One school argued from this verse that the increase is willed, while the other argued from the verse that states that jinn and humanity were created only to worship that God does not will disbelief for anyone.

The second group held that the general verse governs the specific one, and the first replied that the specific statement in this verse remains true alongside the general. Al-Rāzī also records an interpretation on which the particle in the sentence indicates result rather than intention, so that the sense is that the respite ends in an increase of sin; he rejects that reading as contrary to the plain sense of the sentence.

**The Reading About the Battle's Outcome**

One of the interpretations recorded in the commentaries applies the verse to the outcome of the fighting. On that reading, those who deny should not think that their survival at Uḥud was better than the deaths of the men who fought in God's way, since all their survival achieved was further life in a corrupt state.

The reading fits the passage's setting closely. The community had lost men whose deaths the sūrah describes as a state of provision and joy, and the survivors among the enemy had kept their lives and nothing else. The verse tells the community which of the two outcomes is the better, and it does so without disputing the facts of the day.

**The Book's Warnings About Being Given Rope**

The Book warns in several places about the impression created by prosperity that is not corrected. One passage describes people who became oblivious to the warnings and were then given everything they desired, until they were seized by surprise and fell into despair. Another asks whether the long enjoyment granted to a people and their forefathers had made them secure.

A third passage tells the Prophet not to be impressed by the wealth and children of the deniers, since God intends to test them by these things in this life. The verse before the reader belongs to that group of statements, and it explains what the community should think when it sees its opponents flourishing.

**The Punishment That Ends the Verse**

The sentence closes by naming the outcome as a humiliating punishment, and the term describes a treatment that abases the person who receives it. The Book uses the word for those who were arrogant in their denial.

The vocabulary matches the warning. The people who supposed that their respite was a sign of favor will be shown what it was, and the humiliation named in the verse is the reversal of the standing they believed they held. The Book's use of the term elsewhere is consistently for those whose conduct has earned them the loss of the regard they claimed. The verses that follow turn to the community's own question about who is sincere among them, and the sūrah continues to explain how such matters are settled.

---
## Sūrah Āli ʿImrān 3:179

> Allah would not leave the believers in the condition you were in, until He distinguished the good from the evil ˹among you˺. Nor would Allah ˹directly˺ reveal to you the unseen, but He chooses whoever He wills as a messenger. So believe in Allah and His messengers. And if you are faithful and mindful ˹of Allah˺, you will receive a great reward.

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Separation Promised**

The verse states that God will not leave the believers in the state they are in until He separates the bad from the good, and it explains that the means of separation is not a disclosure of hidden knowledge. The sentence answers the community's uncertainty about who among it was sincere.

Al-Ṭabarī took the separation to mean that those whose adherence was hollow are singled out from those whose commitment was genuine. Most commentators read the promise as given to the community about itself: its members would not be left in a state where the two could not be told apart.

Some commentators read the opening words as addressed to the disbelievers and hypocrites, so that the sentence means that God would not leave the believers in the same condition as those who deny. The two readings distribute the sentence's parts differently, and they produce the same assurance.

The difference is worth noting because it shows how closely the comment tradition attended to the question of address. The Book's sentences about the community frequently change their addressee without marking the change, and the commentators tracked those movements as part of their work.

**The Book's Teaching About Testing**

The verse's statement that the separation happens is amplified elsewhere in the sūrah. The Book asks the community whether it imagined that it would reach the garden with no one having been shown to have struggled and endured, and the account of the battle shows the sorting that the sentence describes happening in the course of one afternoon.

The two groups at Uḥud were distinguished by conduct rather than by declaration, and the verse before the reader states the principle that the day had demonstrated. Testing, in the Book's teaching, is not an incidental hardship but the mechanism by which the community's composition becomes visible to those who live through it and to those who come after them.

**The Unseen Not Disclosed**

The verse states that God will not inform the community of the unseen, and the commentators explain this as a statement that God does not reveal what lies in a person's heart. The community would not be given a list of names; it would be given occasions on which character showed itself.

Both al-Rāzī and al-Ṭabarī tie the sentence to the campaign itself, where the pressure of the day brought out what people were. The Book's way of dealing with a community is to let conduct bring to light what a report from the unseen would have settled only by coercion.

**The Occasions Reported for the Verse**

The commentators record two occasions for the revelation of this verse. One report places it after a request from the community for a means of telling who among them was sound and who was not; another has it answering an opponent who demanded that the Prophet name each person's category.

Both reports describe the same desire: a knowledge of people's inner states that would settle the community's uncertainty once and for all. The verse declines to provide it and supplies the community with the method it was going to have anyway.

The verse makes an exception for the messengers, whom God chooses and to whom He grants what He wills of the knowledge of such matters. The Book states elsewhere that God is the Knower of the unseen and discloses it to those He chooses among His messengers.

The sentence therefore keeps the community from expecting the knowledge while acknowledging that God gives it where He decides. The Prophet knew more about the people around him than anyone else, and the verse's exception explains the source of that knowledge without turning it into a general provision for the community. What the community is offered instead is the ordinary means of finding out, which is the conduct that trials bring into the open. The Prophet knew more about the people around him than anyone else, and the verse's exception explains the source of that knowledge without turning it into a general provision for the community.

**The Command to Believe and Its Reward**

The verse ends with an instruction and a promise: the call to place trust in God and in the men He sends, and the assurance that those who hold to that trust and keep their duty will receive a great reward. The sentence is short, and its position at the end of a passage about tests and knowledge gives it the force of a conclusion.

What the community is told to do is what it can do, and the sentence's brevity keeps the instruction within reach of everyone who hears it. It cannot see into the hearts of its members, and it is not asked to; it is asked to hold to God and to His messengers and to conduct itself with the awareness the sūrah has been teaching. The reward named at the end is the same one the sūrah has attached to the same combination in earlier verses.

**What the Verse Teaches About Certainty**

The verse's teaching about certainty is that it comes through trial rather than through revelation of hidden matters, and the community's own history had just demonstrated the point. The Book does not promise its people a way of knowing who is sincere without the cost of the occasions that reveal sincerity.

The spiritual reading recorded in the commentaries draws the same lesson for the individual, describing the purification of the soul as a gradual sorting of what is sound from what is not, and warning against expecting hidden knowledge to be granted as the fruit of the path. What a person is asked for is conduct, and what the verse promises is the reward that follows it.

---
## Sūrah Āli ʿImrān 3:180

> And do not let those who ˹greedily˺ withhold Allah’s bounties think it is good for them—in fact, it is bad for them! They will be leashed ˹by their necks˺ on the Day of Judgment with whatever ˹wealth˺ they used to withhold. And Allah is the ˹sole˺ inheritor of the heavens and the earth. And Allah is All-Aware of what you do.

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Warning to the Miserly**

The verse tells those who are miserly with what God has given them not to suppose that their holding back is good for them, and it states that it is evil for them. The sentence deals with a calculation that people make about their property, and it reverses the calculation's conclusion.

The sūrah has dealt with property at several points: the command to spend, the descriptions of those who give in ease and hardship, and the earlier passage about defrauding the community of what was held in common. The verse before the reader belongs to that sequence, and it addresses the withholding that the community's critics practiced.

**The Bounty Recalled**

The verse describes what the people withhold as what God has given them from His bounty, and the phrase places the property in question within a gift. The word for bounty has appeared in the sūrah in the descriptions of the martyrs and of the men who returned from the pursuit, and its use here is the same.

The placement matters for the warning's logic. What the miserly person holds is not his own achievement but something received, and the sentence treats the withholding as a response to generosity rather than as the prudent management of what one has. The Book's instructions about wealth are consistently grounded in this understanding.

**Material Wealth and Spiritual Knowledge**

The commentators read the verse as covering both material wealth and the knowledge that a person is given, and al-Ṭabarī applied it specifically to the People of the Book who refused to teach what they had received. The verse's wording about the bounty of God supports the wider application.

The two kinds of withholding share a structure. In each case a person keeps something that was given for a purpose beyond his own comfort, and in each case the holding is presented in the Book as a loss to the holder rather than as a gain. The passage about the earlier community's scholars is the clearest instance the sūrah's first readers would have recognised. The sūrah's readers are expected to examine their own case along both lines.

**The Collaring on the Day of Resurrection**

The verse states that on the Day of Resurrection those who were miserly will be collared by what they withheld, and the image is the same one the sūrah used in its passage about the defrauder who carries what he took. The tradition records an account attributed to the Prophet in which a person's treasure appears on that day as a serpent that follows him and wraps itself around him, saying that it is his wealth and his treasure.

The Book's imagery in these passages gives property a body that accompanies its owner. What a person kept and refused to part with becomes the thing that binds him, and the sentence is designed to make the miser see the object of his attachment in its final form.

**The Book's Other Warnings About Miserliness**

The Book returns to the subject in several passages. One describes those who are stingy and encourage others to be stingy, and it reminds them that God is self-sufficient. Another tells the believers that whoever withholds gives up only his own advantage, since God is self-sufficient while people are in need.

The sūrah of the Repentance announces a painful punishment for those who hoard gold and silver and do not spend it in the way of God. All of these passages describe the same error and the same outcome, and the verse before the reader is the sūrah's own statement of the warning. The repetition indicates how persistent the error is in human communities, since each generation is addressed in the same terms.

**The Contrast With Spending**

The Book places the miserly against the image of those who spend, and the contrast is drawn with the same emphasis. One passage compares what is spent in God's cause to a grain that produces seven ears, each containing a hundred grains, and it states that God multiplies the reward as He wills. Another describes those who give of their wealth to purify themselves.

The two pictures stand at the opposite ends of the Book's instruction about property. What the miser believes he is preserving is described as a serpent on his neck, and what the giver parts with is described as a seed that becomes a harvest, and the sūrah's readers are expected to make the comparison.

The verse states that to God belongs the inheritance of the heavens and the earth, and the commentators explained the phrase with care. God is in possession of everything always, and the inheritance is spoken of because all other owners eventually cease while He remains.

The reading makes the sentence a comment on the futility of hoarding, since what a person holds is held for a short time by an arrangement that he did not create and cannot maintain. What a person holds is held for a short time by an arrangement that he did not create and cannot maintain, and the Book's phrasing reminds the reader of the end of every ownership.

**The Closing Statement About Awareness**

The verse ends with the statement that God is aware of everything the community does, and the sentence closes the passage as it has closed several others in this sūrah. The awareness covers the hidden calculations as well as the visible acts.

The community that recites the verse is told that its treatment of what it has been given is known in full, and the sentence makes the accounting of the Day of Resurrection a matter of certainty rather than of speculation. The sūrah's later passages continue to deal with the community's property and its obligations, and the warning in this verse sets the terms for everything that follows.

---
## Sūrah Āli ʿImrān 3:181

> Indeed, Allah has heard those ˹among the Jews˺ who said, “Allah is poor; we are rich!” We have certainly recorded their slurs and their killing of prophets unjustly. Then We will say, “Taste the torment of burning!

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Saying That Was Heard**

The verse opens with the declaration that God has heard what a group said about Him, and it reports the taunt itself: that God is poor while they are rich. The announcement that the words were heard is the first move in the sentence, and it places the speakers in a position they had not considered.

The Book records many statements of its opponents, and it frequently introduces them with a notice that the words have been registered. The formula is a reminder that the speech of human beings about God is not private, and the verse uses it before it states what the words will bring.

**What Prompted the Taunt**

The commentators explain what occasioned the remark. The Book had told the believers that whoever lends to God a goodly loan will have it multiplied, and the same invitation appears in another sūrah as a question addressed to those who might give. Some of the group seized on the wording and turned it into a mockery, saying that the invitation showed that God was in need and they were wealthy.

The sūrah about the Table reports a similar taunt from the same quarter, in which a group among the People of the Book said that God's hand was tied. The Book's answer in that passage is a statement of His generosity, and the verse before the reader answers the taunt in a different way.

**The Intention Behind the Words**

Al-Qurṭūbī records that the group did not believe what they said. Their purpose was to stir up unease among the weaker members of the community, who might be disturbed by ridicule aimed at the revelation.

The explanation fits the pattern of the sūrah's earlier passages about the community's opponents, whose object was to shake the believers rather than to win an argument. The Book elsewhere states the relation between the two groups plainly, telling the believers that God is the rich one while they are the poor, and the verse before the reader supplies the answer to those who turned that statement into a joke.

**The Record Kept of What They Said**

The verse states that God will record what the group said, and the Book describes the record elsewhere as a register that will be produced for each person on the Day of Judgment. The sūrah of the Night Journey describes a record that will be brought out and read, and other passages describe books given to people in their right hands or behind their backs.

The sentence places the mocking words in that register alongside the deeds the same people had committed. The verse joins the two in a single clause, and the joining is the answer to anyone who supposes that speech about God is a lesser matter than conduct.

**The Slaying of the Prophets**

The verse adds the killing of the prophets to what will be recorded, and the phrase about killing without right appears in the sūrah's earlier description of those who deny God's signs. One passage describes the people who were arrogant enough to reject some messengers and kill others, and another describes a community that denied a messenger whenever he brought what they did not want.

The acts referred to belong to the history of the earlier community, and the verse includes them in the reckoning of the people who were speaking in the present. The Book treats the two as connected, and the connection is explained in the comment tradition.

**Approval as a Form of Participation**

Al-Qurṭūbī explains the mention of the earlier killings by observing that agreement with an act is treated as a share in it. The group in question had not committed the killings themselves, and the verse's inclusion of the deed in their record indicates that their approval of what their ancestors did had put them in the same position.

The reasoning is supported by a report in the tradition about the responsibility of those who witness an evil and those who are absent from it but approve of it. The principle is severe, and the verse applies it to a case in which the approval was of the killing of messengers.

**The Punishment Named**

The sentence closes with a command addressed to the group on the Day of Judgment: taste the punishment of the burning. The Book uses the imperative form in its descriptions of the treatment of those who denied, and the command is spoken by the one whose words they had mocked.

The word for the punishment describes the fire's effect, and the sūrah had used the same vocabulary in its warnings about the destination of those who reject the truth. The verse leaves the group with the outcome stated in their own language, since the taunt they had made concerned a matter of wealth and the answer concerns what they will carry away from everything else.

The verse gives the community a lesson about the treatment of revelation by people who have no intention of accepting it. The mocking words of a group that did not believe what it said are recorded as though they had been meant, and the verse teaches the believers to take such speech seriously.

The community at Madinah had been subjected to a steady stream of taunts about its message and its poverty. The sentence assures it that the taunts were heard and would be answered, and the next verse adds the reason for the treatment that has been announced.

**The Answer the Book Gives Elsewhere

The claim that God is poor and the community rich is answered directly in another sūrah, where the Book states that God is the Rich and the people are the poor (47:38). The two statements use the same vocabulary, which is why the commentators treated the taunt as a deliberate reversal of a verse the community had been reciting. The words in question came from the passage that asks who will lend God a goodly loan, and the loan language had been used by the revelation itself; the taunt took that language literally and turned it into mockery. The sentence before the reader records it as speech God has heard, and the answer to it is not a correction of the claim about wealth but the statement of what the speakers have earned.

**The Saying of the Prophet About Approval

The tradition preserved a report the commentators attached to the charge of killing the prophets: when a sin is done on the earth, the person who is present and disapproves of it is like one who was absent, and the person who is absent and approves of it is like one who was present. The report explains how the verse's charge can reach a community whose ancestors committed the acts. Announcing which past deeds one endorses is itself a way of sharing in them, and the Book's statements about the slaying of the prophets are regularly accompanied by this kind of extension. The verse's list of offences, the taunt and the killings together, therefore describes a settled attitude rather than two unrelated incidents, and the recording it announces covers the words as well as the acts.

---
## Sūrah Āli ʿImrān 3:182

> This is ˹the reward˺ for what your hands have done. And Allah is never unjust to ˹His˺ creation.”

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Reason Stated**

The verse explains the punishment announced in the sentence before it by pointing to what the people in question had themselves sent ahead, and by stating that God does not wrong His servants. The sentence is short and functions as the justification of what has just been described.

The Book often follows a description of punishment with a clause of this kind, and the clause prevents the reader from understanding the outcome as an act of arbitrary severity. What people receive, in the Book's account, is the consequence of what they have done, and the sentence states that consequence in the language of a balance rather than of a penalty imposed from outside. The clause about God's justice follows descriptions of punishment throughout the Book, and its function is to close the door on the thought that the outcome could have been otherwise.

**What the Hands Have Sent Ahead**

The phrase about what the hands have sent ahead appears in other passages of the Book, and its image is of deeds that precede the person who will meet them. One sūrah states that a person will be told that the treatment received is for what his hands have done, and another uses the same formula in a context of punishment.

The Book uses the image to make a person's responsibility concrete. What is done in this life is not left behind when a person moves on; it goes ahead of him, and the sentence in this verse treats the punishment of the group as something they had dispatched with their own conduct.

**The Justice of the Sentence**

The statement that God does not wrong His servants is one of the Book's recurring declarations, and it appears in several sūrahs in nearly the same words. One passage states that whoever does good does so for himself and whoever does evil does so against himself, and adds that God is not unjust to His creatures.

Another states that God's word cannot be changed and that He is not unjust to His creation. The verse before the reader belongs to that group, and its placement after the announcement of a punishment gives the sentence its force: what is about to happen is not a departure from justice but an instance of it.

**The Word for Wronging**

The word the Book uses here describes the placing of a burden where it does not belong, or the reduction of a person's due. The negation of the term in this verse means that nothing of what the group is owed will be withheld and nothing undeserved will be added.

The Book's teaching about human responsibility is built on this negation. The sūrah had already stated, in its passage about the defrauder, that every soul will be paid in full and will not be wronged, and the sentence before the reader repeats the principle for the case of those whose conduct has been described in the preceding verse.

**Deeds as a Store Set Aside**

The Book's description of deeds as what is sent ahead belongs to a family of images that includes the account of the miser collared by what he withheld, a few verses earlier in this sūrah. Both pictures treat a person's conduct as something that remains attached to him and is produced at the end.

The two images work from opposite directions. The hoarder's property becomes a weight around his neck, and the deeds of the group in this verse become the reason for what they are told to taste. The Book's imagery of the Day of Judgment makes a person's history into an object that can be presented, and the sentences in this passage use that imagery twice.

**Why the Statement Follows the Taunt**

The verse explains the punishment of the group by their conduct rather than by their words alone, and the sentence includes the deeds in the account that the previous verse began. The taunt about God's poverty was one item among many.

The Book's treatment of its opponents in this passage is consistently cumulative. The verse before the reader gathers their speech and their actions together and states what the sum produces, and the sentence about justice explains why the outcome was inevitable. The sūrah's readers are meant to see the connection between the conduct and the treatment, and the verse exists to make that connection explicit.

**What the Community Learned**

The community that recited these verses was being taught how to think about the treatment its opponents would receive, and the sentence about justice kept it from reading the punishment as evidence of divine anger alone. The Book's descriptions of the next life always attach the outcome to the deed.

The verses also gave the community a way to think about its own case. The sūrah had said the same thing about the community's own losses, and the sentence in this verse states the measure that applies to both: the account is exact, and no one is wronged in either direction.

**The Verse's Function in the Passage**

The verse stands between the announcement of the taunt's consequence and the account of another challenge that the same quarter presented to the Prophet. Its brevity gives it the quality of a conclusion, and its reference to justice prepares the reader for the exchange that follows.

The passage as a whole deals with the refusal of the message by people who had been given the most evidence, and the verses move from one form of that refusal to another. The sentence about what the hands send ahead supplies the principle by which all of them are judged, and the next verse takes up a demand that the group made of the Prophet himself.

---
## Sūrah Āli ʿImrān 3:183

> Those ˹are the same people˺ who say, “Allah has commanded us not to believe in any messenger unless he brings us an offering to be consumed by fire ˹from the sky˺.” Say, ˹O Prophet,˺ “Other prophets did in fact come to you before me with clear proofs and ˹even˺ what you demanded—why then did you kill them, if what you say is true?”

**Expanded Commentary**

The verse reports a claim made by a group: that God had bound them not to believe in any messenger until he brought them an offering consumed by fire from heaven. The sentence presents the claim as the group's own account of its obligation.

The Book records several such claims made by the group in question, and it treats them as conditions that the claimants had constructed for themselves. The verse reports this one in the form the claimants used, and the reply that follows takes up the terms of their own condition.

**The Historical Challenge**

The commentators describe the occasion as a challenge that prominent members of the Jewish community in Madinah put to the Prophet. They asked him to produce a sacrificial offering that fire from heaven would consume, presenting it as the criterion they had always required.

The commentaries observe that fire descending on an offering is described in their own scriptures in connection with a number of prophets, and they list the occasions. The challenge therefore drew on a tradition the group knew, and the verse's reply treats it as a criterion that had been applied selectively.

**Why the Challenge Was Empty**

Al-Rāzī and others note that the sign demanded had not been granted to all the prophets of Israel, and that the practice of animal sacrifice at the temple had ceased long before. By the time the challenge was made, the group was setting a condition that its own history had already made impossible.

The observation explains the reply's tone, since the condition the group had set was one its own tradition had already answered. The Prophet is told to point out that messengers had brought the proofs they asked for, and that the ancestors of the group had killed some of those messengers. The condition the group proposed had been met before and had not produced the belief it was supposed to require.

**The Reply and Its Logic**

The reply is stated as a question: messengers came before me with clear proofs and with that of which you speak, so why did you kill them, if you are truthful? The sentence turns the challenge back on the challengers by using their own criterion as evidence against them.

The Book's manner of arguing in such passages is to show that the objection raised by its opponents condemns them by their own record. The reply does not dispute the value of a spectacular sign; it observes that the sign had been given in the past without producing the result the group claimed it would produce.

**The Killing of the Prophets Revisited**

The verse's closing question refers to a subject that the sūrah has just raised in its account of those who spoke against God. The Book states in another sūrah that each time a messenger came to the people of Israel with what they did not want, they rejected some and killed others.

A further passage describes a community that made a covenant and then broke it, rejecting the signs and killing the prophets unjustly. The verse before the reader takes the same history and uses it as the answer to a demand for further proof.

**The Standard the Group Proposed**

The passage's argument concerns the standards people use to decide what to accept. The group proposed a test that its own history had already answered, and the reply shows what the test had produced when it was applied.

The Book treats such standards with respect when they are honest, and it answers them by referring to the evidence that had already been given. The verse's reply does not dismiss the value of a sign; it observes that the sign had been supplied before, in the history the group itself claimed to honour. One of the sūrah's earlier verses states that a group of the People of the Book recited the signs of God through the night while prostrating, and the Book's argument throughout this section is with those who had evidence and did not act on it.

**The Verse's Connection With the Earlier Statements**

The verse follows the taunt about God's poverty and the general statement about what deeds are recorded, and it continues the sūrah's account of the community's opponents. The two passages together describe the same quarter in the same posture.

The connection between them is the group's treatment of the messengers. The earlier verse mentioned the killing of the prophets as part of the record, and this verse makes the same history the basis of an argument. The sūrah is teaching its readers how the refusal of the message had actually operated in the past, and it does so in a form that its own community could apply to the arguments it was meeting in Madinah.

One of the readings recorded in the commentaries applies the verse to the inner life, describing the soul's refusal to follow the way and its production of excuses designed to satisfy itself. On this reading the demand for a spectacular sign is the mind's way of postponing a decision it has already made.

The reading is offered as an application rather than as the verse's plain sense, and it has been useful in the community's teaching about self-deception. The verse's own reply is a matter of history, and the application draws the same lesson from it for anyone who sets conditions on what he will accept, since a delay in accepting what is evident is usually a matter of the will rather than of the evidence.

---
## Sūrah Āli ʿImrān 3:184

> If you are rejected by them, so too were messengers before you who came with clear proofs, divine Books, and enlightening Scriptures.

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Consolation Repeated**

The verse tells the Prophet that if the people deny him, they had already denied messengers who came before him with the proofs their Lord had given them. The sentence is the sūrah's fourth address to the Prophet's grief, and it uses the same remedy as the others.

The argument is addressed to the experience of rejection rather than to the arguments of the rejecters. The Prophet is told that the response he was receiving had a history, and that the men who preceded him had been met with the same treatment from the people they came to. The sentence's force comes from the fact that the Prophet is not being told to expect anything unusual.

**The Clear Proofs**

The commentators describe the clear proofs as the various kinds of demonstration that accompanied the messengers: the signs they performed, the testimonies they produced, and the arguments they brought. The term is a broad one, and the Book uses it for several kinds of evidence.

The phrase in this verse gathers all of them into a single category, and the point is that the messengers had not come to their peoples without support. The denial described in the sentence was a response to something that had been supplied, and the sūrah has been making the same point about its own community's opponents through its account of the arguments it was meeting.

**The Word for Scriptures**

The term rendered as scriptures is the plural of a word meaning something written, and the commentators note that it refers to books containing wisdom rather than to one specific volume. One of them observes that the term is distinct from the word for the Psalms of David, which has a different form and a narrower reference.

The Book uses the broader word for the revelations given to a range of messengers, and one of the later sūrahs refers to the sheets of Abraham and Moses in describing the teachings of the earlier revelations. The verse before the reader gathers the written revelation of the earlier messengers under one heading.

**The Luminous Book**

The phrase about the luminous Book has been explained as a reference to the Torah and the Gospel, and the commentators discussed whether it is a separate item from the scriptures mentioned before it or the same thing described again. Al-Rāzī read the conjunction as indicating that the two phrases describe a single reality.

The term for luminous appears in the Book's descriptions of the revelation in other places as well, and the quality it names is the light by which a text makes matters clear to the people who receive it. The verse thus lists what the messengers brought in three parts: the proofs that were shown, the books that were written, and the light they carried.

**The Earlier Messengers' Experience**

The Book describes the treatment of the earlier messengers in several passages. One states that every time a messenger came to the people of Israel with what they did not want, they rejected some and killed others. Another describes the covenant that was taken from them and the messengers who were sent and rejected.

The verse before the reader places the Prophet's own experience within that record, and it asks the community to read its own difficulties as a repetition of a pattern that runs through the history of revelation. The community at Madinah had seen its message dismissed by groups with every reason to accept it, and the sentence tells it that such a reception is not evidence that the message was false. What the community was facing had been faced before, and the messengers who faced it had been vindicated in the end.

**What the Community Gains From the Sentence**
