The consolation in the verse extends beyond the Prophet. Any community that carries a message meets the same treatment, and the sentence supplies the response in advance: the denial of the present does not distinguish the messenger from those who came before him.

The sūrah had already told the believers not to be grieved by those who rush into disbelief. This verse adds the historical frame to the same instruction, and the community is given a way of reading its own difficulties that does not depend on the reaction of the people it addresses. What has been refused is not a new message but the latest in a long series, and the series has a record that the community can examine.

**The Book's Names for the Earlier Revelations**

The Book refers to the revelations that preceded it by several names, and it treats them as a single stream of guidance given to successive messengers. One passage lists the prophets who received revelation and mentions the Psalms given to David along with the books given to others.

Another passage asks the believers to declare their faith in what was revealed to them and in what was revealed to the earlier prophets without distinguishing among them. The verse before the reader belongs to that treatment of revelation as one continuous work, and it uses the general language of the Book's own vocabulary.

The verse closes the sūrah's answer to the arguments of those who demanded signs and mocked the message, and it prepares the reader for the statement about death and reward that follows. The two movements are connected by the subject of what endures.

The community had been told that its messenger would not be treated differently from his predecessors. The next verse states what every soul will experience and where the final account is settled, and the passage's concerns are gathered there in a single sentence that the community has recited ever since.

---
## Sūrah Āli ʿImrān 3:185

> Every soul will taste death. And you will only receive your full reward on the Day of Judgment. Whoever is spared from the Fire and is admitted into Paradise will ˹indeed˺ triumph, whereas the life of this world is no more than the delusion of enjoyment.

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Sentence About Death**

The verse opens with the declaration that every soul will taste death, and the sentence appears in two other sūrahs in almost the same words. The commentators note that the Arabic construction also permits the sense that every soul is a taster of death, which suggests that death is not only an event at the end of a life but a condition that touches a person throughout it.

The verse is the sūrah's third statement on the subject, following the declaration that no soul dies except by God's permission and the reminder that those destined for death would have gone to the places where they were to die. The repetition in the course of the passage is deliberate, and the sentence in this verse gives the teaching its widest form.

**The Full Reward on the Day of Resurrection**

The verse states that the reward will be paid in full on the Day of Resurrection, and the phrase echoes the sūrah's earlier statements about the exactness of the settlement. The community had been told that every soul would be paid what it earned and would not be wronged, and this verse repeats the assurance in a form that covers all people.

The sentence places the completion of the account at a definite point, which is the resurrection rather than the moment of death. The Book's teaching in these passages is that the full settlement waits until every player in the story has been gathered, and the community's patience in this life is connected to that arrangement.

**The Definition of Triumph**

The verse states that whoever is kept away from the fire and admitted to the garden has triumphed, and the definition rearranges the meaning of success. The community had been measuring its fortunes in terms of the events of the battlefield and the position of its opponents, and the sentence supplies a different measure.

The Book uses the word for triumph in its descriptions of the reward, and it uses it in the verse about the exchange of lives and wealth for the garden. The sentence in this verse is the clearest statement of the Book's understanding of success: it consists of two events, one of them the avoidance of the destination the sūrah has been warning about throughout.

**The Book's Other Statements**

The Book declares the passing of everything that exists in several places. One passage states that everything is bound to perish except God's own self, and another declares that all that is upon the earth will pass away while the face of the Lord remains.

The verses about the tasting of death in other sūrahs add that humanity is tested with good and evil and that all will be returned to God. Read together with the verse before the reader, these statements describe a world in which nothing lasting is held by human hands, and they make the sentence about triumph a statement about what survives.

**The Life of This World as Delusion**

The verse closes by describing the life of this world as nothing but the enjoyment of a delusion, and the word carries the senses of vanity, deception, and peril. The Book uses the same phrase in the sūrah of Iron, where it compares the world to rain that produces a crop the planters admire until it withers, and it describes the Hereafter in that passage as either severe punishment or forgiveness and pleasure.

Another passage states that the present life is play and amusement and that the home of the Hereafter is better for those who are mindful. A third states that the Hereafter is the real life. The verse before the reader is the sūrah's own statement of the contrast, and the word it uses for the world's attraction is the one that describes being taken in.

**The Report About the Garden**

The commentary tradition records a statement attributed to the Prophet that a space in the garden the size of a whip's length is better than this world and everything in it. The report is used in the commentaries to illustrate the verse's judgement about the value of the two lives.

The sentence in the verse makes the same point in the Book's own words. What the community had been fighting over was of the order of the world, and the sentence about the garden's value places that order in a scale that does not require the community to despise its own life in order to assess it correctly.

**The Verse in the Community's Memory**

The verse has been among the most quoted in the community's life, and al-Qushayrī observed that the cup of death has been placed in the hand of every living being, so that a person either drinks it well and finds bliss or drinks it with a grimace and a wail. The recitation of the verse at funerals is a long-established practice.

The sentence is short enough to be carried in memory and complete enough to be used on its own. The community that recites it on such occasions is reminded of the destination of every soul and of the standard by which the outcome is measured, and the two ideas are given in the order the verse presents them.

**What the Verse Establishes**

The verse gathers the sūrah's teaching about death, reward, and the value of the present life into a single statement, and it does so at the point where the sūrah turns to its final instructions. The community is told what it will experience, where the accounting takes place, what success consists of, and what the world it was fighting over amounts to.

Those four claims form the basis for the conduct the sūrah asks of its readers in the passages that follow. The verses ahead deal with generosity, truthfulness, and the community's dealings with one another, and the sentence about the tombstone's worth of difference between the two lives is the ground on which all of those instructions rest.

---
## Sūrah Āli ʿImrān 3:186

> You ˹believers˺ will surely be tested in your wealth and yourselves, and you will certainly hear many hurtful words from those who were given the Scripture before you and ˹from˺ the polytheists. But if you are patient and mindful ˹of Allah˺—surely this is a resolve to aspire to.

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Trial Announced**

The verse tells the believers that they will certainly be tested in their property and in themselves, and that they will hear painful words from two groups. The sentence is stated as a prediction, and its certainty is part of what it conveys.

The Book announces trials to its communities in several places, and one passage lists the forms they take: fear, hunger, loss of property, loss of life, and loss of crops. The verse before the reader names two of those categories and adds the specific form of harm that comes through speech, and the community is told all of it in advance.

**What the Reference to Souls Covers**

The phrase about being tried in one's soul can be read as referring to the person himself, and al-Ṭabarī records another reading on which the word means one's own kin and the members of one's household. On that second reading the verse predicts the loss and the suffering of the people closest to the believer.

Both readings describe what the community at Madinah had already experienced. Its members had lost relatives on the field, and the survivors had borne the strain of the losses in their own persons. The verse's phrasing gathers the different forms of the trial into two words, and the commentators' disagreement reflects how much those two words were expected to carry.

**The Hurt From the Two Groups**

The verse states that the community will hear much that is painful from those who were given the Book before it and from the idolaters, and the word used covers both physical harm and verbal attacks. Al-Ṭabarī explains that it includes mockery, slander, falsehoods, and blasphemous statements about God and His prophets.

The sūrah had already reported examples of such speech in its account of the taunt about God's poverty and the challenge about the burnt offering. The community was being prepared for what it would continue to meet, and the verse names the source of the hurt rather than describing the community's reaction to it.

The community's situation in Madinah involved constant dealings with both groups, and the taunts came in the course of ordinary conversation and argument rather than only in open hostility. The verse places the experience in the category of a trial rather than of an accident.

The Book's teaching here is that the words of opponents were among the things that the community was going to be tested by, and the test is described in the same sentence as the losses of property and life. What the community would need in order to pass it is named in the clause that follows.

**Patience and Reverence as the Prescription**

The verse states that if the community is patient and mindful of God, then its conduct belongs to the matters that require resolve. The two qualities named are the ones the sūrah has been recommending throughout its account of the community's difficulties.

Patience in this context covers endurance under provocation as well as under loss, and mindfulness covers the awareness that governs how a person responds. The verse places both of them in the same clause, and the Book's descriptions of steadfastness elsewhere use the same pairing when the affliction takes the form of insults rather than blows.

**The Course Worthy of Resolve**

The phrase that closes the verse appears again in the Book in the advice given to Luqmān's son about enduring what befalls him, and in the statement that whoever endures and forgives has undertaken something that requires determination. The expression describes a course of action that a person must decide to take, and the determination is part of what it requires.

The community is therefore told that the endurance of insult is not a passive condition but a course of conduct. The Book's treatment of the matter in all three passages is the same, and the word it uses places the conduct among the things that human beings choose rather than among the things that happen to them.

**The Book's Counsel of Forbearance**

The Book counsels restraint in the face of rejection in several passages. One records the instruction to Moses and Aaron to speak gently to Pharaoh in the hope that he might be reminded. Another tells the believers to respond to evil with what is better, and promises that the person with whom one is in a feud may become a close friend. A third tells the believers to forgive those who do not look for the days of God.

The verse before the reader belongs to this body of teaching, and the community's conduct at Madinah was meant to be shaped by it. The Book's instruction about the manner of conveying the message is as consistent as its instruction about the message itself.

**The Question of Abrogation**

Al-Rāzī and al-Qurṭūbī considered the argument that this verse was set aside by the passages that permit fighting, and they rejected it. Their reasoning is that patience and leniency in the face of insult were the practice of the Prophet and his companions throughout their lives, including the periods in which fighting occurred.

The point is a useful one for the verse's later readers. The Book's permission to defend the community does not cancel the requirement to bear provocation patiently in the ordinary course of dealings with opponents, and the sūrah's placement of this instruction after its account of the battle makes the same point in its own way.

---
## Sūrah Āli ʿImrān 3:187

> ˹Remember, O Prophet,˺ when Allah took the covenant of those who were given the Scripture to make it known to people and not hide it, yet they cast it behind their backs and traded it for a fleeting gain. What a miserable profit!

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Covenant Recalled**

The verse recalls the time when God took a covenant from those who had been given the Book, and it states the content of the obligation: to make the revelation clear to people and not to conceal it. The sentence reports a commitment that the recipients had accepted.

Al-Ṭabarī records an interpretation on which the covenant was made through the prophets with their peoples, so that the obligation to teach the revelation was undertaken by the communities that received it. The verse's phrasing leaves the question of the parties to the covenant open, and the obligation it names is clear in either case.

**The Obligation to Make It Plain**

The command to make the message clear covers both the transmission of the text and its explanation, and the Book uses the vocabulary of clarification for the work of the messengers. The community addressed in the covenant had been given a scripture that was supposed to be taught rather than reserved.

The Book's instructions about knowledge are consistent on this point. What has been given for the guidance of people is not to be kept within the group that received it, and the verse states the obligation in the form of a quotation so that its terms cannot be mistaken.

**What Was Concealed**

The pronoun in the sentence refers to the Book, and some commentators understood the reference more narrowly as pointing to the foretellings of the coming of the Prophet that the earlier scriptures were believed to contain. The Book names the recognition of the messenger among the things the recipients of the earlier revelation were expected to acknowledge.

Both readings concern the same failure. The group had been given a text whose meaning obliged it to speak, and it withheld what it knew. The verse places the concealment in the same category as the harm described in the preceding verse, since silence about the truth was a form of the same conduct the community was being warned against.

**Casting It Behind Their Backs**

The verse describes the group as casting the covenant behind its back, and the image is one the Book uses elsewhere when it describes people who abandoned what they had undertaken. One passage describes a community that had been given the covenant and then disregarded it, and another describes the Book being thrown away as though it were not known.

The physical image of something dropped behind a person describes an abandonment that requires no decision at a particular moment. The covenant was not renounced in a formal act; it was simply left where it fell, and the verse's picture of the careless gesture is more telling than an account of a deliberate breach would be.

**The Paltry Price**

The verse states that the group sold the covenant for a small amount, and the Book uses the same commercial image for those who trade their commitments for advantage. One passage describes those who trade God's covenant and their oaths for a fleeting gain and states that they will have no share in the Hereafter. Another describes those who hide God's revelations and trade them for a small gain, and states that they consume nothing but fire.

The verse before the reader belongs to that group of statements, and its closing exclamation states that the sale was evil. The Book's treatment of the concealment of knowledge as a commercial transaction is consistent, and the price is described the same way in every passage.

**The General Application**

Al-Qurṭūbī read the verse as a general condemnation of anyone who is given knowledge and does not teach it, even though the sentence speaks specifically of one group. On this reading the obligation to teach what one has received applies to every community that possesses it.

The tradition supports the reading with a report in which the Prophet states that whoever conceals knowledge from his people will be bridled with one of the bridles of the fire, and with a statement attributed to ʿAlī that God does not require an ignorant person to learn until He requires a learned person to teach. The community's scholars have applied the verse in that sense ever since.

**The Book's Other Warnings Against Concealment**

The Book returns to the subject in several passages. One states that those who hide the clear proofs and the guidance after it has been made clear to humanity will be condemned by God and by those who condemn. Another asks why the recipients of the scripture mix truth with falsehood and conceal the truth while they know it.

The frequency of these warnings indicates how serious the Book considers the failure. The concealment in question is not an oversight; it is a decision made by people who know what they are doing, and the Book's language in every passage treats it as a betrayal of the trust on which the whole enterprise of guidance depends.

**What the Community Learns**

The community that recites this verse stands on the other side of its obligation. It has received a message, and the verse's account of what was done to the earlier one is a warning about what the same conduct would mean in its own case.

The sūrah's placement of the verse after its description of the trials of the community connects the two subjects. The community would be provoked by the taunts of the two groups, and it was being reminded that the withholding of knowledge had brought those groups to their present condition. The next verse continues to describe the conduct of people who had been given knowledge and had misused the position it gave them.

---
## Sūrah Āli ʿImrān 3:188

> Do not let those who rejoice in their misdeeds and love to take credit for what they have not done think they will escape torment. They will suffer a painful punishment.

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Warning About Self-Satisfaction**

The verse warns against supposing that people who exult in what they have brought about, and who want to be praised for what they have not done, are safe from punishment. The sentence describes a combination of satisfaction with oneself and a desire for credit that is not deserved.

The Book's warnings about hypocrisy usually concentrate on one of these elements, and the verse before the reader names both of them in a single sentence. The result is a portrait of people who are pleased with their own record and who also solicit approval for accomplishments that are not theirs, and the Book treats the combination as a single condition of the heart. The warning also addresses the community that recites it, since the desire for credit is not a condition confined to the group at which the verse was first aimed.

**The Repetition of the Prohibition**

The verse states its prohibition twice, at the beginning and in the middle of the sentence, and the repetition is a feature of the Book's rhetoric when a matter requires emphasis. The second occurrence interrupts the description of the people and resumes it after the warning has been restated.

The construction is unusual even by the standards of the Book, and the commentators noted it as a mark of the seriousness with which the conduct described is regarded. The effect is to make the sentence a warning about the people described rather than a statement about them, and the hearer is placed on guard before the description has been completed.

**What the Two Traits Involve**

Al-Rāzī explains the combination as a state in which a person takes his happiness from the goods and pleasures of the world while wishing to be regarded as sincere and devout. The two parts of the description belong together, since the desire for a reputation for piety is what makes the self-satisfaction dangerous.

The Book's warnings about the desire for praise run through its instructions about giving, praying, and fasting, and the sentence in this verse states the matter in its most compact form. A person who wants credit for what he has not done has made his reputation the object of his effort, and the verse places that condition among those that lead to punishment.

**The Reports About the Occasion**

The commentators record several occasions to which the verse has been connected. One report links it to hypocrites who stayed behind when the Prophet marched out, sought his pardon on his return, and then asked to be praised for conduct they had not engaged in. Others refer it to the hypocrites in general, who wanted credit for a belief they did not hold.

Al-Rāzī records further possibilities: that it refers to the People of the Book who distorted their scriptures and then expected to be honoured as devout, or that it refers to the concealment mentioned in the verse immediately before this one, where the concealing was combined with a claim to learning. All of the occasions describe the same pattern, and the verse covers it whichever report is preferred.

**Hypocrisy as Social Conduct**

The Book treats hypocrisy not only as a matter of belief but as a pattern of public behavior, and the passage describes people who were visible in the community and knew how to present themselves. The conduct described in this verse is social in character: a person seeks credit from others.

The Book's warnings about self-exaltation elsewhere make the same point. One passage asks whether those who elevate themselves have not noticed that God raises whom He wills, and another tells people not to claim purity for themselves since God knows best who is mindful. The verse before the reader states the social form of the same error.

The verse states that the people described are not outside the reach of punishment and that a painful punishment awaits them. The wording denies the assumption the people themselves were making, which is what the repeated prohibition is designed to address.

The phrase about not being delivered echoes the language used earlier in the sūrah for those who traded belief for disbelief. The Book's descriptions of punishment in this section are stated in almost identical words, and the repetition ties the various forms of the same conduct to the same outcome.

**Why the Sentence Is Repeated**

The double prohibition is the sentence's most distinctive feature, and its function is to leave no room for the assumption that the people described had nothing to fear. The Book uses repetition in this way when it addresses a condition that people do not recognise in themselves.

The community that recites the verse is asked to examine its own attitude toward reputation and toward the credit it expects for its conduct. The conduct described is common enough that the warning cannot be read as applying only to the hypocrites of the first generation, and the sentence's emphasis serves the later readers as much as the first ones.

**What the Community Learns**

The verse teaches the community to be suspicious of its own satisfaction and of its desire for the credit that comes with a good name. What the Book recommends instead is stated in the verses that follow, which describe people who remember God in every posture and reflect on the creation.

The sūrah is drawing toward the close of its long argument, and the sentences in this section deal with the difference between the people who use religion for their standing and the people whose conduct is aimed at God alone. The next verse states who owns what the first group is trying to secure.

---
## Sūrah Āli ʿImrān 3:189

> To Allah ˹alone˺ belongs the kingdom of the heavens and the earth. And Allah is Most Capable of everything.

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Ownership Stated**

The verse states that to God belongs sovereignty over the heavens and the earth and that He is powerful over all things, and the sentence supplies the fact that governs everything the passage has been discussing. The Book states the same ownership in many places, and it usually does so where claims of power or standing are in question.

The sentence's position in the passage is significant, since it follows a description of people who were pleased with their own standing. It follows a warning to people who took pleasure in their position and expected credit for what they had not done, and it states where the position they valued actually belongs. The sovereignty over the heavens and the earth is not distributed among the people who believe they hold it.

**The Book's Recurring Formula**

The Book states that the kingdom of the heavens and the earth belongs to God in a series of passages, and the contexts vary widely. One passage uses the statement to answer those who said that the Messiah was God, and it asks who could prevent God if He willed to destroy the Messiah and his mother and everyone on earth.

Another passage states that the kingdom belongs to God and that the final return is to Him. A third states that whatever is in the heavens and the earth belongs to Him, and that He will call people to account for what they reveal and what they conceal. The sentence in this verse belongs to that group, and its function is consistently to place every claim of authority under a higher one.

The verse adds that God is powerful over all things, and the phrase is one the sūrah has used at several points, including the close of the passage about the affliction after the battle. The declaration covers the exercise of the sovereignty that the first half of the sentence has asserted.

The Book's pairing of ownership with power is deliberate. The claim that the heavens and the earth belong to God is a statement of right, and the statement of power explains why the right cannot be contested. The two together leave the reader with no place to stand outside the arrangement the verse describes.

**Why the Sentence Follows the Warning**

The verse before the reader comes after a description of people who were pleased with themselves and sought praise for what they had not done, and it names the owner of everything they were competing over. The connection between the two verses is the subject of standing.

The community's opponents had their positions, their learning, and their claims to be the people of God. The verse states that sovereignty belongs elsewhere, and the placement gives the sentence the quality of a correction. What the earlier verse warned against was a misreading of one's position, and this verse supplies the correct account of where position comes from, since all standing in the world is held on terms set by its owner.

**The Sūrah's Earlier Treatment of Dominion**

The sūrah has already dealt with the subject at its opening, where it addresses God as the owner of all dominion who gives it to whom He wills and takes it from whom He wills. The passage describes the granting and removal of authority as matters within a single hand.

The verse before the reader states the same principle in general terms. The sūrah's argument with the community's opponents has repeatedly touched on the question of who holds authority over guidance, and the answer is given here in the form of a statement about the whole creation, which leaves no room for a rival claim.

**The Final Return Joined to the Sovereignty**

The Book frequently pairs the statement of ownership with the statement that the return is to God, and the pairing gives the ownership a practical consequence. The one who owns everything is the one to whom everything returns, and the account of human conduct is settled within that ownership.

The verse before the reader states the first half of that pair, and the passages in the other sūrahs supply the second. The community that recites it is being given a fact about the arrangement of the world rather than an instruction about a particular matter, and the Book uses such statements to reorder the reader's sense of what matters.

**The Position of the Oppressed**

The verse has a particular resonance for people whose cause is being defeated and whose opponents appear to hold every advantage. The sentence states that the sovereignty they see exercised is held on loan from the one to whom it belongs, and the Book's uses of the formula consistently occur in such settings.

The community at Madinah had seen its enemies gain ground and had been told about the fate of the groups whose conduct the sūrah has been describing in the passages about the People of the Book and the idolaters. The verse's statement of ownership supplies the frame in which all of that is to be read, and the sentences that follow turn to the signs of God in the creation.

**A Statement of Fact and Its Use**

The verse is short and consists of two declarations, and the community has used it as a statement of the ground on which its confidence rests. The Book places such sentences at the ends of arguments, and their function is to leave the reader with the fact that resolves the particular difficulty.

The sūrah's closing movement begins with this declaration and continues into a description of the people who draw the right conclusion from what they observe in the world around them. The next verse turns to that observation, and the passage builds from the statement of ownership to the reflection of those who understand.

---
## Sūrah Āli ʿImrān 3:190

> Indeed, in the creation of the heavens and the earth and the alternation of the day and night there are signs for people of reason.

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Signs Named**

The verse states that in the creation of the heavens and the earth and in the variation of night and day there are signs for those who possess understanding. The sentence opens the sūrah's closing movement, which is built on the observation of the world.

The Book invites this observation in several passages. One lists the creation of the heavens and the earth, the alternation of day and night, the ships that sail the sea, the rain, the creatures scattered throughout the earth, the shifting winds, and the clouds, and concludes that in all of it there are signs for people of understanding. Another passage states that in the alternation of night and day and in what God has created there are signs for those who are mindful. A third states that in the creation of the heavens and the earth there are signs for the believers.

**The Word Behind Creation**

The word rendered as creation can refer both to the act by which the heavens and the earth were brought into being and to the character of what was created. The commentators noted that the verse can therefore direct attention both to the making and to the nature of what was made.

The distinction widens the scope of the observation. A person reflecting on the sentence can consider the act of creation and the power it displays, or he can consider the arrangement of the created world and the order it exhibits. Both lines of reflection lead to the same conclusion, and the verse leaves room for either.

**The Possessors of Understanding**

The phrase describing those for whom the signs exist is one of the Book's terms for people who use their minds in the right way. The Book uses it in passages that commend reflection, and it uses it in passages that commend the fear of God and the acceptance of admonition.

The term is not a description of intelligence in the ordinary sense. The Book's usage connects it with the ability to draw the right conclusion from what a person observes, and the passages that use the term consistently place it close to the qualities of humility and attention. What the verse requires is not cleverness but the willingness to see what is in front of one.

**The Prophet's Practice**

The commentaries record that the Prophet recited the closing verses of this sūrah every night, and they report the occasion on which the passage was first revealed. He is said to have stood in prayer, and when Bilāl came to call the congregation and found him weeping, Bilāl asked why he wept when God had forgiven him all his sins, past and future. The Prophet answered by asking whether he should not be a grateful servant, and he named this verse as the reason for his tears.

The report adds that he said that the one who recites the verse and does not reflect on it is in a bad way. The tradition has preserved the account because it shows how the passage was received by the person who first recited it, and the community's teachers have used it ever since.

The report places reflection alongside recitation, and the community's practice has followed the distinction. The Book's verses are to be read and to be considered, and the passage before the reader is one of the places where the second activity is explicitly invited.

The verse's own structure supports the practice. It names specific features of the world and states that they are signs, which amounts to an instruction to look at them and to draw the conclusion. The invitation is repeated in the sūrah's following verses, which describe the people of understanding as those who remember God in every posture and reflect on the creation.

**The Book's Appeal to Observation**

The Book's arguments frequently begin from what its readers can see. It points to the rain, the growth of crops, the cycles of the sky, the variety of creatures, and the order of the seasons, and it asks its audience to draw conclusions about the one who arranged them.

The appeal is not to a special kind of knowledge but to the ordinary experience of anyone who lives in the world. The Book's reasoning in such passages is that the ordinary facts of existence are enough to establish what it is asking people to accept, and the verse before the reader is a compact statement of that argument for a community that had seen unusual events.

**What the Signs Lead To**

The next verses describe the people of understanding in action: they remember God while standing, sitting, and lying on their sides, and they reflect on the creation and ask what it all means. The explanation of what they conclude and what they ask for continues through the close of the sūrah.

The passage therefore moves from the observation of the world to the conduct of those who observe it, and the sūrah ends with their prayer. The community is given a portrait of the quality that the Book most values in its people, and the portrait begins with the sentence in this verse and continues through the prayer that ends the sūrah.

**The Function of the Closing Movement**

The sūrah ends with this reflection and the prayer that follows it, and the placement gives the whole sūrah its conclusion. The community has been taken through the battles, the failures, the warnings about property and speech, and the arguments with its opponents, and it is left contemplating the heavens and the earth.

The close of the passage returns to the note on which the sūrah opened, where the Book described itself as a guidance for those who guard themselves against God. The last verses turn that guidance back toward the world it explains, and the community that reaches the end of the sūrah is asked to look up.

---
## Sūrah Āli ʿImrān 3:191

> ˹They are˺ those who remember Allah while standing, sitting, and lying on their sides, and reflect on the creation of the heavens and the earth ˹and pray˺, “Our Lord! You have not created ˹all of˺ this without purpose. Glory be to You! Protect us from the torment of the Fire.

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Three Postures of Remembrance**

The verse describes the people of understanding as those who remember God while standing, while sitting, and while lying on their sides, and the three positions cover the ordinary conditions of a human life. The sūrah about Women uses the same three modes in its instruction about remembrance after the prayer.

Al-Rāzī observed that no human being is ever outside one of those three positions, so the instruction covers the whole of a person's waking and sleeping life. The verse's description is therefore of a life rather than of a ritual, and the community that reads it is being shown what the constant awareness of God looks like in practice.

**The Forms the Remembrance Takes**

The commentators explained the remembrance in several ways: as the movement of the heart, as the words of the tongue, and as the positions of the canonical prayer, including those adopted by people unable to stand. Ibn Kathīr included the positions of the prayer among the meanings, and others extended the phrase to every form that remembrance can take, the recitation of the Book among them.

The verse has consequently been treated in the tradition as one of the foundations of the practice of remembering God at all times, and the Sufi tradition in particular drew on it. The wording supports the practice: the three postures leave no part of a person's day outside the activity the verse describes, and the sequence traces a person from activity through rest.

**Reflection on the Creation**

The second act attributed to the people of understanding is reflection on the heavens and the earth as made things, and the Book invites this activity in many passages. It directs attention to the rain, the growth of plants, the differences among creatures, and the order of the sky.

The Book's argument in such passages is that the created world displays the qualities of the one who made it. The people described in this verse move from the observation of the world to a conclusion about its maker, and the conclusion they reach is stated in the quotation that follows.

**The Creation Is Not in Vain**

The words the verse places in the mouths of these people are a declaration that God has not created the world in vain. The Book states the same in other passages: one declares that heaven and earth and all that lies between them were not made in play, and another states that they were not created without purpose, contrary to the thought of those who deny.

A third passage asks whether people imagined that they had been created without purpose and would never return to God. The sentence in this verse belongs to that group, and the community's reflection on the creation leads it to the conclusion that the arrangement of the world is neither accidental nor pointless.

**The Distinction Between Creation and the World's Allure**

The commentators drew a careful line between the created order, which the Book presents as a sign, and the present world, which other passages describe as play and diversion. The two are not the same thing.

The distinction matters for the verse's instruction. What the people of understanding reflect upon is the act of creation and the qualities it displays, and what the Book warns against is the absorption in worldly desire that turns the same world into an end in itself. The same objects can be a sign or a distraction, and the difference lies in what a person does with them.

**Meditation and Its Limits**

Al-Rāzī drew from the verse the principle that a person may meditate on God through His creation and through the signs of His qualities within it; the essence itself, however, is not a subject for such meditation, since no limited consciousness can grasp it.

The Book supports the distinction in a passage that promises to show people the signs on the horizons and within themselves until it is made plain to them that the message is true. The instruction is to look at what God has made rather than to attempt what the verse's own limitation describes.

**The Tradition of Reflection**

The tradition preserved statements about reflection that the commentators attached to this verse. One report states that an hour of reflection is better than a night spent in vigil, and the practice appears in the reports about the companions: Abū Dharr's wife said that he passed his days thinking in a corner of his home, and the account from Abū Bakr's household says the same of his nights.

Ḥasan al-Baṣrī is quoted as saying that speech which carries no wisdom is empty, that silence which carries no reflection is heedlessness, and that thought which carries no contemplation is amusement. The community's teachers have used these sayings to explain what the verse asks of its readers.

**The Petition That Ends the Verse**

The verse closes with a request to be shielded from the Fire's punishment, and the prayer places the reflection and the request side by side. The Book uses the same petition in other passages, including the prayer of the believers in the earlier part of this sūrah and the request in the sūrah of the Forgiver.

The order of the sentence is instructive: the people of understanding observe the world, conclude that it has a purpose, and then ask to be shielded from the destination of those who fail to draw that conclusion. The request is short, and its brevity matches the confidence of those who make it. The next verse continues their prayer and states what they understand about the fate they are asking to avoid.

---
## Sūrah Āli ʿImrān 3:192

> Our Lord! Indeed, those You commit to the Fire will be ˹completely˺ disgraced! And the wrongdoers will have no helpers.

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Disgrace of the Fire**

The verse continues the prayer of the people of understanding with the statement that whoever is made to enter the Fire has been disgraced, and it adds that the wrongdoers have no helpers. The sentence explains why the petition in the verse before it was made.

The word for disgrace describes the loss of honour before others, and the verse treats the entry into the Fire as the greatest form of it. The people of understanding, who have just reflected on the dignity of the creation, ask to be spared the condition that would undo the standing of a human being.

**The Explanation of the Disgrace**

Al-Quṭūbī and al-Ṭabarī record the view that the disgrace described here belongs specifically to those who enter the Fire and never leave it, rather than to everyone who is punished there for a period. Al-Ṭabarī records a remark of Ḥasan al-Baṣrī on the subject: sinners will be admitted to the fire, yet at some stage they will be brought out of it on account of the belief that remains within them.

The distinction reflects the Book's teaching that punishment and dismissal from God's favour are not the same thing, and the community's discussions of the subject have turned on that difference. The verse's own wording leaves room for the reading, since the disgrace is attached to the entry described in the petition rather than to a general statement about all punishment.

**The Spiritual Suffering of the Hereafter**

Al-Rāzī observes that the disgrace named in this verse is not a material punishment, which shows that the Hereafter includes suffering of a kind that has no physical counterpart. He makes the same observation about the rewards of the garden, where the Book describes conditions such as hearing nothing but peace.

The point widens the reader's understanding of what the Book's descriptions of the Hereafter involve. The Fire is described through its physical images, and the sentence before the reader names a form of loss that has to do with a person's standing, and the community's teachers have used the verse as evidence that both kinds of experience belong to the next life.

**The Debate the Verse Entered**

The verse has been used in the theological discussions about the believer who commits a serious sin. One side argued that the Book states elsewhere that the Prophet and the believers will not be shamed on the Day of Judgment, so no believer can enter the fire, since entering it would involve the disgrace described here.

The discussion belongs to a larger set of questions about the relation between faith and punishment, and the verse's contribution is the weight it gives to the disgrace itself. The community's scholars have treated the sentence as one of the texts that must be held together with the passages about forgiveness and the passages about punishment.

**The Statement About Helpers**

The verse closes by stating that the wrongdoers will have no helpers, and the phrase is used in another sūrah for those who associate others with God in worship. There the Book states that their home will be the Fire and that the wrongdoers will have no helpers.

The sentence in this verse applies the same declaration in the context of the prayer of the people of understanding, and its placement at the close of the petition gives the prayer its final note. What they are asking to be spared is a condition in which no assistance from any quarter can change the outcome, and the verse states that condition in the plainest terms available.

**The Prayer as Instruction**

The sūrah places these petitions in the mouths of the people it has just described, and the community that recites them is being taught how to pray. The Book's practice of recording the prayers of the righteous is a form of instruction in itself, and every clause of this passage can be turned into a lesson on what to ask for.

What the people of understanding ask for in this passage is protection, forgiveness, company, and the fulfilment of what God has promised. Each of those requests is stated in a short clause, and the community is given a set of petitions that covers the whole of what a person needs, in the order in which the needs arise.

**The Order of the Petitions**

The passage moves from the protection of the Fire in this verse to the request for forgiveness in the next, and then to the request not to be disgraced on the Day of Resurrection. The order reflects the sequence a person follows when he considers his own case, and it mirrors the movement of the whole passage from the world above to the fate of the person who contemplates it.

The prayer begins with the greatest danger, proceeds to the faults that make the danger real, and ends with the standing a person hopes to have at the end. The community's manuals of prayer have used the passage in that sequence, and the sūrah's shaping of the petitions gives them their model.

**What the Verse Teaches**

The verse teaches the community to think about the Hereafter in terms of both the fire and the loss of standing, and it teaches it to place both under the petition for protection. The people of understanding are described as people who are aware of what is at stake.

The sūrah is drawing toward its close, and the prayer scene is one of its final movements. The community that follows the passage to its end is given a picture of the state of the righteous in the presence of their Lord, asking for what they need and stating what they know, and the answer to their prayer is given in the verse that follows their last request.

---
## Sūrah Āli ʿImrān 3:193

> Our Lord! We have heard the caller to ˹true˺ belief, ˹proclaiming,˺ ‘Believe in your Lord ˹alone˺,’ so we believed. Our Lord! Forgive our sins, absolve us of our misdeeds, and allow us ˹each˺ to die as one of the virtuous.

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Caller and the Call**

The verse continues the prayer with a report of what the community heard: a caller calling to faith, urging belief in their Lord, and the community's answer that it believed. The identity of the caller is most often given as the Prophet, and al-Rāzī records the view that the call is the Book itself, since the message reaches everyone while only a limited number heard it from the Prophet directly.

Both readings describe the same event from different angles. What the community is testifying to is that it was called and that it responded, and the prayer's next clause asks for the forgiveness that the response makes necessary. The report is made in the first person, so the community speaks as one body about what it heard and accepted.

**The Response Reported in the Prayer**

The words the community uses are a simple statement that it believed, and the simplicity is characteristic of the prayer. The Book's descriptions of faith in such passages avoid elaboration and place the emphasis on the act of accepting the message.

The believers in this verse are not described as having understood everything or as having fulfilled the obligations that followed. They are described as having heard a call and responded to it, and the remainder of the prayer asks for what they need in order to carry the response through to the end.

**The Request for Forgiveness**

The prayer asks for the forgiveness of sins, and the vocabulary is the same as that used by the believers who pray in other passages of the sūrah, where they ask forgiveness and protection from the punishment of the fire. The request for protection from the fire in the preceding verses is followed here by the request for the removal of what would bring it.

The Book's prayers consistently include a request for the forgiveness of the one praying, and the community's model in this passage does the same. The people who are described as reflecting on the creation do not regard themselves as beyond the need of pardon, and the community that recites the verses is taught the same posture.

**The Removal of Evil Deeds**

The second request is for the removal of evil deeds, and the wording is fuller than a simple plea for pardon. The Book elsewhere promises that those who repent, believe, and do good will have their evil deeds changed into good ones, and it describes the covering of faults as one of the effects of forgiveness.

The petition asks for a treatment of the record rather than merely for the avoidance of punishment. What the community is requesting is that its worst actions should not be left standing against it, and the same request appears in the prayers of the believers in the sūrah about the Night Journey and elsewhere.

**The Company of the Pious**

The prayer's final request is to be taken to God among the company of the pious, and the request is for association rather than for a rank. The Book describes the company of the prophets, the truthful, the martyrs, and the righteous as the companions of those who obey God and His messenger, and it describes that company as excellent.

The petition reflects the Book's understanding of what a person should want for himself: not only safety but presence with those who were faithful. The community's literature has used the verse in its teaching about choosing one's company, and the prayer in this sūrah places the desire for good company among the requests of the people of understanding.

**The Prayer's Place in the Community's Devotion**

The sūrah's closing prayer is one of the most widely repeated in the community's worship, and the commentators note that it appears in many manuals of supplication. Its use is not restricted to the recitation of the sūrah, and it has served the community as a model for private supplication as well.

The prayer's content explains its circulation. It combines a statement of what the believer has heard and accepted, a request for the pardon of his faults, and a request for the company of the righteous at the end. Each of those elements is teachable on its own, and the community's teachers have used the passage to instruct new Muslims in what they should say.

**The Language of Calling in the Book**

The Book describes the message as a call in several places, and it uses the image of a voice summoning people to a position. One passage describes a caller among the jinn telling his people to respond to the one who calls to God and to believe in him.

The image of the caller shapes the community's understanding of what the message is. A call is either answered or ignored, and the Book's descriptions of the two responses occupy much of its instruction. The verse before the reader places the community's answer in the prayer it recites, and the answer is stated without self-congratulation.

**What the Prayer Teaches About Faith**

The prayer describes faith as a sequence: hearing a call, responding to it, and then asking for what the response requires. The three movements belong together, and the community's teachers drew on the passage for that reason.

The sequence also describes the community's own history, which the sūrah has been recounting through its account of the battle and its aftermath. The people described in the closing passage are the ones who heard the call and continued to keep their standing, and their prayer is the sūrah's final instruction on what such a people should ask of God. Faith, on this account, is not a single moment but a course that the requests of the prayer are meant to sustain.

---
## Sūrah Āli ʿImrān 3:194

> Our Lord! Grant us what You have promised us through Your messengers and do not put us to shame on Judgment Day—for certainly You never fail in Your promise.”

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Petition About the Promise**

The prayer asks God to give what He promised through His messengers, and the commentators record two ways of taking the phrase: that God made the promise to the messengers themselves, or that the messengers conveyed the promise to the people, or that both senses are intended. The Book's promises to the believers are stated in both forms, so the readings are not exclusive.

The petition's content is therefore a request for the fulfilment of what the community had been told to expect. The people of understanding ask that the promise reach them, and the request is expressed in the language of a claim that rests on nothing but God's own word.

**Al-Rāzī on Praying for What Is Certain**

Al-Rāzī discusses the apparent difficulty in asking God for something He has said He will do. He observes that such prayers are not attempts to change God's action; they are expressions of humility and deference on the part of the one who prays.

He cites the Book's other prayers of this kind, including the request of a prophet for his Lord to judge with truth and the prayer of those who ask God to forgive those who repent and follow His way. On his reading, the supplication is a response to what God does rather than a cause of it, and the community's prayers of this kind are exercises in the posture they express.

**The Request Not to Be Disgraced**

The second half of the verse asks God not to disgrace the community on the Day of Resurrection, and the request echoes the previous verse's statement that those who enter the fire will be disgraced. Al-Rāzī notes that the earlier verse concerned the material punishment of the fire while this prayer seeks deliverance from the shame that belongs to the Day.

The two passages together give the reader a sense of what is at stake at the end. The community is described as asking to be spared both the fire and the exposure, and the prayer places the second request in the context of the gathering on the Day of Resurrection.

**The Book's Assurance About the Meeting**

The Book states the certainty of the gathering in several passages, and one of the sūrah's earlier verses puts the declaration in the form of a prayer: that God will gather all humanity on a Day about which there is no doubt, and that He does not break His promise.

Another passage describes the righteous in the garden saying that God has fulfilled what He promised them. The verse before the reader belongs to that group and asks for the same outcome, and the community's prayers in this passage are shaped by the certainty the Book states elsewhere. The prayer takes that assurance as its ground and asks that the believer be among those who receive what has been promised.

**The Repeated Address**

The prayer in this passage addresses God as its Lord at the start of each petition, and the repetition shapes the way the whole scene reads. The community's requests are made by people who place themselves under the authority of the one they address.

The pattern appears in the Book's other recorded prayers, and the community's own supplications follow it. The address establishes the relation between the one who asks and the one who gives, and it keeps the petitions within the bounds of what a servant may ask of his Lord: nothing in the passage requests what lies outside God's promise or His will.

**What the People of Understanding Ask For**

The passage's petitions together cover the whole of a person's need: protection from the fire, forgiveness, the removal of evil deeds, the company of the righteous, the fulfilment of the promise, and deliverance from disgrace on the Day of Resurrection.

The list is arranged in the order of the prayer and the needs are stated one after another, each in a clause of its own. The community that recites the passage is given a complete set of requests, and the closing verses of the sūrah show how the requests were received. The requests are made in the plural and cover the community as a whole, so the individual prays with the body of the believers rather than for himself alone.

**The Certainty Expressed in the Final Clause**

The verse ends with the declaration that God does not fail the appointed meeting, and the sentence is a statement of confidence placed at the end of a request. The community's prayer does not end with uncertainty about the outcome but with an assertion about the one being addressed.

The Book's prayers frequently close in this way, with a statement about God that serves as the ground of the petition. The community is taught to end its requests with an acknowledgment of what God is, and the form has shaped the way the community's own supplications are constructed, ending with what God is rather than with what the supplicant wants.

**The Prayer as the Sūrah's Close**

The passage is the sūrah's final movement and its closing prayer, and the choice of this material for the end is deliberate. The sūrah has taken its readers through the community's history, its failures, its obligations, and its arguments with its opponents, and it leaves them with the community at prayer.

The address is made to God on behalf of people who have been described as remembering Him in every posture and reflecting on the creation. The next verse reports the answer that their prayer received, and the sūrah's account of what God granted them is the last major statement of the passage.

---
## Sūrah Āli ʿImrān 3:195

> So their Lord responded to them: “I will never deny any of you—male or female—the reward of your deeds. Both are equal in reward. Those who migrated or were expelled from their homes, and were persecuted for My sake and fought and ˹some˺ were martyred—I will certainly forgive their sins and admit them into Gardens under which rivers flow, as a reward from Allah. And with Allah is the finest reward!”

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Answer Given**

The verse opens by stating that their Lord answered them, and the sentence follows the prayer that reaches through the end of the previous verse. The Book records the answers to such prayers in several places, and the community in this passage is told that its petitions were heard.

The transition from request to answer gives the closing movement of the sūrah its shape. The people of understanding reflect on the creation, make their requests, and are answered by the one they address, and the reply is reported in the first person.

**The Promise That No Work Is Wasted**

The answer begins with the declaration that God will not let the work of any worker be in vain, and the sentence is the sūrah's broadest assurance on the subject. The sūrah had earlier stated that God does not neglect the reward of the believers, and the two statements belong together.

The declaration covers the whole range of what a person does, without specifying a category of deeds or a rank of people. The answer to the community's prayers begins with that general assurance, and the specific promises that follow are applications of it to the people whose history the sūrah has been describing.

**Male and Female Alike**

The answer states that no worker among them will be denied the fruit of his work, male or female, and then adds that each of them is like the other. Al-Rāzī explains the phrase as meaning that the reward for obedience and righteous conduct is not differentiated among men and women, and he notes the further sense that the phrase may mean that each is of the other.

The Book makes the point in several places. One passage states that whoever does good, whether male or female, and believes will be given a good life and rewarded according to the best of what he did. Another lists the qualities of believing men and women together and promises both forgiveness and a great reward. A third states that those who do good, whether male or female, and have faith will enter the garden and will not be wronged in the least.

**The Sufferings Listed**

The answer then names the experiences of the people it concerns: those who emigrated, those who were expelled from their homes, those who were hurt in God's cause, those who fought, and those who were killed. The list follows the community's history, beginning with the migration from Makkah and continuing through the fighting that the sūrah has described.

The commentators identify the emigration and expulsion with what the believers suffered in Makkah and the migration that followed it to Madinah. The list is therefore a summary of what the first community had undergone, and the answer to the prayer is addressed to the people who had borne all of it.

**What Being Hurt Covers**

The phrase about being hurt in God's cause is explained by the commentators as covering insults and mockery as well as physical injury. The verse that preceded the prayer in this sūrah told the community that it would hear much that was painful from the two groups, and the answer to the prayer returns to the same experience.

The inclusion of insults in the list of what earns the reward is significant for the community's self-understanding. What the believers had endured was not only the loss of possessions and the dangers of the road but also the daily pressure of being mocked for their position, and the answer names it as part of what God will not allow to be wasted.

**Absolution and the Gardens**

The answer promises to absolve the people described of their evil deeds and to bring them into gardens with rivers running beneath them. The two elements had appeared in the sūrah's earlier description of the reward of the righteous, and the closing passage repeats the promise.

The gardens with rivers beneath them are the Book's standard image for the reward, and the absolution of deeds is the removal of what would otherwise stand against the people who receive it. The answer to the prayer thus grants both the removal of the debt and the gift that follows it, and the community is told what its sacrifices were exchanged for.

**The Reward Attributed to God**

The verse describes what is given as a reward from God, and it closes with the statement that with God is the most beautiful reward. The attribution places the reward outside the system of exchange the community might have imagined, since what is given is described as coming from God rather than as earned by the recipients.

The sūrah's earlier passages used the same language when they described the reward of the believers and the bounty of God toward the community. The closing sentence of the verse gathers all of it into a single phrase, and the passage ends with the community's aspirations directed to the source rather than to the gift.

**What the Answer Teaches the Community**

The answer teaches the community that its hardships have been registered and that the account will be settled in its favour. The sūrah has been describing a community that lost a battle, was mocked by its neighbours, and had members who failed and members who stood firm, and the closing movement places all of them within the answer given to the prayer of the righteous.

The verses that follow this one add a warning about the conduct of those who trade faith for disbelief, and the sūrah ends shortly after. The passage's last word on the community's situation is the promise stated here, and it is given to people who had asked for exactly what the answer grants.

---
## Sūrah Āli ʿImrān 3:196

> Do not be deceived by the prosperity of the disbelievers throughout the land.

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Delusion Named**

The verse addresses the Prophet with a warning against being misled by the ease with which those who deny the message travel the land and prosper in it. The sentence names a conclusion that a person could draw from appearances: that the comfort of the deniers is a sign of their standing before God.

The warning is stated in the negative because the impression itself is the danger, and the verse denies the conclusion before it can take hold. The counsel is needed because the conclusion it forbids is one that a reasonable observer might reach from the facts alone. The sentences that follow in the sūrah supply the reason, and the next verse states what the freedom of movement actually amounts to.

**The Occasion Reported**

The commentators record an occasion for the passage. Some believers are said to have remarked on the contrast between their own hunger and hardship and the freedom with which the idolaters moved about the land and profited from commerce. Others report that the remark came from the hypocrites, who used the same contrast to cast doubt on the message.

Al-Rāzī observed that although the sentence is addressed to the Prophet, its audience is wider, as though a listener were being addressed directly. The verse is therefore read as a warning to anyone who measures the truth of a claim by the comfort of the people who reject it.

**Freedom of Movement as Appearance**

The observation that the deniers range over the earth appears again in the sūrah, where the same impression is addressed: they are given length of days, and their going about the land looks like success. The thought occurs to the observer because the world's arrangement places no visible obstacle in the path of those who oppose the message.

The two passages belong together, and the earlier statement had already warned the believers against drawing conclusions from the length of the interval granted to their opponents. Both treat the ease of the deniers as a postponement rather than a verdict, and both turn the reader's attention to what comes after the interval. The community is taught to read the delay as a part of the story rather than as its ending.

**The Respite Described Elsewhere**

The Book states in several passages that the comfort granted to those who deny the message is a delay and not a reward. One passage tells the prosperous to eat and enjoy themselves and be diverted by false hope, adding that they will come to know. Another states that ornaments and pleasures of that kind are no more than the passing enjoyment of the present life, while what is with God belongs to those who are mindful of Him.

A third passage states that the present life has been made attractive to those who reject the truth and that they mock the believers, while those who are mindful will rank above them on the Day of Judgment. The verse before the reader depends on the same judgment about appearances.

**The World's Standing in the Book**

The tradition preserved a statement attributed to the Prophet that explains the paradox the verse addresses: the world is a prison for the believer and a garden for the one who denies. The sentence expresses what the verse assumes, since the ease of the deniers and the hardship of the believers are not evidence about the next life and may indicate its opposite.

Al-Rāzī and the other commentators made the same point in their explanations of the passage. What appears to be a favour to one group and a deprivation of the other is measured by a scale that the world's own indications cannot reveal.

**The Judgment on the Worldly Life**

The Book describes the worldly life as a brief and delusive possession in many places. One passage states that after being rescued people transgress in the land unjustly, and that their transgression is against their own souls, with the present life being only a passing enjoyment before the return to God. Another compares the present life to play, amusement, display, and rivalry in wealth and children, and calls it the delusion of enjoyment.

The sentence before the reader rests on that estimate. What looks to the observer like the freedom of the deniers is measured against a scale in which the whole of the worldly life weighs very little, and the next verse states what remains for them when it is over.

The sūrah has been contrasting the two groups throughout its closing movement. It has described the reward of those who revere God and the destination of those who rejected the message, and the sentence before the reader applies that contrast to the observers themselves.

The members of the community were the ones tempted by the comparison, and the verse answers them by forbidding the conclusion they were drawing. The reader is asked to hold two facts together: the appearance that impresses him and the account of the outcome that the Book supplies. What they were to rely on was the account the sūrah had already given of both outcomes, and the reminder was addressed to people who had been given that account.

**What the Verse Corrects**

The verse corrects a reading of the world in which success is identified with the condition of those who appear to be succeeding. The Book's teaching is that the present arrangement is not the final one, and that comparisons drawn from it do not hold.

The correction is delivered as a prohibition addressed to a person, which is how the Book often states a conclusion it wants drawn. The community is told not to let what it sees mislead it, and the sentence leaves the reader with the fact that overturns the impression. What the deniers have secured has a limit, and the verse that follows states what that limit is.

**The Verse and the One It Echoes

The sentence is the second in the sūrah to deal with the ease of those who deny the message. The earlier passage, which comes a few verses before this one, states that the delay granted to such people should not be mistaken for an advantage, and it warns that their respite is a form of drawing them on. The sentence before the reader repeats the warning from the side of the observer rather than in a statement of fact, since the temptation it answers is the one the community felt when it watched its opponents travel and profit while it went hungry. The Book addresses the same temptation in another sūrah, where it asks those who trade in falsehood to enjoy themselves and names their destination (40:4). The three passages together show a single concern treated from three angles, and the community's teachers used them together when they explained why hardship and prosperity are not the measures of a person's standing.

---
## Sūrah Āli ʿImrān 3:197

> It is only a brief enjoyment. Then Hell will be their home—what an evil place to rest!

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Brief Enjoyment**

The verse follows the warning of the sentence before it and states what the freedom of the deniers amounts to: a small enjoyment, followed by the Fire as their refuge. The sentence is the answer to the impression that the previous verse had told the reader to resist.

The Book uses the vocabulary of a little or a brief span for the present life in several passages, and the word in this verse carries the same sense. The community was expected to adopt that measure as its own rather than the estimate that appearances suggest. What the deniers have secured is measured in the sentence as small, and the word chosen for it settles the comparison that the community had been tempted to make.

**The Word for Little**

The Arabic term rendered as a little names something slight in extent or duration, and the commentators applied it to the span of worldly comfort. The sentence does not deny that the deniers enjoy their position; it denies that the enjoyment is large.

The Book's descriptions of the worldly life elsewhere use the same kind of measurement, and the consistency of the judgment is what the community's teachers pointed to when they warned against envy of the prosperous. A passage says that the present life compared with the Hereafter is nothing but a fleeting enjoyment, and another states that its ornaments are a passing enjoyment while the Hereafter with God belongs to the mindful. The verse before the reader states the same estimate in a single word.

**The Refuge Named**

The second half of the verse names the Fire as the refuge of the people described, and the choice of the word is deliberate. What the deniers thought of as the world's open land ends in a place described as a destination they cannot leave.

The Book names the Fire as the destination of the arrogant and the deniers in many passages, and it does so with the same vocabulary of arrival. The word for refuge carries the sense of a place to which a person is brought, and the Book applies it to those who spent their lives opposing the message. One passage tells those who treat others as rivals to God to enjoy themselves, since their destination is the Fire, and another states that the wrongdoers will ultimately be returned to it.

**The Resting Place Inverted**

The verse closes with the exclamation that the resting place named is evil, and the term carries the sense of a place where a traveller stops or a person lies down. The image of the present life as a journey appears in the sentence through the word for movement in the previous verse.

The Book applies the same term to the Fire in other passages, where it is described as an evil place of rest for those who arrive there. The contrast is between the welcome that the next verse promises to the mindful and the destination named here, and the two are set side by side in the sūrah's closing lines.

**The Book's Other Descriptions of the Destination**

The Book describes the Fire in similar terms in several passages. One states that the people of the Fire will burn there, and asks what an evil place of rest it is. Another describes the wrongdoers being sent back to their place in it, and a third describes it as a home for those who transgressed.

The repetition of the same images across the Book gives the sentence its weight. The verse before the reader is one of a series of statements in which the destination of those who rejected the message is named in identical language, and the community's teachers used those passages together when they explained the verse.

**The Comparison With the Welcome That Follows**

The construction of the passage places this verse directly before the one that describes the gardens promised to those who revere God. The word for refuge in this sentence and the word for welcome in the next are set against each other, and the two destinations are the alternatives the sūrah has been presenting.

The last verses of the sūrah therefore close with a comparison rather than with an argument. The community that recites them is shown the two endings and left to draw the conclusion, and the sentence before the reader is the darker half of the pair.

The verse consists of two brief statements and an exclamation, and its brevity is part of its effect. What the previous verse described at length is dismissed in a clause, and the dismissal carries the judgment.

The Book uses short sentences in this way when it states the outcome of a long dispute. The reader is given the fact without embellishment, and the terseness of the sentence leaves the impression that the matter requires no further elaboration.

**What the Verse Teaches**

The verse teaches the community that the comfort of those who deny the message has a limit that is fixed in advance. It also teaches it to describe that comfort with the word the Book uses for it rather than with the estimate that appearances suggest.

The instruction belongs to the preparation the sūrah has been giving its readers for their life in a world where the two groups live side by side. The sūrah's closing verses repeat the same distinction, and the community is given the two outcomes as the frame within which it should read its own circumstances. The next verse turns to the portion of the other group, and the transition makes the two destinations the sūrah's final subject.

---
## Sūrah Āli ʿImrān 3:198

> But those who are mindful of their Lord will be in Gardens under which rivers flow, to stay there forever—as an accommodation from Allah. And what is with Allah is best for the virtuous.

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Contrast Stated**

The verse begins with a turn that sets the destiny of the mindful against the destination described in the sentence before it. Those who revere their Lord are promised gardens with rivers flowing beneath them, and the promise is given in the same terms the sūrah has used earlier for the reward of the righteous.

The sūrah has been contrasting the two groups from the beginning of its closing movement, and this sentence completes the comparison. The turn at the start of the verse is the Book's familiar way of placing two outcomes side by side. What the wrongdoers receive is named in the previous verse, and what those who revere God receive is named here.

**The Gardens Described**

The gardens are described through the rivers that run beneath them, which is the Book's most frequent image for the reward. The phrase recalls the promise made earlier in the sūrah to those who are mindful, and it recalls the promise made to the believers and the doers of good in the second sūrah, where the same rivers are named.

The community that hears the description is being reminded of what it has been promised. The image is used consistently across the Book, and the repetition of the same words ties the rewards promised in different passages to the same reality. It conveys both the abundance of what is given and the permanence of the home in which it is enjoyed.

**The Word for Welcome**
